answer:
Google Analytics doesn’t seem to offer a built-in way to combine stats from separate, unrelated properties into one total view. The closest supported options are:

- Use Universal Analytics on a new profile, which can use the same tracking code across sites.
- For Classic Analytics, use cross-domain tracking for multiple domains.
- If you want combined server usage or real-time load estimates, a web analytics tool for server logs may be easier.
- For capacity planning, monitor server resources directly with tools like top or Task Manager.

The thread does not include an answer, so it doesn’t confirm whether one property can show combined stats for all sites.

Closest supported guidance: the setup you described suggests creating one account, one property, and separate profiles for each site, with “All Web Site Data” as the default combined view. That implies you may be able to see combined statistics there and individual site stats in the other profiles, but the thread does not verify it or mention any special tracking code.

If you want, I can help infer the likely Google Analytics configuration from this setup.

Changing hosting servers by itself should not affect your SEO page ranking. Hosting doesn’t determine content quality or relevance.

The main thing to watch is site speed and downtime. If the new host is much slower, or if the move causes significant downtime, rankings could be affected. A smooth transition with minimal interruption is the safest approach.

To keep the domain registration unchanged and move hosting to GoDaddy, change the domain’s nameservers to GoDaddy’s in your GoDaddy account. Go to Domains > Manage My Domains, select the domain, then use the Nameservers dropdown and choose “Set name server.” Select “Standard,” and that should point the domain to the new hosting.

The evidence doesn’t cover the exact nameserver values to use or the steps at CrazyDomains, only that changing nameservers is the needed configuration.

jQuery runs in the browser, so changing hosting companies should not affect whether your jQuery works. Hosting mainly matters for server-side features like PHP, WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or any AJAX/server interaction you may use.

So if your site is “very jQuery driven,” any normal professional web host should be fine. Just make sure the host supports whatever server-side language or platform you need.

Google could have found them through discovery paths other than a direct link from your site, such as being pinged as new content, being shared publicly on places like Twitter/Facebook/YouTube, or being linked from other sites with high crawl rate. The advice also says linking the new page from your home page or another strong page on your site helps Google find it faster.

So if the pages were unlinked from your site, the most likely explanations supported here are external mentions/links, CMS pings, or another page with authority pointing to them.

Google can discover a new site even if there are no public links to it. The supported answer here is that Google is a registrar, so it may use registrar-related information to find new domains and index them. The evidence does not say exactly whether it uses WHOIS records or another specific source, only that registrar access could explain how it found the site.

Google may have found those old URLs from somewhere in the cloned WordPress files or database, even if the pages were deleted. The suggested way to track this down is to download the site files and database and search them for the old domain and/or IP address. In WordPress, old links can be hidden in serialized database strings, so be careful when editing.

The evidence doesn’t show exactly how Google discovered the links, only that they may still exist somewhere in the cloned files or database.

To check whether your site is indexed, search for your domain name in the search engine. If it appears, your site is indexed.

To check ranking, search for the terms you expect to rank for and see whether your pages appear in the results. If they don’t show up, that usually means they rank poorly rather than not at all.

If you want a more objective or easier way to do this repeatedly, the guidance suggests using tools to automate the checking process.

To check your ranking objectively, first verify whether Google has manually penalized your site in Google Webmaster Tools. If there’s no manual-action message there, the drop may be from an algorithmic update, so you’d need to review whether your SEO activity follows Google’s guidelines.

If you want a more detailed diagnosis, you’d need to provide the site URL.

Because a sitemap is only a discovery list, not a guarantee of indexing. Google decides which URLs to include in its index, and may ignore some sitemap URLs if it considers them thin, duplicate, poor quality, or otherwise unsuitable. So it’s possible for Google to index fewer URLs than are in the sitemap, and also to index URLs it found through other paths outside the sitemap.

Google can index URLs even if they are not in your sitemap, because a sitemap is only advisory. It tells Google which URLs you want crawled, but it does not limit Google to only those URLs. Google may find URLs through links or other discovery methods and index them independently.

So if Google has more indexed URLs than your sitemap contains, that can happen naturally. Also, Google may not have crawled or indexed every submitted URL yet, especially if the sitemap was submitted recently.

It can happen because a sitemap is not a complete inventory of all indexed URLs; it’s just one way to tell Google about URLs. Google may discover URLs through links and other sources, so it can index more than are listed in the sitemap.

The evidence also suggests a practical fix for large, changing sites: split the sitemap into multiple sitemaps using a sitemap index, ideally by logical site sections or categories. That helps manage large sets of URLs and makes maintenance easier if a full rebuild takes too long.

I can’t tell you the exact method from the available material because the thread has no answer on record. It only indicates that the issue is about setting an expiry date or maximum age in HTTP headers for static assets like CSS, JS, and images.

Closest guidance supported here: you need to configure your web server to send caching headers for those files, rather than setting cookie/session expiry. Look for settings related to “Expires” or “Cache-Control” in your server configuration.

For CSS, JS, and images, the provided guidance doesn’t describe expiration headers. It only says that if you want non-HTML files out of search results, you can use the x-robots-tag HTTP header with noindex, or block crawling with robots.txt.

If your goal is cache expiration, you’d need server/CDN cache-control or expires settings, but that isn’t covered here.

Use Apache’s mod_expires, which is easier to maintain:

ExpiresActive on
ExpiresDefault "access plus 24 hours"
ExpiresByType image/jpg "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType image/gif "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType image/jpeg "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType image/png "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType text/css "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType text/javascript "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType application/javascript "access plus 1 months"

This sets expiration for CSS, JS, and common image types.

You can’t make your router “dynamically” keep a static public IP by assigning it locally. The supported ways are to get a static IP from your ISP, or use a dynamic DNS service that automatically updates your DNS record when your IP changes.

If you want the host URL itself to change with your IP, dynamic DNS is the closest fit. It will keep the DNS pointing at your current address, but there can be delays unless you use a very short TTL, which has performance tradeoffs.

The available information only discusses dynamic sitemap change frequency, not changing the host URL itself. It suggests that dynamically generating sitemap values may be unnecessary and that leaving the changefreq tag out is often fine. If your goal is to vary sitemap metadata based on page activity, that approach is supported. For changing the host URL dynamically, this evidence doesn’t provide a method.

Use your hosts file instead of trying to rewrite the Host header in the browser. That lets you point the domain to the desired IP while keeping the Host name correct, and it works for more than just GET requests.

A self-hosted analytics tool like Urchin can run on your own servers, which makes it suitable for intranets. It also supports processing historical logs, robot and spider reports, status/error code reports such as 404s, and individual visitor history drilldown. One downside mentioned is cost: US$9995.

Your tracking snippet should be inside the page’s HTML body, not outside the `<html>` tag. If it’s placed incorrectly, Analytics may not record goals properly.

If the issue is specifically misattribution to Facebook and accounts.google.com, this evidence doesn’t fully cover referral exclusion or attribution settings. The closest supported guidance is to first fix the tracking code placement, since broken tracking can cause goal recording and attribution problems.

To avoid misattributed goal conversions, don’t rely on the page URL changing if the form submits without loading a new page. Instead, fire a Google Analytics event when the form is submitted, and create the goal from that event. That tracks the actual form completion rather than whatever referrer or session source may be present, which can help prevent conversions being counted under Facebook or accounts.google.com.

If you’re tracking the whole domain and subdomains, use only the path for the goal, like /conversions/. Google Analytics will count visits to that page on either the main domain or the subdomain, so you don’t need to enter the subdomain name in the goal URL.

This answer covers subdomain goal tracking, but it doesn’t address misattribution to Facebook or accounts.google.com. For that issue, the closest guidance here is that the goal should be defined by the page path, not the referrer domain. If the conversions are landing on the expected page path, GA will track them as conversions regardless of whether the visit came from a subdomain or main domain.

If you mean adding http:// to internal links, the only supported fix here is to make the /en/ URL redirect server-side to /en/home/. The example solution is to place a PHP/ASP/JSP redirect in /en/ so clicking /en/ lands on /en/home/ instead of 404ing.

If you don’t have that kind of server-side access, the closest guidance here is that you’re “pretty much out of luck”; browser-side workarounds would be long-winded and cumbersome.

If you mean adding http:// to internal links, that’s not addressed here. The guidance here is that putting a NOFOLLOW meta tag on every page is not a good idea because it can stop search engines from crawling the whole site. A sitemap can help pages be crawled and indexed, but pages without internal links may still not rank well. A better approach is to block only the API-dependent URLs in robots.txt if they follow a predictable pattern, or pre-generate the pages so they’re already in your database and load quickly.

Adding `http://` in internal links is not what causes `nofollow`. The `.htaccess` file cannot add `nofollow` to links in your HTML.

The evidence says something else is causing it, likely a CMS plugin, module, or theme setting. Internal links should generally not be `nofollow`; that is usually meant for links you do not control.

Your redirects for `www` and `index.html` can stay, but you need to inspect the page source or CMS settings to find where `rel="nofollow"` is being added and remove it there.

No. The guidance shown says you may not encourage users to click Google ads, directly or indirectly. Examples it lists as prohibited include phrases like “click the ads,” “support us,” and “visit these links,” or similar language. So wording like “check out our sponsors” could be risky if it is meant to prompt ad clicks.

If your AdSense ads aren’t showing, the likely things to check are:

- Whether your AdSense account is under review or banned
- Whether the code was copied and pasted correctly
- Whether JavaScript is enabled and no ad blocker is interfering
- Whether you have more than 3 AdSense ad units on the page
- Whether your site content is suitable for AdSense
- Whether Google can crawl your site without errors

The thread also suggests checking if the page shows white space or PSAs, and using Google Webmaster Tools to see how Google views your site.

If your AdSense account was disabled, the answer suggests it may not be recoverable. To investigate invalid-click abuse, you can temporarily replace AdSense with a simple dummy ad that logs IP address, time, and user agent, then look for suspicious patterns. You can also report invalid clicks to Google using their invalid-clicks contact form.

For prevention, one suggested approach is to show ads only to visitors coming from search engines. The answer also notes you don’t need to know what software attackers use.

Hyphens aren’t necessarily “bad” for domain names, but multiple hyphens may reduce any exact-match keyword benefit. In the example, the site is indexed, so it doesn’t appear to be blacklisted. The likely issue is that the hyphenated domain may not get the same exact-match bonus as the non-hyphenated version, which could hurt rankings.

Hyphens aren’t inherently bad, but the guidance here is to avoid them if you can. They add noise and can make a domain less user-friendly, especially when people have to say or spell the address aloud.

That said, a well-placed hyphen can sometimes help readability and prevent confusing meanings, like separating words in a domain.

So the closest answer supported here is: generally avoid hyphens in domain names, unless they clearly improve clarity.

Use an SMS gateway/API rather than building SMS handling yourself. The suggested search term is “International SMS Gateway.” Twilio is noted as very developer-friendly and worth contacting for a referral. Another provider mentioned is cdyne’s SMS service. The thread doesn’t give a specific international provider for Sydney, Australia, but it does support looking for an international SMS gateway with an API you can code against.

The provided information suggests using an HTTP-to-SMS gateway service. One example mentioned is Clickatell, which has been used to send and receive SMS with PHP. The note also mentions that details are on their SMS Gateway page.

So, the closest supported guidance is: choose an HTTP-to-SMS gateway provider, then integrate it with your website’s PHP or ASP code to send and receive text messages.

The simplest option described here is to embed the Google Talk chatback widget on your website. It uses an HTML snippet provided by the service, and visitors can contact you through it while you’re logged in to Google Talk.

The provided information doesn’t explain how to send the messages. It only says the person already researched that part and was asking about setting up the subscription service. The suggested guidance is to use PayPal’s built-in monthly subscription/subscriber service, configure the billing frequency, and make cancellation easy. For messaging, you’d need to use a separate text-message/SMS service, but no specific one is named here.

To send messages from your website, the closest guidance here is to use an SMS gateway/API. The exact phrase suggested is “International SMS Gateway.” Twilio is mentioned as a strong option for developer-friendly SMS sending, though it was noted as US-limited in your post. Another service suggested is cdyne’s SMS service.

From the described flow, your website would receive incoming SMS, process the votes on your backend, and later use the API to send an outgoing SMS to the selected winner. If you want international providers similar to Twilio, the answer only suggests searching for international SMS gateways and contacting Twilio for references.

For a simple site search, the guidance here is not to try to get Google to index the AJAX search result pages. Instead, create an XML sitemap of your actual content pages and keep it updated. Google can then crawl those pages directly.

The concern is that letting Google crawl search results can waste crawl budget on an almost infinite set of possible result pages, and those pages may become stale quickly. So for your case, the supported approach is to index the underlying content pages, not the search results themselves.

Google has changed how it indexes sites and can now index AJAX pages directly. Googlebot can see the page the same way an end user sees it, including interactive JavaScript and AJAX-powered content, so no special AJAX-specific changes are needed for Googlebot.

So the issue with the “Submit to Google index” button not doing anything for that AJAX URL is likely not something you need to solve with AJAX crawling anymore. The closest guidance supported here is to rely on Google’s normal indexing rather than the old AJAX-crawl setup.

It’s not necessarily a problem for SEO as long as the snapshot HTML contains the same content a user would see in the browser. Different markup structure, like using different tags such as h1 or h2, is okay if the visible content is equivalent. It becomes a problem only if the snapshot shows materially different content than the user page.

If the script isn’t meant to be accessed directly by clients, the answer is to stop trying to block bots and instead make the script only work when included by your own PHP. Define a constant in the main page, include the script, and in the script check whether that constant exists; if not, return a 403 or blank page.

This requires using include, not file_get_contents, and using a file path rather than a URL. Another better option is moving the script outside the document root, if your host allows it.

You can use several anti-bot measures:

- Add a fake hidden field or hidden link; if it’s submitted or followed, ignore it and optionally ban the source.
- Use CAPTCHA like reCAPTCHA.
- Add a simple human question field, like “what is 5 + 3?”; reject missing or wrong answers.
- Use a token stored in the session and included in the form; if it’s missing or doesn’t match, treat it as automated.
- Watch for repeated submissions from the same IP and temporarily block it if it spikes.
- Use Akismet to help identify spam.

The evidence doesn’t specifically confirm the cookie/JavaScript timestamp idea, but it does support token/session-based checks and rate limiting as stronger options.

Filter search engines by user agent, not by IP addresses. The provided answer does not mention a website or always-up-to-date list of bot IPs, so it doesn’t support using IP-based filtering for this purpose.

Yes—because Google Analytics treats bounces as 0 seconds for “Avg visit duration” / “Avg time on site,” but still counts their full reading time in “Avg time on page.”

So if many users land on one page and leave without viewing another page, the site duration average gets pulled down, while page time can stay higher. That’s why “Avg time on page” can be larger than “Avg visit duration.”

In short: single-page visits reduce visit duration to zero, but not page time.

This can happen because “Avg. Visit Duration” includes all visits, even ones where the user left after the first page loaded, so many sessions may be recorded as 00:00:00. “Avg. Time on Page” is calculated only for pages where Google Analytics can measure time between pageviews, so it can be higher.

In other words, a session can count as a visit without producing measurable visit duration if the user lands on one page and leaves quickly. That’s what the evidence supports; it does not specifically indicate robots or a broken script.

Yes. In Google Analytics, “Avg. time on page” can be larger than “Avg. visit duration” because they’re calculated differently.

“Avg. time on page” measures the time between that pageview and the next pageview on your site, and it excludes single-page visits from the calculation.

“Avg. visit duration” is based on the time between the first and last pageviews in a visit. Since the last pageview’s time can’t be measured, it tends to be shorter than the actual visit.

So if you want to estimate how long users stay on that page before moving on, “Avg. time on page” is the better metric.

To exclude a specific page from Google Analytics, go to the view you want to change, then Admin > Filters > New Filter > Custom Filter.

You can filter by page title if it’s unique, or filter by URL by entering all or part of the page URL. That will stop that page from being monitored in that view.

If you meant hiding the “All Traffic” row in a report, this doesn’t cover that directly; it only supports filtering traffic/page data out of a view.

You can’t just hide the “all traffic” line in the regular plot-rows view. The closest workaround is to use the Motion Charts view instead:

Select your date range.
Go to Traffic Sources > Sources > Referrals.
Make sure the referrers you want are on the first page.
Click the Motion Charts icon (three black dots at the top right of the graph).
Change the metric on the left to Visits.
Then switch to the line-chart tab and use the checkboxes to select only the referrers you want.

That gives you a comparison graph without the oversized “all traffic” line dominating the chart.

Those 404s are being caused by a bad link on your site, not by Google itself. In the example shown, the “want to advertise” banner at the top of every page contains a relative link like `href="_#"`.

That makes the crawler try to visit a URL like `/_`, which returns 404 on every page where the banner appears.

Fix the banner’s link so it points to a valid URL, or remove the broken link. Once Google recrawls the site, those 404s should stop appearing.

Google can report 404s for URLs that never existed because search engines sometimes request random, made-up paths to check whether your server returns a proper 404 for missing pages. The example page name may not have been created by a human at all.

So the 170 “not found” errors may include these kinds of crawler-generated requests. This usually means Google found URLs that returned 404, not necessarily that those pages were ever on your site.

If the 404s are from random URLs, that is generally normal. If they’re from real old URLs, you’d want to check for broken internal links, bad external links, or removed pages.

If Google Webmaster Tools is showing 404 errors, the fix is on the site first: correct the broken URLs or remove the bad links. After that, mark the errors as fixed in Google Webmaster Tools.

If you already fixed them, they may still remain in the report until Google recrawls the site. Once Google checks again, the errors should disappear if the problem no longer exists. If the same 404s happen again later, Google will report them again.

Google’s error is usually triggered when the product markup is missing a supported property on the Product item. In the code shown, the product uses `data-vocabulary.org/Product`, and the visible properties shown are `name` and `image`; the snippet does not show any `price`, `review`, or `availability` markup.

Closest guidance supported by the evidence: make sure the Product item includes one of those properties on the same item, and verify the markup being output in the page source. If the values are present in your data, the issue may be that they are not marked up in a way Google recognizes, or not attached to the Product item correctly.

That warning usually means Google can see the markup but can’t use it for rich results because the marked-up content doesn’t match the main page content. In the resolved case, Google’s testing tool reported that the marked-up content “does not appear to be the main focus of the page,” and there was also a duplicate makesOffer property.

Closest guidance supported here: make sure the structured data matches visible page content, and remove duplicate properties. Google may then be able to recognize it properly.

For discontinued products, use a 410 Gone so search engines know the page is removed. On the page, tell users the product has been discontinued and provide links to similar products plus your home page, sitemap, and contact page.

If the item is seasonal and will return, don’t use 404/410. Mark it as currently out of stock or seasonal, keep the page indexed, and optionally let users register for restock notifications.

For removed pages, 404 is the closer choice. The accepted guidance says to use a custom 404 page with useful internal links, like the homepage, search, or a main topic page. It also says this should not negatively affect the site in general, as long as you handle a few things: update your XML sitemap, remove or adjust internal links, and if possible notify external sites that link to the removed pages.

A 301 to the homepage is not what this guidance recommends for deleted content. If you want to avoid losing visitors, a helpful 404 page is the supported approach.

If a page is truly removed and not coming back, 404 is the closest match. If you 301 it to the home page or another unrelated page, Google will treat the old URL as moved and pass any value to the new URL.

From the evidence: a 404 is fine when the page doesn’t exist yet; if it later appears and returns 200, Google will notice. A 301 to the closest valid page can pass “juice” sooner, but it’s only appropriate if that redirect really represents the old content.

So for removed pages: use 404 if they’re gone; use 301 only when there’s a relevant replacement.

From the SEO perspective in the example, the closer the domain is to the target keyword, the better. A shorter, keyword-focused .com would be the safer choice if you want broad use and easier memorability.

So between alltogether.com and all-different-words.com, all other things equal, alltogether.com would likely have the advantage because it’s shorter and closer to a clean brandable domain, while the longer hyphenated version is less ideal for users.

That said, SEO is not just about the domain name. The answer also emphasizes usability and memorability matter a lot.

The more SEO-friendly choice is the cleaner, path-based URL like alltogether.com rather than a longer, parameter-style or more cluttered alternative. The cited guidance says the first format is both more SEO-friendly and more user-friendly. If you need the convenience of dynamic parameters, you can still present clean URLs using mod_rewrite so they look like the better SEO option while behaving like the parameterized version.

A JavaScript redirect is not a good idea for SEO. Search engines may not handle it well, and it doesn’t clearly signal a permanent move, so PageRank/association may not carry over properly.

If you need to move a page, the supported approach is a server-side 301 redirect. If the issue is replacing the homepage, the best option is to just serve the new homepage directly rather than redirecting it.

This guidance doesn’t specifically address non-existing posts, but it does support avoiding JavaScript redirects and using 301s for moved pages.

Redirecting non-existing posts to the homepage is not ideal for SEO. The guidance here says 404 pages are fine, and generally 404 errors don’t impact ranking in Google. Problems arise when your site keeps linking to lots of broken pages, which can hurt user experience and look poorly maintained.

If a page truly doesn’t exist, it should return a real 404 status. A custom 404 page with a search box is fine. If the URL is meant to be handled as an old or moved page, then a relevant redirect is better than sending everything to the homepage. Redirecting unrelated broken URLs to the homepage can confuse users and search engines.

Use a CMS or routing system that lets you change the site structure without tying it to the physical file structure. Then define a clear, user-friendly taxonomy and map old URLs to the new ones.

For the link update itself, the closest supported guidance is to avoid changing things arbitrarily and preserve usability: use custom routing/redirects so old links still work, and organize the new structure around user segments, terminology, and common use cases.

If you’re asking specifically how to migrate existing links after a redesign, the practical best practice is to redirect old URLs to their new equivalents rather than leaving broken links.

If you change the site structure, keep the old URLs and set up 301 permanent redirects from each old URL to its new target. That is the best-supported approach here.

Without redirects, existing links can break, and Google may treat the new URLs as duplicates of the old ones, which can hurt ranking. With 301 redirects, Google should be able to update to the new targets over time.

So the practical guidance is: map old pages to new pages one-to-one and redirect every old URL permanently to the corresponding new URL.

Best practice here is to use 301 redirects for old URLs to the new ones. The guidance also suggests:

- Roll out the new structure in parallel where possible, rather than switching everything at once.
- Update sitemaps to point search engines to the new URL paths.
- Use a canonical link/header if duplicate URL paths will exist.
- Avoid doing the migration right around domain renewal/expiry.
- If link structure changes a lot, make sure the changes are genuinely in users’ best interest.

If you mean internal links on the site, update them to the new URLs as part of the redesign, while keeping 301 redirects from the old URLs so existing links still work.

If you have no backup, the closest option mentioned is Warrick. It can scrape Google Cache and a few other sources to try to recover lost site content. The provided info does not say that full website recovery is guaranteed, only that it may help recover lost content from cached copies and related sources. If your site is visible in Google Cache, that content is a possible recovery source.

If you have no backup, the closest recovery options in the thread are to rebuild from caches: use search engine/web crawler caches to recover HTML page content, then restore images from readers’ browser caches.

The described approach is:
- Recover the page list and individual posts from Google/Yahoo/Bing caches, often manually if automated tools fail.
- For images, restore the HTML first, then have readers load URLs and save any images that still exist in their browser caches, since some may have recently viewed the site.

This can help recover parts of the site, but the thread also notes browser caches may not go back far enough, so full recovery isn’t guaranteed.

No. Based on the provided information, adding a Google Map to a page does not appear to improve page SEO or rankings. A large-scale site with Google Maps on over 1 million pages saw zero ranking effect with or without the map. The closest guidance supported here is that Google may execute some JavaScript, but this mainly seems useful for link discovery and detecting spammy redirects, not for boosting SEO.

The available information only says that for a Google Maps Premier license, you should contact their sales department from the referenced page. It does not provide any details about SEO for Google Maps applications.

If your question is about improving search visibility for a Google Maps-based app, this evidence doesn’t cover that. The closest guidance it supports is to use the Google Maps sales contact page for licensing or product inquiries.

A .nl domain is already geo-targeted to the Netherlands, and you can’t manually change that in Google Webmaster Tools for a country-code TLD. That doesn’t stop it from appearing on google.com, google.co.uk, etc. if Google thinks it’s relevant.

If your page is indexed but not showing for searches, the issue is more likely relevance/language rather than indexing. In the example, the site appeared on google.com and google.co.uk for a name search, and on google.nl it showed up only when English was chosen as the search language because the site is in English.

So the closest guidance is: you generally can’t make a .nl domain “global-targeted,” but it can still rank worldwide if the content matches the search terms and language.

If `site:ecservice.ro` shows pages, Google has likely indexed them. Not appearing for keyword searches usually means the pages don’t have enough relevance or authority for those terms.

In the cited case, the site was described as full of unrelated links, which search engines may treat as spam. That can prevent it from ranking for any searches even if it is indexed.

Closest guidance supported here:
- Make sure the page content matches the search terms.
- Remove unrelated or spammy links.
- Build up reputation with relevant links from other sites.

New sites can also take time before they start showing in normal search results.

Google likely isn’t showing authorship because the author link is hidden from humans. Google says the rel="author" link should not be invisible with techniques like display:none or CSS, and it won’t display information that cannot be viewed by humans. So if the link is created but hidden, that can prevent authorship from appearing. The answer also suggests the whole purpose of authorship is to connect visible content with your Google+ profile. The `nofollow` part wasn’t identified as the main issue here; the visibility of the link was.

Google may simply be choosing not to display the authorship image/profile, even if the markup tests correctly. In the answer provided, the likely reason is that your Google+ profile may not look active enough—only 4 people have you in their circles—which could make Google decide it’s not worth showing in search results.

So the guidance supported here is: keep adding authorship to new posts and build up your Google+ account/activity.

You may already be using the correct microdata format. The issue described is that SEOquake does not report on any type of markup, so there’s no need to change your microformat just to satisfy that tool. It mainly reports off-site parameters, and the only on-site parameter it can report on is page titles.

So the best guidance here is: keep the markup as-is if it follows the documented format, and don’t rely on SEOquake to validate it. If you need SEOquake to report markup, that would require creating custom parameters for it.

The evidence doesn’t address “microformatting accepted, then ignored” directly. It only says that programming/code-focused sites may have a harder time getting Adsense approval, while sites about broader programming practices, tips, advice, or a knowledge base are more likely to be approved. It also suggests reviewing Adsense guidelines. If your issue is that microformatting was accepted but later ignored, this source doesn’t explain why that happens. The closest guidance it supports is to make sure the site has substantial, useful content and fits Adsense policies.

The markup is mostly right, but acceptedPaymentMethod should be expressed with link and href, not meta and content, because it’s a URL/URI value.

Use:
<link itemprop="acceptedPaymentMethod" href="http://purl.org/goodrelations/v1#PayPal" />
<link itemprop="acceptedPaymentMethod" href="http://purl.org/goodrelations/v1#PaymentMethodCreditCard" />

The rest of the example looks fine at first glance.

Google appears to have removed authorship images from all SERPs as part of a rollout, not just from your site. The closest supported guidance is that Google made official statements about the change and provided an updated support page. No specific reason is given in the evidence beyond that it was a broader rollout affecting everyone.

No, hiding the rel="author" link with CSS like display:none is not expected to work. Google’s guidance says the rel="author" link should be visible to humans, and it won’t display information that can’t be viewed by users. The accepted answer also says the purpose of authorship is to connect content with a visible author profile for credibility.

The evidence doesn’t say that nofollow alone would break authorship, but it does indicate that the hidden link is the main problem. It also suggests you may need to be reasonably active on Google+ for authorship to show.

The most likely issue is that the rel="author" link is hidden with `display:none`. Google generally won’t show authorship information that isn’t visible to users, so the photo may appear only in limited cases or not at all for others.

What this covers:
- Your markup uses `rel="author"`.
- The author div is hidden from view.
- Google may not display hidden author info.

Closest guidance supported here:
- Make the author link visible on the page.
- Use Google’s structured data/testing tools to verify it can be extracted.
- Also note Google never guaranteed authorship would always appear.

Google’s disavow process is about the spammy links pointing to your site, so for a reconsideration request you’d identify those bad inbound links and disavow them. The evidence here doesn’t explain how to find them all, but it does support that you should focus on links Google may view as link spam and that disavowing them won’t hurt other sites. The closest guidance supported is to review your backlink profile and list the spammy links to your site for disavowal.

The evidence doesn’t say how to find all the links to disavow. It only says you should work to have the unnatural links removed, regardless of age, and if you can’t resolve all issues, document your efforts clearly when submitting a reconsideration request. It also suggests it’s okay to submit a reconsideration request even if you’re unsure whether the issue is algorithmic or manual.

If you know for sure the links are spammy, artificial, or low-quality, you can disavow them. The only harm described here is accidentally disavowing links that were helping your rankings, which could make the affected pages drop in search results.

This doesn’t explain how to find all links for a reconsideration request. The closest guidance supported is to review backlink data carefully and disavow only links you’re confident are harmful. If the links were clearly built by a competitor as negative SEO, then disavowing them is considered okay.

A hyphen doesn’t make a domain inherently better or worse for SEO just because of a stop word. The answer says modern Google doesn’t really use stop words in the old sense, and searches like “green giraffes” and “about green giraffes” are not identical, only similar. So “aboutgreengiraffes.com” is not necessarily as good as “greengiraffes.com” for SEO value. The evidence doesn’t support the idea that shorter filler characters like “e” or “z” are better either. The closest supported guidance is that stop words are not treated as equal ignored terms in modern Google, so domain choice should not rely on that assumption.

I’d avoid hyphens in the domain name. They add noise and make the name less pleasant to say and spell out, so from a user-friendliness standpoint “stackoverflow.com” is better than “stack-overflow.com.”

There can be exceptions where a hyphen improves readability and avoids a bad misreading, like “experts-exchange” versus “expertsexchange.” So the closest guidance is: use a hyphen only if it clearly improves clarity; otherwise, prefer no hyphen.

Not all of them by default. The main risk is disavowing links that actually help your rankings, which could make your pages drop in search results.

If you know a set of links is truly spammy or was built by a competitor, the guidance here says it’s reasonable to disavow them. If you’re unsure, only do it with caution and only for links you believe are causing problems.

A mobile XML sitemap won’t directly affect rankings, whether positively or negatively. The bigger issue is making sure Google gets the right version of your pages into the right index.

If your desktop and mobile pages use the same URLs but generate device-specific HTML, the important thing is the Vary HTTP header so Google knows the content changes by device.

So if the mobile sitemap would just duplicate the desktop sitemap, it should not itself change ranking; it also isn’t the main fix for same-URL device-specific pages.

You need a separate vhost or an alias-based setup; the example as written can cause a loop if the non-www host is also handled by the same redirect.

The accepted approaches shown are:

1. Two virtual hosts:
- one for example.com with your site
- one for www.example.com that issues `Redirect 301 / http://example.com/`

2. Use `.htaccess` with a redirect rule if you want to avoid a second vhost.

3. One vhost with:
`ServerName example.com`
`ServerAlias www.example.com`
and then a rewrite rule in `.htaccess` to redirect `www` to non-www.

If you avoid `.htaccess`, the supported guidance here is to use two virtual hosts, with the `www` vhost doing the 301 redirect.

Use one version and 301-redirect the other. The choice between www and naked domain is mostly up to you; the key is that both shouldn’t serve as separate pages. If the domain is short, dropping www is often preferred; if it’s longer, keeping www may look better. As long as you redirect one to the other, it shouldn’t really matter.

Use an .htaccess redirect for the www host to the non-www version:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www.example.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://example.com/$1 [R=301,L]

Put the .htaccess file in your site’s root directory.

This specifically redirects requests from www.example.com to example.com. The provided guidance does not cover the reverse case or a wildcard “all works” setup.

It’s not “essential” in the sense that either `www.domain.com` or `domain.com` can be the preferred version. The important part is to choose one and redirect the other to it with a 301 so both versions don’t serve the same content.

If both www and non-www work without redirecting, they can behave like two different URLs, which can cause duplicate content and make canonicalization unclear.

So the best-supported guidance is: pick one version, then set a 301 redirect from the other to it.

If you’re the site owner, there isn’t really a way to make DNS propagate faster. The closest useful step is to first verify the nameservers are correct. In cPanel, check under Addon Domains that the domain isn’t already listed; if it is, delete it and re-add it. If you still get the same error, contact your host, because it suggests something is misconfigured in your cPanel account and they can fix it.

The provided information doesn’t actually explain how to make DNS propagate faster. It only suggests that a slow site load may be caused by WordPress performance, and the top answer recommends installing a caching plugin for WordPress.

If your issue is the initial GET request taking too long, the closest guidance here is to improve site-side performance with caching. If you want DNS-specific help, this evidence doesn’t cover it.

Changing the nameservers only tells the internet which DNS server is authoritative for your domain. If you point the domain to 000webhost’s nameservers, you still need to add the domain/zone and the needed DNS records there, usually an A record for the root domain and a www record, using the IP or hostname 000webhost gives you.

If you prefer, you can switch back to whois.com’s nameservers and manage the DNS records there instead. The message you see in whois.com means their DNS management won’t work unless the domain uses whois.com nameservers.

Domain privacy only hides the registrant/owner info in Whois. It does not hide DNS servers. Whois for the domain can still show which name servers you’re using.

If you want less visible DNS-related information, you can either:
- remove DNS records if you’re not using the domain, or
- use a DNS service and create/manage records there instead of exposing unnecessary details.

The answer provided also notes that DNS servers and IPs can have their own Whois records, but that’s separate from your domain’s Whois.

There isn’t a guaranteed “foolproof” switch here. The guidance supported is to use an image sitemap and point Google to the actual image URL with `image:loc`, associated with the page’s `loc`. That can help Google discover the real image instead of only the thumbnail. I can only say this covers image indexing generally; it doesn’t guarantee Google News will always choose the exact thumbnail you want.

There’s no answer on record for a foolproof way to make Google News pull the correct thumbnail image. The only related information is that the thread discussed compiling many RSS feeds into a WordPress news section similar to Google News, but it did not provide any solution.

So, based on this, I can’t confirm a guaranteed method. The closest guidance supported here is that this is a feed aggregation/curation problem, but the thread itself doesn’t say how to control Google News thumbnails.

No foolproof way. Even if you do everything right, Google News may still not show your image or may pair the article with a relevant image from another source.

Closest guidance supported here: use JPEG/JPG images, make them at least 60×60, keep reasonable aspect ratios, place them inline and near the article title, add clear captions, avoid robots.txt blocking, and host images on a domain included in Google News. If images are on a separate domain, Google is unlikely to crawl them.

The best way is to create high-quality content on your Malayalam or English site, because good content naturally attracts backlinks from other websites.

Lower-quality ways to get links include:
- forum signatures
- directory submissions
- link exchanges
- blog comments
- article directories

These can help with quantity, but they are usually much less valuable than links from established sites that rank well for your keywords.

Also, make sure the links are not nofollow if your goal is SEO value, and avoid spamming other sites.

To get backlinks for Malayalam sites, whether in English or Malayalam, the key is to have links from relevant, trustworthy sites. You can make a landing page that includes Malayalam content and links to your Malayalam site, and use lang for the language of the content and hreflang on the target links.

You can’t force search engines to show different titles/descriptions for different languages on the same page. A single page has one title, so it’s best to use a neutral title like the domain name.

For backlinks, focus on getting other Malayalam-related or English-related sites to link to your page naturally. The evidence here supports multilingual landing pages and language-marked links, but not a specific backlink-building method.

If multiple HTTPS page URLs show the same content, the supported fix here is to use `<link rel="canonical">` to point search engines to the primary URL. That tells them the pages are duplicates and which one should be treated as the main version, avoiding duplicate-content issues.

This only covers the case where multiple URLs produce the same content. It doesn’t address other issues like pagination, tag pages, or whether to use `noindex`/`nofollow` on those pages.

Use a 301 redirect from the old URL structure to the new one. That’s the supported way to get Google to replace the old URLs in its index. It may take time, but it should happen.

A robots.txt Disallow on the old URLs is not the suggested fix here, since the guidance given is specifically to redirect the old pages to the new pages.

The answer given says SSL certificates don’t have to be expensive, and that your host could fix this without you buying one. The suggested fixes are for the hosting company to reconfigure Apache SSL/virtual hosts or add an htaccess rule on the SSL site to block access via the wrong domain name. If they won’t do that, moving hosts may be the practical option. It also says there’s nothing you can do entirely on your own to solve it without help from the host.

Use a canonical tag to tell search engines which URL is the preferred version of a page. That was suggested specifically for http/https duplication issues.

For users, don’t redirect someone from HTTP to HTTPS after they’re already logged in if that would expose the session cookie over HTTP. They should log in again from a secure HTTPS page.

If a user hits the HTTPS version while not logged in, you can either leave them on HTTPS or redirect them to HTTP depending on your site’s needs and traffic. The advice here does not give a single required redirect strategy, only that keeping them on HTTPS may be acceptable.

If other sites republish your content, that is duplicate content, but the republishing sites are the ones typically affected. Google has improved how it handles this so the original publisher can get credit, though it is not perfect.

To help reduce the risk of duplicate-content issues, include a hard link to the original article in your RSS feed so republishers show you as the original source.

For site-wide HTTPS specifically, the provided guidance does not cover SSL migration or redirects. The closest supported advice is to make the original version clear and ensure republished copies point back to it.

The provided guidance only covers changing from HTTP to HTTPS or back: if the host and path stay the same, rankings should not be lost, though Google will re-index the pages. It does not directly address duplicate-content SEO when forcing HTTPS site-wide on an existing site.

Closest supported advice: make the HTTPS version the canonical one by consistently using the same host/path and ensuring Google re-indexes it. If you’re changing protocol only, the main expectation is reindexing rather than a ranking loss.

For a two-word search, the best SEO URL name is usually the exact keyword phrase, with words separated by hyphens, if it reads naturally. The answer you have here mainly says to choose keywords based on search traffic, value, and competition; it doesn’t give a specific URL naming rule. Closest guidance: use the exact target phrase in the URL, keep it short, and don’t force awkward wording. If you’re choosing between two-word terms, pick the one with good SEOT/SEOV and manageable competition, then use that phrase in the URL.

If the search term you want to target is the full name “John Smith,” the fuller URL, /johnsmith, is the better match. The accepted guidance says that matching the exact search term more closely is preferable, so /johnsmith would be more SEO-friendly for that query than /john.

The first format is more SEO-friendly and more user-friendly: `/x/y/z/t` is preferred over `/x?var1=y&var2=z&var3=t`.

If convenience is the reason you like the second form, you can still make URLs look like the first while handling them like the second by using mod_rewrite.

Google does not treat content inside an iFrame as part of the domain doing the framing, so the forwarded domain won’t be seen as the real site. Based on this, that setup is unlikely to help the business appear in Google Maps or the right-hand knowledge panel.

The closest guidance supported here is to use a proper site for the business rather than an iFrame-based forward. If the business still doesn’t show, the issue is likely related to how Google is associating the website/listing, not just the address or Webmaster Tools.

If your business or site isn’t appearing on the right side of Google search, the main thing supported here is that it can simply take time to show up. Even if your keywords are on the site, that doesn’t mean it will appear immediately in search results.

A suggested next step is to add your site to web directories with good PageRank, which may help it get discovered. But the key point is that visibility in Google can still take time, even after that.

To get a business shown in the right-hand side of Google search, the guide suggests creating a Google+ page for your business, choosing the Local Business or Place category, and entering an accurate, complete street address and direct phone number. If your business already exists in the drop-down, select it; otherwise choose the option saying it isn’t listed. Then submit and complete verification if offered. For non-local pages, Google says it helps to link your Google+ page and website to each other. If you want, I can also help you check whether your business should be set up as local or non-local.

To add a domain/subdomain on a VPS with Webmin, you need a web server such as Apache running first. Then you set up DNS so the domain points to your VPS; Cloudflare is suggested for DNS, or you can run your own DNS with BIND. If you want multiple domains/virtual hosts, Webmin can be used with Apache virtual hosting.

The provided guidance does not give the exact Webmin clicks for creating a subdomain, but it supports this setup: install/configure Apache, add DNS records for the subdomain, and create a virtual host for it in Webmin.

To add the Google SPF, create a TXT record and set its value to:

v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all

The Webmin/BIND DNS server record types help page is the place to look for adding DNS records. This doesn’t specifically describe creating a subdomain, but for SPF you’re adding a TXT record for the domain or subdomain you want to use.

To create a subdomain virtual host in Webmin, set up a separate Apache virtual host for that subdomain with its own Server Name and Document Root. The accepted setup was:

Address: seopanel.mydomainlolfake.com  
Port: Any  
Server Name: seopanel.mydomainlolfake.com  
Document Root: /var/www/vhosts/seopanel

This allowed two separate virtual hosts to work correctly.

Using keywords in URLs can help a little, but only as a very small SEO factor. It can also make links clearer to users. Great content, titles, and link text matter much more.

If your URLs already work and you have a link structure in place, the safest guidance here is not to change them just to add keywords. Whether a different URL structure would help is debatable and may or may not make a difference.

Google ranks pages, not your whole website. The meta keywords tag is not used for ranking and has not been for a long time. So the better approach is to focus each page on the keywords relevant to that page, rather than trying to expose 100,000 keywords sitewide.

Creating random keyword lists in the footer and linking each keyword to the same content with different URLs would create duplicate content, which is not a good solution.

The guidance supported here is: use page-specific keywords and avoid duplicate URLs for the same content.

This can happen when someone actually searches Google for a page’s URL, not a keyword phrase. Google can return that page in results, and Google Analytics may then record the URL as the organic “keyword.” Common reasons include checking whether a page is indexed, viewing a cached copy, or finding a page directly.

If you’re seeing only a single visitor for each URL, it’s very likely just individual users searching for those exact URLs.

A domain name matching the keyword has only minor SEO significance. It’s more likely the competitor ranks higher because of backlink quality and quantity, not because their domain contains the phrase.

In your case, changing the URL to getbraodband.com/reliancebraodband.html did not help, which also suggests the domain name itself is not the main issue. If you have only around 30 backlinks, that may be too few, and a single strong backlink can matter more than many weak ones.

Creating a subdomain is unlikely to fix the ranking problem by itself. The best supported guidance here is to improve high-quality, indexed backlinks and overall SEO strength rather than relying on an exact-match domain.

If you’re using SortSite from PowerMapper, the spelling checker appears to support only English and French. That means non-English content can be flagged as misspelled even when it’s correct.

The evidence doesn’t say that these warnings affect Google rankings. It only says that whether spelling errors influence ranking is a separate question and would need more details.

So, based on this, the closest guidance is: you likely can’t make that tool ignore all non-English text if it doesn’t support the language, and the permalink text in Georgian may be fine for SEO, but there’s no evidence here that it causes a ranking problem.

No, it should not be a problem for SEO. The remote desktop connection uses a specific port, and that is not part of normal SEO crawling, so search engines won’t treat it the same as the website domain.

If two URLs differ only by case and show the same content, search engines won’t necessarily “penalize” you, but they may treat them as duplicate URLs and choose one version themselves.

Best practice is to make one URL the forced canonical version with a 301 redirect. That works for search engines, users, bookmarks, caches, and other tools. If a 301 redirect isn’t possible, use `rel="canonical"` as a fallback.

So for lowercase vs uppercase, prefer redirecting the nonpreferred version to the preferred one rather than relying only on canonical tags.

Lowercase and uppercase in querystring parameters are different URLs, so Google can initially treat them as separate pages if it discovers both variants. If the content is the same, Google is generally smart enough to recognize them as the same page and avoid duplicate-content issues. The clearest fix is to pick one preferred URL version, usually all lowercase, and add a canonical tag pointing to it.

Use 301 redirects from the old URLs on www.example.com to the matching URLs on blog.example.com. That tells Google and visitors the content has moved, and Google will update its index after reindexing.

Example for Apache:

Redirect 301 /blog http://blog.example.com

Or with mod_rewrite:

RewriteRule ^/?blog(/.*)?$ http://blog.example.com$1 [NS,L,R=301]

If the old and new URLs are too mixed to redirect cleanly, you can also handle it in your 404 error handler.

It appears Google Webmaster Tools’ Change of Address feature does not work for a destination that is a subdomain. The best-supported explanation here is that this is why it says no usable sites are in the account, even though the new site is verified.

The guidance supported by the thread is that this likely won’t hurt you if you’re already using correct 301 redirects, but it may slow the transfer process.

The only supported conclusion here is that the issue was not fixed by adding an add-on or changing app config; it started working later without any known change, so it appears to have been a Heroku-side problem.

So, based on this, there isn’t evidence of a reliable way to “use SSL on Heroku without paying Heroku for SSL” beyond Heroku’s built-in SSL behavior on the platform. If you’re seeing “SSL is not enabled,” the closest guidance supported here is to wait and retry, since the original case resolved on its own.

Use a 301 Moved Permanently redirect to the new URL. That will pass most or all PageRank/link juice to the new page. The loss of Facebook likes, tweets, or +1s on the old URL should not affect PageRank, since PageRank is based on inbound links, not social counts.

You may lose the visible social counters on the old page when the URL changes, but the redirect is the right way to preserve SEO value.

I can’t tell from the available info how to rewrite a URL without losing Facebook likes, tweets, or similar social counts. The only related detail here is that Facebook likes can be tied to either a fan page or a URL, and they are treated differently.

Closest guidance supported here: if you want likes to accumulate on one target, make sure everyone is liking the same canonical URL or the page itself, rather than multiple variants. If you change the URL, existing counts may not carry over automatically.

The evidence doesn’t say how long Data Highlighter markup takes to appear in the structured data tool. It only says the Product page for Data Highlighter is currently not available, and that Product rich snippets use schema.org/Product markup. If you’re waiting for changes to show up, the closest guidance supported here is that Google uses Product/Offer properties like price, currency, quantity, and offerURL/url for rich snippets, but no timing is provided.

If you’ve already added structured data in the page markup, the Data Highlighter adds nothing. The best guidance here is that on-page structured data is better because it can be consumed by all bots, while the Data Highlighter only makes the data available to Google. The evidence doesn’t say how long it takes for highlights to appear in the Structured Data Tool.

To get reviews from your site shown in Google Places/Maps, the supported approach is to use microformats, which Google refers to as rich snippets. That’s the mechanism cited for helping Google recognize review content from your site. The evidence does not mention a separate API or a direct submission process for review sources. It only supports using microformats/rich snippets and following Google’s documentation on that topic.

Google did not provide a widget for embedding Google+ reviews on a website. The supported widgets at the time were only Google+ badge widgets. So if you want to show review details like stars, name, date, and text, the evidence does not show a Google-provided way to do that.

The review box in Google Search results is part of the Google Knowledge Graph. Google decides what to show there from sources like businesses listed in Google Local/Google+, data submitted to Freebase, and often Wikipedia entries.

This does not describe a direct way to “provide” Google reviews information yourself. The closest guidance supported here is to make sure your business/listing data is present in Google Local/Google+ and related sources, since Google selects from those sources when displaying the panel.

For SEO, neither domain has a real keyword-ranking advantage. Exact match domains are no longer beneficial for Google SEO, so it’s better to choose the one that best supports your brand.

If choosing between those two, the version without a hyphen is preferable if possible, since it’s easier to type and remember. The answer also suggests the second option may be more identifiable, but the main guidance is to prioritize branding over SEO keywords.

Both choices are equally relevant for SEO, based on the advice here. The guidance is not to worry much about “learn” vs “learning,” since either would be fine in principle. The bigger issue mentioned is that both domains are already taken, so that may be the deciding factor.

The first format, with path segments like domain.com/x/y/z/t, is more SEO-friendly and more user-friendly. The second format with query parameters is more convenient to manipulate, but the accepted answer says the first is better for SEO. You can also make URLs look like the first while they behave like the second using mod_rewrite.

Use a rewrite that maps the requested subdomain to the matching folder and serves files from there. The code shown in the accepted answer is aimed at turning folders inside a specific `/subdomains/` directory into subdomains, not at making `/sub/` become the main site root.

If you want `domain.com/site` or `site.domain.com` to show content from a subfolder, the supported approach is to rewrite requests for that subdomain into the corresponding directory and check whether the file or directory exists there:

`RewriteCond %{DOCUMENT_ROOT}/subdomains/%1/$1 -f [OR]`
`RewriteCond %{DOCUMENT_ROOT}/subdomains/%1/$1 -d`
`RewriteRule (.*) /subdomains/%1/$1 [L]`

Replace `example.com` with your domain. This should let URLs like `sub.domain.com/2/3/4.html` load from the matching subfolder, if that folder/file exists.

Use a 301 redirect with RedirectMatch if you want everything under a subfolder sent to another location. For example, to redirect all /portfolio URLs, you’d use:

RedirectMatch 301 ^/portfolio/(.*)$ http://new-domain.com/portfolio/$1

If you want the main index to go to a subfolder like domain.com/site, this same kind of 301 redirect is the closest supported approach. The example shown only covers subfolder paths, not the bare domain root, so for the exact root-to-subfolder case you’d need a similar redirect rule targeting “/” specifically.

Yes—based on the example, you can make `domain.com/site` serve `domain.com/site/index.html`, and also redirect `domain.com/site/` and `domain.com/site/index.html` back to `domain.com/site`.

A pattern like this should work in `.htaccess`:

```apache
DirectorySlash Off
RewriteEngine on

RewriteRule ^site$ /site/index.html [L,E=LOOP:1]

RewriteCond %{ENV:REDIRECT_LOOP} !1
RewriteRule ^site/$ /site [R=301,L]

RewriteCond %{ENV:REDIRECT_LOOP} !1
RewriteRule ^site/index.html$ /site [R=301,L]
```

This covers:
- `/site` → shows `/site/index.html`
- `/site/` → redirects to `/site`
- `/site/index.html` → redirects to `/site`

It does not specifically address other files in the folder, but the example says those should still be shown normally.

Your rule is redirecting to the same host, which can cause a redirect loop. To send `demo.example.com` to `example.com/my-demo`, use an absolute URL in the rewrite target:

`RewriteEngine On`
`RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} =demo.example.com`
`RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://example.com/my-demo/$1 [R=301,L]`

This keeps the path and changes both the host and destination directory.

To keep sub.domain.com in the browser while serving content from another server, the supported approach here is a reverse proxy, not a normal redirect. The example given uses Apache ProxyPass/ProxyPassReverse to forward requests for the subdomain to another backend while preserving the .com URL.

A second workaround mentioned is a full-page iframe, but it is less suitable, especially for SEO, and can be problematic with SSL.

If your goal is actually to map the subdomain to a subdirectory on the same site, this evidence does not cover that directly, but the closest supported guidance is still to use reverse proxying.

Yes. Moving PHP/MySQL parts to a different server can be a wise move if that server has the same or greater resources.

For SEO, subdomains and subdirectories are treated as analogous by Google, so there may be a temporary ranking drop while redirects are processed, but the long-term impact should be minimal if the old URLs are properly redirected.

The Nginx rewrite you showed is a server configuration question; the provided guidance doesn’t confirm whether it correctly sets 301 redirects.

Yes. Once you switch your MX entries, new email will start arriving at the new provider. For a short time, some senders may still use cached old MX records and deliver to the old place.

To avoid disruption, you need to be able to receive mail from both the old and new providers during the transition. If you can do that, you should be fine. After about 3 days, all email should be arriving at the new place.

You should be okay transferring the domain and hosting as long as you keep the existing DNS mail records, especially the MX records, unchanged. The MX records tell mail where to go. If the mail hosts are part of the domain, keep those related records too.

So the key is not the transfer itself, but making sure DNS continues to point email the same way during and after the move.

If the email is currently forwarded, you can preserve it by recreating the forwarding on the new email hosting. If you want to keep using the local/work server directly, you need to use that server’s full MX records instead of the hosting package’s mail settings.

To reduce disruption, lower the domain TTL to 1 hour and wait about 24 hours for it to propagate before making the transfer. Then make the DNS changes during a low-traffic time, such as a weekend or evening.

Make sure private registration/ID protection is turned off before starting the transfer. You’ll also need the EPP/transfer auth code from your domain control panel.

If you can access the hosting panel, the primary domain can be changed to 50cccycle.com there; otherwise you’ll need to contact the hosting provider.

The provided guidance does not cover preserving email during a transfer, but it does show you should check what hosting platform you’re on, since the answer asks whether it’s Linux, Windows, or Java hosting.

Not in the case you described. If the PHP page only sends a redirect and no content, search engines follow the redirect and the final landing page is what gets indexed and credited. The original PHP URL itself has no SEO value in that setup.

If your PHP-generated main page actually returns normal content instead of only redirecting, the evidence here doesn’t say for sure whether it would be indexed, but it does say redirects made in PHP are treated the same as other redirects.

Yes, but only if Google can actually fetch the content behind it.

Google can index an AJAX-based PHP main page if the site is set up so Googlebot can receive the server-side version of each page. Simply having `index.php` with 5 internal pages, or using 301 redirects to `#!/page_Example`, is not enough by itself.

The guidance here is to:
- list the AJAX URLs in your sitemap, and
- make sure the server supports Google’s AJAX crawling method by handling the `_escaped_fragment_` parameter and serving the corresponding content.

If Google can’t load the AJAX content, it will only index the main page. Using “Fetch as Googlebot” would help verify whether Google can see the content.

Yes. The evidence suggests Google can index pages served as `index.php?module=test&param=1`, and it says the old idea that `.html` URLs were better is no longer believed to be true for Google. If you have very similar pages, use `rel="canonical"` so Google knows which one is the main version and your rank is not split.
