If the spam is manual, it’s hard to eliminate completely. Validation, captcha, math checks, and server-side checks may stop automated spam but not a person paid to submit it.

The best additional protection mentioned is a client-side timer: require the visitor to stay on the page for a set time, such as 1 minute, before the submit button becomes active. This can help block quick cut-and-paste submissions and some semi-automated spam.

Even then, it won’t stop all manual spam, so it’s more of a filter than a full fix.

Blocking 127.0.0.1 is not recommended just based on that alone. Seeing many requests from 127.0.0.1 usually suggests you have a cache/proxy setup like Varnish, or possibly another server-side issue, rather than normal visitors. It would be safer to investigate why local requests are showing up and check whether the server has been compromised or is making local requests itself.

This doesn’t directly answer the best anti-spam method for web forms, but the closest guidance here is: don’t rely on blocking that IP as a spam solution; first identify the source of the requests.

Blocking all comments from the same IP is not a good spam-defense system. IPs change over time, so you could delete legitimate older or future posts, and malicious flagging could unfairly affect real users.

Better options are tools built for this fight, like ReCAPTCHA or Akismet. If you want to build your own approach, require verified accounts and avoid automatic deletion. Let moderator review happen before removing anything. You can also slow spammers down by making posting less immediate and less anonymous.

A good remaining option is a plugin like Cyb that requires a minimum post count before users can post links. Pair that with restricted profile permissions so users with fewer than 5 posts can’t add URLs in their profile.

You can also consider:
- a waiting period plus a minimum number of prior posts before link posting is allowed
- a daily post limit set just below the number needed to start posting links

These measures tend to discourage spammers because they don’t like multiple-step requirements.

Check the site files for malicious code and remove it, especially main.php, its header and footer, thumb.php/Timthumb, and any index.php files. Then search all files for the same injected code and clean anything else found. After that, update WordPress to the latest version, update the theme/template, and update all plugins.

If your goal is to stop spam inquiries on the site, the provided guidance doesn’t directly cover that. The closest supported advice is to clean the injection first and then update everything, since the site was compromised.

Yes, changing URLs by removing “.php” can affect SEO because search engines may treat the pages as new URLs. Existing links, bookmarks, and indexed results can be disrupted unless you set up 301 redirects from the old .php URLs to the new URLs. That lets search engines transfer indexing and most link value to the new addresses.

Removing index.php is generally considered a better practice for SEO-friendly URLs, and the cited answer says you “don’t have to do it yourself” because plugins can do it. It does not say SEO is harmed by the change; rather, it suggests cleaner URLs are preferable.

So, based on this, changing from .php/index.php-style URLs to cleaner URLs is not indicated as a negative for SEO and may be beneficial. If you want the safest approach, use the existing routing/plugin support rather than manually changing URL structure.

Based on the provided info, using PHP includes themselves does not affect SEO, because PHP is processed on the server and Google only sees the resulting HTML.

It does not directly answer whether changing a URL from “.php” to a URL without “.php” affects SEO. The closest supported guidance is that search engines care about the HTML/content they receive, not how it was generated. If the content stays the same, the extension change alone is not indicated to affect SEO by this evidence.

A good approach is to keep the email address from being easily harvested by spambots: render it encoded and decode/display it with JavaScript after page load, or show it as an image. For the submission form, use a CAPTCHA or a similar anti-bot challenge. This won’t eliminate all spam, but it should cut down most automated submissions.

A practical approach is to make the user prove they’re human, measure how fast the form is filled out, or obfuscate the form fields in the HTML. CAPTCHA is the most effective of those, but it’s also the most annoying. Timing checks can block obvious bots, but bots can adapt. Obfuscation can help, especially if JavaScript populates field names later, but it also has limits. In practice, it’s a cat-and-mouse game, so no method is perfect.

A good approach is to filter the submissions themselves, not try to block the linked images via .htaccess. The evidence says .htaccess won’t help because those image requests don’t come from your server. Instead, add a filter that checks anonymous comments/submissions for .ru links and blocks them, or use a spam filter plugin like Akismet.

- set up DomainKeys
- set up SPF

To reduce spam, the evidence suggests hiding the email address through the web interface and using spam-prevention features in the contact form, such as bot traps, required preview, captcha, and disallowing HTML in messages. Don’t use a fake sender address; that strongly looks like spam. Use a real address on your own domain and set up DomainKeys and SPF for that domain. Also include an unsubscribe link. If mail is still landing in spam, check whether your sending IP or domain is listed on blacklist databases; if so, request a new shared IP or use a dedicated IP.

- If Gmail keeps classifying it as spam, the content or sending pattern may also be contributing.

Gmail is probably not flagging you because other domains share the same IP. The quoted line is a recommendation for your own bulk mail, not a warning about shared hosting.

Shared servers commonly send mail for multiple domains. The more likely causes are message content, recipients marking mail as spam, or the server IP having a poor reputation because another site on it has sent spam.

A good next step is to check your server IP reputation or blacklist status with services like senderscore.org or senderbase.org. If the IP is listed, the hosting provider may need to address it.

Check that your SPF and DomainKeys/DKIM are set up correctly and actually valid for the emails you send. A useful test is to send a message to spf-test@openspf.org; it will reject the mail and reply with details of the SPF test results. In one case, the issue was that the host was sending mail through a different server, so the configuration needed further tweaks. If Gmail is the only provider marking mail as spam, this is the closest concrete step supported here.

The most supported explanation is that Gmail is flagging that specific message because of email authentication or sending-path issues, not because all your mail is bad. A common cause is SPF or DomainKeys/DKIM being misconfigured or invalid for that message. Set up a proper SPF TXT record and sign outgoing mail with DKIM through Sendgrid. From the material here, the main performance factors are:
- non-blocking SMTP handling, so one slow DNS/SMTP target doesn’t stall everything
- how many recipient domains you’re sending to
- available bandwidth
- fast DNS responses if you host your own DNS
- reusing SMTP connections by sorting recipients by domain

It also suggests that encryption/authentication and packaging are usually minor costs compared with waiting on slow remote mail servers. Two mail servers with enough bandwidth may outperform one faster server.

This was caused by malformed headers in the email code, not by Gmail randomly rejecting specific recipients. In the accepted answer, two lines were duplicating header fields:

$headers .= "To: $nameto "
$headers .= "From: $namefrom "

That header duplication made Gmail reject some messages with the RFC 2822 error. The fix was to correct the header construction so those fields are not added twice.

It redirects `www.example.com` to `example.com` using a 301 redirect. The `.htaccess` rules check the host name, and if it matches `www.example.com`, they send the same path to `http://example.com/` instead. Place the `.htaccess` file in the site’s root directory.

“www” is usually just a subdomain, often used to name the web server. A site may work only with www if the DNS or server configuration is set up so that www.mysite.com points correctly but mysite.com does not.

If both names resolve to the same IP, the web server/vhost setup may be misconfigured. If they resolve differently, the DNS setup may be the issue.

People often include www because of long-standing Internet naming practice. It isn’t technically required.

WWW is not special in Google Analytics by itself. If `www.anothersite.com` uses the same Analytics tracking ID as `www.mysite.com`, Google can include that traffic in your reports too.

A server-side redirect from one site to another does not trigger client-side JavaScript, so no pageview is recorded from the redirected page. A JavaScript or Meta Refresh redirect can be tracked if Google Analytics loads before the redirect happens.

To avoid unwanted traffic, use filters to include only your own domains.

It doesn’t really matter for SEO between a folder-style URL and a filename-style URL. The important part is to make URLs short and descriptive for users.

For spaces in URLs, browsers will automatically encode them as %20 if the link is written properly. That makes spaces workable, but it’s not ideal for naming or linking files. The guidance here is to prefer renaming files to use hyphens/dashes instead of spaces.

This evidence does not address whether `+`, `_`, or `-` is best specifically.

For SEO, the main point is that Google needs to be able to fetch the asset. URL-encoded references are fine, and Googlebot can URL-decode them. The advice here is to always use proper URL encoding in your links so requests stay standard and don’t break.

For “+”, “_”, or “-”, this doesn’t provide a ranking difference. The only supported guidance is: use valid, standard-encoded URLs and make sure Google can access the files. The example notes no apparent ranking change for maintenance windows of 1–3 hours. For longer downtime, the safest guidance from this is still to use temporary status responses, not a permanent redirect.
503 everything is the best strategy, together with a Retry-After HTTP header. This is presented as the best way to handle planned site downtime so search engines are less likely to be affected.

Put this in the .htaccess on the old domain:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^www\.example\.com [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.example.com%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]

This redirects all requests from the old domain, including folders and subdomains, to the new domain while preserving the requested path. Replace example.com with your new domain. If the old and new domains point to the same server, the same .htaccess may be used.

Yes. That rule will 301 redirect everything on oldsite.org to the same path on http://newsite.com. It matches the host and preserves the requested path, so /page becomes /page on the new domain.

Blank lines and spacing in .htaccess generally don’t matter here. The key parts are RewriteEngine On, the RewriteCond for the old host, and the RewriteRule with [R=301,L].

If you want to redirect to a different path on the new site, you’d change the target URL accordingly.

The provided guidance says to use a permanent redirect from the old domain to the new one, and points to a page that explains how to do this with common web languages under “Redirect Old domain to New domain.” It also recommends reading Google’s site-move guidance for what to consider when moving a site.

It doesn’t give the exact redirect code itself, but it supports setting up a permanent redirect at the web/server level rather than just pointing both domains to the same DNS target.

Yes—this will redirect the old domain and any path like /folder, subdomains included, to the new domain, as long as the .htaccess is applied on the old domain:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^www\.newdomain\.com [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.newdomain.com%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]

If your old and new domains point to the same server, the same .htaccess can handle it. This covers all reachable URLs and sends them permanently to the new domain.

There’s no problem with keeping the old domains in Google Webmaster Tools if you still own them. The guidance given does not say you must delete the ccTLDs after redirecting.

It also notes that country-specific domains are generally favored over using subdomains on a single TLD, though your setup uses subdirectories, not subdomains.

So the closest supported answer is: keep the old domains in GWT if you still control them, and make the 301 redirects to the relevant new subdirectories.

Using paths with slashes is generally preferred for new sites because it encourages a clearer site hierarchy, which helps navigation and can improve how users and search engines understand the site. It can also help you think through routing and controller design earlier. Query-string parameters are still handled well by search engines, so they’re not “wrong,” but clean URLs are usually the better choice if you’re starting fresh.

If you want PHP to access the files, they generally must remain reachable on the server side; if they’re hidden by returning 404 to web requests, they may no longer be available the way you expect. The suggested fix is to put files that should only be used by PHP outside the web/http root.

If the files are meant for browsers too (images, CSS, etc.), they must stay accessible to clients, so you can’t truly hide them from HTTP while still serving them normally. Also, hiding a directory or returning 403/404 doesn’t add real security by itself.

Using shorter, meaningful directory names is generally preferred. The answer recommends keeping a simple structure like js, img, css, and lib rather than using single-letter names, which are too ambiguous, or longer names like styles and images, which are fine but less concise.

There’s no strong functional advantage beyond tidier URLs and a small byte savings in repeated references. The main guidance is to use names that are clear, consistent, and not overly abbreviated.

`www` is not automatic. If `http://example.com` works but `www.example.com` returns no results or doesn’t load, the likely issue is your DNS setup.

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www.example.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://example.com/$1 [R=301,L]

This makes both forms resolve consistently by sending `www` traffic to the non-www domain.

The likely cause mentioned is your robots.txt file. It shows:

That blocks all crawlers, including Google, from accessing your site. Remove that rule so Google can crawl your pages normally.

If indexing is still slow after that, the evidence doesn’t say more, but fixing robots.txt is the clearest first step supported here.

The guidance here favors subdirectories if you want the most reliable SEO benefit, because subfolders always share link/trust/ranking signals with the main site. Subdomains may or may not pass those signals.

Country-specific TLDs generally don’t get special ranking weight by themselves. A .cn site can rank in English results, and .us sites can be in Russian, Chinese, or Spanish.

What matters more is the locale used when publishing and branding/vanity. A country-specific domain can help signal a local presence, like a UK business using .co.uk. They can also be useful for organizing infrastructure, for example separate hostnames by country when using geo-based redirection.

So the closest guidance is: use multiple country-specific domains if you want local branding or operational separation; use one global domain if that fits your publishing and marketing goals.

Put the location block in an included file, then include it inside each server block. Nginx doesn’t allow `location` outside `server`, so this is the closest way to avoid repeating it.

Example included file:
`location ~* \.(png|jpg|jpeg|gif|ico)$ { expires 1y; }`

Then in each `server` block:
`include includes/gfx-expires-header.conf;`

Use Apache mod_rewrite before the request reaches Django/mod_wsgi. In the working example, two fixes were needed:

- Match the path with a leading slash: `^/modules\.php` not `^modules\.php`
- Stop Apache from appending the original query string by adding a trailing `?`

Working rule:
`RewriteEngine on`
`RewriteCond %{QUERY_STRING} sid=([0-9]+)`
`RewriteRule ^/modules\.php /news/story/%1/? [R=301,L]`

This redirects old URLs like `/modules.php?name=News&file=article&sid=600` to `/news/story/600/`.

- avoid unnecessary redirect chains
- make sure the page source contains the content and metadata
- avoid dubious markup like scripts after the closing body tag

If you only want URLs like `http://www.my-website.com/click-4559226-10388358`, the closest matching rule is:

`RewriteRule ^click\-([0-9]+)\-([0-9]+)$ http://www.newdomain.com/click-$1-$2?%{QUERY_STRING} [R=301,L]`

That keeps the two numeric parts and passes along the query string.

If you want to redirect the exact path plus everything after it, the broader rule shown is:

`RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.newdomain.com/$1 [R=301,L]`

The provided example only covers redirecting matching paths on the same pattern; it doesn’t explain handling more complex variations.

If you want URLs like /course-compilers instead of /course-compilers.html, use this in .htaccess:

RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME}.html -f
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ $1.html

This rewrites requests to the matching .html file if it exists, while avoiding directories. If you later restructure into folders like courses/compilers, you’d need to adjust the rewrite rule to match that layout.

As long as your main domain’s A record points to your hosting IP address, you can create as many subdomains as your host allows.

Websites use contact forms for a few practical reasons: they reduce spam, let messages be routed to different people or departments, and allow the site to change the receiving email without updating public contact details. Forms also work for users without an email address or email client, can attach site usage info automatically, and avoid typos in the recipient address.

So an email address can be enough for some sites, but a contact form gives the site more control and convenience.

That way Google should replace the HTTPS results with HTTP over time.

Changing from HTTP to HTTPS alone isn’t the issue here. In the provided case, Google wasn’t indexing the site well because the content was duplicated from another domain. Google was already showing the original site instead of the copy.

If you still have both HTTP and HTTPS versions accessible with the same content, that can confuse indexing. Remove duplicates and ensure Google sees only the preferred version.

If someone searches on Google over HTTPS, you may only get a referer like https://www.google.com/ without keywords. You could use that as a signal to redirect to your HTTPS site, but that’s only a workaround on your side.

So if you switch your site to HTTPS, Google search results won’t “sort themselves out” based on the search being HTTP vs HTTPS.

Google isn’t being “convinced” to list the HTTPS version here; the issue described is duplicate content. If you want your HTTPS site indexed, it needs to have unique content, and duplicate pages on the other domain should be removed. Google does not provide a way to make it list your HTTPS site only when the user searched on Google over HTTPS. You can’t rank HTTPS for HTTPS search and HTTP for HTTP search separately.

- keep the 301 redirects from HTTP to HTTPS in place

Google should handle it as the same domain, so there’s no need to use change of address. The https:// property will also let you use “Fetch as Google.”

- Use Graph by -> Hour
- Review visits for the hour you care about

- Report visitors per hour in standard reports, which gives volume by hour but not true concurrency.

If you need peak concurrent users historically, you’d need a different tool or service designed for that.

So you can’t calculate peak concurrent users for an hour from the hourly Audience Overview number alone; it only tells you total activity during that hour. To estimate peak concurrency, use the real-time report or a tool that records simultaneous active users over time.

Negative SEO is treated here as a real risk: it can involve black hat tactics like DDoS attacks, hacking, copying content, injecting bad links/content, removing backlinks, social engineering, and fake social profiles. Negative SEO appears to be possible, but its impact is inconsistent and not guaranteed. The cases cited include reports where sites believed they were harmed by bad backlinks, and also reports where lots of bad links did not hurt rankings.

If multiple page URLs show the same content, use rel="canonical" to tell search engines which URL is the primary one. That’s the simplest way to handle duplicate content from pagination, tag, index, or similar pages.

The behavior was likely caused by Google treating the inner quotation marks as query control characters, not just literal text. So the first query was effectively split into multiple quoted and unquoted parts, which can change ranking and return a different result set. When the quotes were removed, or when Google later reprocessed the query, Stack Overflow ranked first for all versions.

In short: the inner quotes altered how Google interpreted the search terms, and quoted vs unquoted searches can produce different results.

Stack Overflow questions appear quickly in Google mainly because each question has its own unique URL. The page template may be the same, but the URL includes the site, the question number, and often a text slug from the title. Google uses that unique URL to see each question as a separate page, even though the content is pulled from a database.

So it’s not that Google sees one page and guesses there are many questions; it sees many different URLs, each mapping to a different question.

Google appears to treat Stack Overflow and similar forum sites specially. In search results for discussion forums, Google shows extra details like dates and number of replies, which suggests it uses custom parsers for popular forum engines rather than a standard Stack Overflow microformat or schema.org Q&A markup. The evidence doesn’t say Stack Overflow does anything special itself; it only supports the idea that Google is extracting and displaying forum metadata quickly from those sites.

Bounce rate doesn’t mean only 15,000 users created the 86,000 page views. Visits and page views are different, and there isn’t a strict one-to-one relationship.

If the stats are measured consistently, each visit usually creates at least one page view. With a 54% bounce rate, about 54% of visits likely leave after that first page, while the remaining 46% view more pages. So 30,000 visits could still produce 86,000 page views.

Alexa ranking is relative to other sites, so your rank can get worse even if your traffic stays the same, if other sites improve faster or get more traffic.

Visits and pageviews are different, so there’s no exact 1:1 relationship. In the simplest case, each visit creates at least one pageview. With a 54% bounce rate, about 54% of visits leave after that first page, while the remaining 46% may generate additional pageviews.

So 30,000 visits can produce 86,000 pageviews; it does not mean only 15,000 users created them. The average would be about 2.87 pageviews per visit, and about 3.78 pages per non-bounce visit.

Alexa rank is relative, so your ranking can still drop if other sites are growing faster, even if your pageviews stay the same.

Visits count how many sessions occurred, pageviews count how many pages were viewed, and bounce rate is the share of visits that viewed only one page. So if pageviews per visit drops, bounce rate can rise. The example suggests a site slowdown or a change such as a JavaScript ad could affect how many pages people load and whether they leave after one page.

There likely isn’t a white paper for an Evernote-like service’s per-user bandwidth. The closest guidance is to estimate it yourself with a sample of real or target users.

A practical approach is:
- Recruit a small local group and more remote users.
- Survey their usage patterns: devices, purposes, notebooks, notes, how often they create/edit/share.
- For the local group, measure actual traffic with monitoring software.
- Segment users by behavior and extrapolate average monthly bandwidth from the sample.
- Scale that estimate up to your projected user base, such as 2.5 million users.

It’s hard to estimate bandwidth from the information given. The best approach is to test the app with a smaller group, like 10, 50, or 100 users, measure the bandwidth used, then scale that up to estimate 10,000 users.

The real requirement also depends on what the app does, whether all 10,000 users are active at the same time every day, and how much growth or file storage you expect.

For hosting, the choice depends on whether you want a US server or another region, your budget, whether disk usage will grow, and whether you want managed or unmanaged hosting.

Use the first formula as a starting point:

(Average daily visitors × average page views per visitor × average page size)
+ (average daily file downloads × average file size)
then multiply by 31 and a fudge factor.

The main caveat is that it can be far off if your site uses lots of external images, client-side caching, or AJAX that loads only small amounts of data. Also, “average page views” should mean the average number of pages each visitor views, not total site page views.

So, estimate with that formula, then adjust for how your application actually delivers content.

Google doesn’t treat subdomains and subdirectories as fundamentally different for duplicate-content purposes. If the same tip appears on multiple activity pages, that’s not automatically a problem; Google will generally try to keep one version in results and filter the others.

The main risk is if too much of a page is repeated across subdomains. The more duplicated content a page has, the more likely it is to be treated as duplicate content and filtered out. To reduce that risk, make sure each page has a substantial amount of unique content, not just shared tips.

So you’re not necessarily hurt by using subdomains, but if you want to minimize duplication issues, focus on making each page meaningfully unique.

A standard SSL certificate from a trusted CA will still be trusted by browsers and will not, by itself, cause warning messages just because it isn’t EV. EV mainly means the issuing CA has done more identity checking; it doesn’t make the technical encryption much more secure.

It does not fully prevent MITM attacks, but it makes silent MITM much harder. Security still depends on correct SSL use and avoiding insecure mixed content. If your goal is basic trusted HTTPS for a website, a non-EV certificate from a recognized CA is generally sufficient.

Based on this, buying through a reseller can be fine if the certificate and verification process are the same. In the resolved case, the buyer said the verification and everything else still went through the original certificate seller; only payment was handled by the reseller.

So the supported guidance is: if the reseller is reputable and provides the same certificate/validation process, there was no difference noted in practice. The evidence does not compare trust levels, browser behavior, or whether a more expensive host-issued certificate is better for your exact use case.

If you only need to encrypt traffic for a site that collects general personal information, a basic certificate is usually enough. Those are typically easy to get: the issuer verifies your domain by email and then issues the cert.

If the site is e-commerce or handles credit card/bank details, you should get a higher-validation certificate that verifies your company identity, which costs more and takes more checks.

The main thing to compare is browser compatibility, especially older browsers as well as newer ones like Chrome. RapidSSL or GeoTrust are suggested as reasonable starting points, and your hosting or registrar may offer similar certificates.

A non-EV SSL certificate still helps protect data in transit and makes silent MITM attacks much harder, but it does not guarantee protection if SSL is implemented incorrectly or if the site loads insecure resources.

It should not show browser warnings just because it is not EV, as long as the issuing certificate authority is trusted by the client browser and the certificate is installed correctly. EV mainly adds stronger identity verification, not much extra technical security.

In the provided material, the only clear meaning of `//` is the standard pair after `http:` in `http://example.com`. The thread itself is about a different case: a double slash in the path, like `http://example.com/search//filter2/...`. It says that this seemed to work in browsers tested and showed no server-side errors, but no recorded answer explains what the double slash means or whether it has downsides.

So, based on this, the closest supported guidance is: the double slash in the path appears to be treated as just part of the URL and may work, but the material does not define its meaning.

A leading slash means the path is rooted at the site’s top level, not relative to the current page. So `/somedir/somepage.html` on `www.mysite.com` becomes `www.mysite.com/somedir/somepage.html`.

Without the leading slash, the URL is treated as relative to the current directory, so on `/cream-cakes/` a link like `blah.html` would go to `/cream-cakes/blah.html`.

Using `/` is generally safer if you want the link to keep working when the site structure changes.

`rel="canonical"` can be used on paginated pages to point to the main or “view all” version when that is the version you want search engines to show. It’s not limited only to exact duplicate content. In the example given, page 2 also changes by sort order, so it’s reasonable to canonicalize those component pages to the main question URL.

So, if you have paginated or sorted component pages, use canonical to indicate the preferred version. Don’t use it just to hide genuinely different content; the tag is best for consolidating signals when pages are part of the same content set.

Use rel="canonical" on a link element to indicate the preferred URL for a page when there are duplicate or very similar URLs. The supported link relation values are listed in official registries, including the microformats rel registry and the IANA link relations list.

A practical way to use it is:
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/preferred-page">

The evidence does not provide detailed rules for when to use canonical, but it does show that canonical is a recognized rel value and that the authoritative lists of rel types are the microformats registry and IANA link relations.

Google has indexed the site, so this may be less about indexing and more about Google not yet reflecting the updated homepage title/description. The advice given is that JavaScript may be interfering, and some Google fetch features have also been problematic.

If by “mobile app” you mean an App Store app, the provided answer says that would not count as duplicate content. If you mean a mobile website such as m.yoursite.com, then it can be treated as duplicate content.

No. The guidance supports that forcing www is not only about SEO or duplicate-content concerns.

A key non-SEO reason is performance: if cookies are set on the root domain, browsers may send them with every request, including requests for static assets. That adds unnecessary overhead. Restricting cookies to a subdomain like www.example.com and serving static content from another subdomain can improve page speed.

So for a corporate/franchise site, using a consistent authoritative domain convention can help both SEO consistency and web performance.

A supported option is to use a rel="canonical" tag on the duplicate pages so search engines treat one version as the preferred copy. If that’s not suitable, rewrite the content so it becomes unique. Another approach is to keep the duplicate content for users but prevent indexing with meta robots “noindex, follow.” If possible, linking to the original author’s page is also a sensible alternative.

If you recently set up the 301 redirect, you’ll likely need to wait—Google can take time to recrawl and update the description shown in search results.

Make sure the `www` version has a relevant meta description, because that’s the one Google should eventually use after it recrawls the site. Re-crawling in Webmaster Tools may not update it immediately.

To get Google to update changed pages, set up 301 redirects from each old URL to its new URL. That tells Google the pages have moved and helps transfer signals from old links to the new pages.

Also submit an XML sitemap in Google Webmaster Tools, and make sure you have an HTML sitemap as well. Using the sitemap alone may not be enough if the old URLs still exist without redirects.

You can’t force Google to use your meta description. Google decides whether to show it, and it may instead use page content relevant to the search query.

To encourage Google to use your description, make sure it is:
- unique for each page
- an accurate summary of that page’s content
- reasonably short, since Google typically displays about 150 characters

If there’s no meta description, Google may use a snippet from the page text instead. If you don’t want a snippet shown at all, you can use:

<meta name="robots" content="nosnippet">

Google may be crawling your site, but the search index and cached results can update on different schedules. Even after you remove robots.txt/noindex issues, it can take from minutes to about a week for the title or description to refresh in search results. If Google is already crawling your pages and your title tags are correct, the closest guidance here is to wait and be patient.

Google’s cache and search indexing aren’t updated together. Google may have the latest cached page but still show the old meta description in search results until its indexing system refreshes that data. Resubmitting the page doesn’t necessarily speed this up. Updates can take days or even weeks depending on how important Google considers the site. The closest guidance here is to wait for Google to recrawl and reindex the page; the accepted answer also points to Google’s webmaster forums for further help.

No. The URL path does not have to match the page’s title.

A page can have a short, stable URL and a different, longer title. The example given is YouTube, where the URL is an ID-based link and the title is descriptive. So if Google shows a title that doesn’t match your page’s `<title>`, that mismatch alone is not a problem.

This does not cover how to get Google to show a specific title, only that the URL and title do not need to match.

Google may ignore the exact contents of your `<title>` tag and use other page text instead. In the example, it appears Google couldn’t create a title from the Danish in the title tag, so it used the page’s `<h1>` text, which is why the search result showed a different title and seemed to show it twice.

The closest fix suggested is to provide a title in English when submitting to google.com, and consider building multilingual versions of the site if you don’t already have them.

Google may keep showing an old title for some time, even after the page has been updated and crawled. The supported remedy here is mainly to wait. Google can also rewrite titles in search results based on the search query, sometimes preferring an older title if it seems more relevant to the searched keywords.

The evidence doesn’t support that adding an alt tag for the logo would trigger the title change.

Yes. The guidance here says text placed only in the title attribute/tag is not indexed by search engines in the way you want. Google also needs readable HTML content on the page, and you should use alt text for images too.

So if your site’s content is mostly in image titles and not in visible text or descriptions, that can prevent proper crawling/understanding. The closest fix supported here is to add regular HTML text that visitors can read, and use alt attributes for images rather than relying on title text alone.

Google can rewrite your page title in search results even when the <title> tag is correct. Since 2012, Google has said it uses many signals to choose the title shown to users, and may generate an alternative title if it thinks that works better for the query. It also uses page content and references to the page on the web, not just the title tag.

So in your case, “sitename: blah blah blah” can be Google’s chosen display title, not proof that the title tag wasn’t crawled. It may still be using your title tag as one signal. If you want, I can suggest ways to reduce title rewriting.

If you can’t edit .htaccess on Yahoo shared hosting, the workaround shown is to handle it in PHP before any output: check `$_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"]`, and if it is `/index.php`, send a redirect with `header('Location: http://myapp.com/');`.

Another possibility mentioned is using JavaScript to change the URL, but PHP redirect is the cleaner option. The answer also notes this can be done in Yahoo Stores, but not in the shared hosting setup described.

There isn’t a way to force Yahoo Answers–style rich results in Google. Google may show those snippets when its algorithms decide they improve the search result, often using structured data to help understand the page.

The closest guidance supported here is to add microdata/structured data to your Q&A pages, so search engines can identify the question, answers, and related details more easily. But even with that, display is not guaranteed.

The thread only shows one suggestion: “Try DreamHost.” It does not mention a hosted version of Yahoo! Answers or any broader comparison. If you’re looking for a free web hosting service to show temporary beta versions of Drupal sites, DreamHost is the only option supported by this thread.

Yes—based on the evidence, TinyMCE is a common WYSIWYG/graphical editor used in PHP-based CMSs like Drupal and Joomla. If you’re looking for a visual editor instead of working directly with code, TinyMCE is the closest supported recommendation here.

If Google crawls a `nav.php` file that isn’t meant to be a page, the links inside it may be wrong because `$main_url` is blank there. That can create crawl errors, but a 404 is a correct response for a non-existent or unintended URL.

The closest fix supported here is to stop Google from crawling the folder that contains reusable files like `nav.php`, for example with `robots.txt`. Also make sure only the intended `nav.php` is included in pages, and avoid leaving extra accessible copies of it in other folders.

So: different IPs alone won’t make SEO better, and using the same IP does not automatically cause a penalty. The more important point is that backlink schemes are increasingly ineffective; better SEO comes from good content and legitimate, independent links.

Dedicated IP addresses should not improve SEO. The answer says IP addresses are irrelevant for SEO; what matters is having unique, non-cloned content. Google can detect duplicate content and may treat many domains promoting one company as a site farm, even if they have different content.

Dropping IE6 lets you use several CSS features IE6 doesn’t support, including child selectors, adjacent and general sibling selectors, chained class selectors, attribute selectors, descendant selectors after :hover, chained pseudo-classes, :hover on non-anchor elements, :first-child, virtual dimensions with absolute positioning, min/max height and width, transparent border colors, position: fixed, and background-attachment: fixed beyond the root element.

This is not a complete list, so it’s safest to test the specific CSS and JavaScript features you want to use rather than assuming everything modern is available.

It depends entirely on your user base. If you support organizations with old computers or locked-down systems, you may need to keep IE6 support for a while. If your audience is more cutting-edge, IE6 support is less necessary and you can drop it sooner.

A practical approach is to let the site degrade gracefully in IE6: keep it usable, but allow unsupported features to fail gracefully. Dropping IE6 will affect some users, so the real question is whether those users matter for your project.

IE7 is expected to become the next “IE6,” but it’s not fully out the door yet. On the mobile page:

The thread doesn’t provide a definitive rule or legal line. It only shows the concern: using a trademarked term in a domain name, even for a noncommercial blog like “youtubepuppies.com,” may raise legal or other issues, and the asker was wondering whether permission from the brand owner would help. The closest guidance supported here is to be cautious when a domain includes a trademark, especially a well-known brand name, even if the site is small or noncommercial. You can display ads on your site, but the risky part is using a domain that contains a trademarked term to talk about that trademark owner’s product/service or competitors. If the trademark is in a completely different business, the risk may be lower, and in Germany the branch of trade matters more, so similar names can sometimes coexist. But the safest takeaway is: if you have a bad feeling, be cautious, because even if you might win, it can still be expensive.

It also notes that some “private” registrars may still release your information with little pressure, so privacy is not guaranteed.

What it doesn’t fully cover is trademark-specific risk. For that, the closest supported guidance is to avoid false registration details and be aware that anonymity services can have legal and ownership consequences.

You can tell Google to target a geographic area using the Geographic Target setting in Google Webmaster Tools. That can help your site be treated as region-specific in search results.

If the site is already country-specific but you want to focus on a smaller district or region, the only extra suggestion here is to make your address visible on the site, such as in the footer, so search engines can see it often. Use Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. After registering your site with both, they can track average position, impressions, click-through rate, and other metrics by keyword. The same answer says Google does read alt attributes, so if you want descriptive image text for SEO and accessibility, use a meaningful alt attribute instead. The title attribute can be omitted if you’re concerned about it being unrelated, and keyword stuffing it could have negative effects.

Google may still be showing an old, cached version of the page title if the <title> tag was changed after indexing. In that case, the updated title should appear after Google re-indexes the page.

This only addresses page <title> tags, not title attributes. The provided information does not explain why title attributes would or wouldn’t be indexed.

Search engines generally don’t index or use title attributes to judge keyword relevance. The title attribute is meant to give users extra, advisory information, often shown as a tooltip or read by assistive technology.

So repeating your heading in a title attribute usually won’t help SEO. It may even look like keyword stuffing and risk over-optimization penalties.

If you use a title attribute, make it meaningful and useful to users, not just a keyword variation.

<!--[if lte IE 7]>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="ie7-or-less.css" type="text/css" />
<![endif]-->

This targets only Internet Explorer 7 and earlier. The provided material doesn’t give broader “best ways” for all cross-browser CSS, only this IE-specific method.

The best-supported choice is the cleaner, more relevant URL. A URL like domain.com/apple is preferred over one that includes only a number, because SEO depends on more than just the URL, and relevance matters. If you need an ID for lookup, it may be better to include a meaningful word in the URL rather than just the number. Between the two formats you gave, domain.com/[id]/title and domain.com/title/[id].html, the guidance only supports making the URL SEO-friendly and relevant, not choosing one of these exact patterns. If possible, favor the format that keeps the title prominent and avoids unnecessary numbers.

Both formats can work well for search engines. The evidence says the best example is an action/id/slug-title style URL, but it also says truthfully both are optimized. So neither format is clearly better from an SEO standpoint based on this. If you want the closest supported recommendation, use a clean, readable URL with the id included somewhere, such as domain.com/[id]/title.

The first format is better for SEO and for users: domain.com/[id]/title. 

The supported guidance says the first style is more SEO-friendly than a query-string style, and that you can still make URLs look like the first while handling them like the second using URL rewriting.

So between your two options, domain.com/[id]/title is the closer match to the more SEO-friendly choice.

Affiliate links are not inherently bad for SEO, and the answer does not support removing all of them to avoid a penalty. It says affiliate links can be used, and a legal way to keep them out of indexing is to put them on noindexed pages. It also says cloaking affiliate links is considered legit in that context. What it does support is separating affiliate stuff from indexable content if you want to reduce mixing monetized links with pages you want ranked. It does not give a direct Google rule, and it does not confirm that a single Amazon affiliate link on a review page would cause a penalty.

The guidance here is that adding many links to sites of uncertain quality could risk your own ranking if those links are followed. The suggested safeguard is to use the nofollow attribute on outgoing links, which is described as the proper way to avoid that risk.

So, if you’re linking to lots of customer sites and can’t vouch for their quality, the closest supported advice is to mark those links nofollow. Without that, the cited answer says you could experience a penalty.

Linking to a site from the same server/IP is not known to hurt SEO. The guidance here says your rankings do not go down just because links come from the same IP, and only Google knows how much value such a link gets. It also suggests there are many variables involved, but no harm is implied. If you want to be cautious, adding rel="nofollow" would avoid passing link value, but based on this information, same-server links themselves are not bad.

The title/slug in the URL is mainly for readability and usability, but it can also help SEO in a few ways.

A keyword-rich slug can:
- make the URL more descriptive to users
- act like anchor text when people paste the raw link elsewhere
- improve click-through rate if the searched keyword appears in the URL

The title part is also useful because it appears in the browser title bar, bookmarks, and can be reused by other websites. The numeric ID is there to uniquely identify the page; the slug adds human and search-engine friendly context.

If each URL corresponds to a genuinely different page with enough unique content, that’s generally fine. Google can understand keywords in both the path and the query string, so switching to query parameters doesn’t really change how the keywords are treated.

That said, stuffing lots of keywords into URLs isn’t necessary and can look spammy. A shorter, cleaner URL with 3–4 relevant terms is the closest guidance supported here. The evidence also says these kinds of URLs are acceptable for categorized pages, especially when they represent distinct results rather than a single page with only minor variations.

Use a rewrite rule that maps a clean path segment to the query parameter, like:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^([a-zA-Z0-9_-]+)$ user.php?username=$1
RewriteRule ^([a-zA-Z0-9_-]+)/$ user.php?username=$1

This covers URLs like `/boats_for_sale` by rewriting them to a script with a parameter. It does not show a complete generic solution for hiding all query strings, but it’s the closest guidance provided: define rewrite patterns that capture the path and pass it internally as a query value.

Google Analytics calculates bounce rate as the percentage of single-page visits out of total visits for a given dimension. In other words, if a session contains only one pageview and no further interaction, it counts as a bounce.

Google Analytics bounce rate is based on sessions where the user leaves after a single interaction. The evidence says you can change what counts toward bounce rate by using Event Tracking on a specific click action and setting that click event so it is not included in the bounce rate calculation. It also implies that clicks to an external site and simple exits may otherwise be mixed together in the bounce rate. It does not explain the full formula Google uses, but it does show that tracked events can prevent a particular action from being treated as a bounce.

A site is not penalized just for having functionality or content that exists elsewhere. The key question is whether it adds something meaningfully different or better.

If your site copies other content, or is just a thin version of what many other sites already do, that can be a problem. But if it has its own value, such as unique insight, better navigation, better prices, better service, a different game variation, or a focused product selection, that can count as original enough.

Google is not said to automatically refuse indexing just because similar pages already exist. The guidance here is to ask whether users would miss your site, or whether it answers something only it can answer.

The supported fix in the thread is to add a robots meta noindex tag to the old pages:

<meta name="robots" content="noindex">

If a domain is already registered, you can usually start with a WHOIS lookup to find the current holder and contact them directly.

Also make sure you meet any registrant requirements, since some country-code domains require a physical presence in that country. If you don’t qualify, you may not be able to register it yourself, even if a seller exists.

If the domain name was trademarked before you registered it, or it was already in use and popular when you bought it and was trademarked later, the company may be able to claim it and take it away. If the trademark was filed after you purchased the domain, and the name was already in use or popular, then they generally cannot take it away as long as you do not use the domain in a way that relates to them or their business.

If you want the closest guidance from this: ownership depends on trademark timing and how you use the domain.

If you didn’t renew the registration for the domain, you generally lost the right to use it, and it could be released and registered by someone else. Domain registration is not the same as owning a physical object; it’s more like a time-limited right to use the name.

If you were the registered name holder and paid the renewal fees, you would typically need to check with the registrar about whether the domain expired, whether there was a grace period, or whether it was transferred.

If you want a domain that someone else already owns, the usual path is to contact the current registrant and try to buy it from them. For .by domains specifically, the guidance here is only that you can try registrars such as 101domain, and you should verify any registrant requirements first.

Some country-code domains require a physical presence in that country, such as residence or an office, before you can register them. If you can’t meet those requirements, you may not be able to register the domain even if it becomes available.

If the domain is already registered by someone else, you generally can’t just register it again. The closest path depends on why you want it back:

- If the domain contains your company trademark and the registrar is in the U.S., you may be able to reclaim it under the Anticybersquatting Consumer Protection Act.
- If it’s a generic domain and you did not trademark it, then you likely can’t take it back through that route.

So the answer is: you usually need to buy it from the current owner or pursue a trademark-based claim if applicable.

Use a robots meta tag on that page, not robots.txt. The setting you want is `noindex,follow`: the robot can read/crawl the page and follow links from it, but it won’t index the page content.


If you block the page in robots.txt, crawlers may not access it at all, so they may not discover the links on it.

robots.txt can disallow crawling of a folder, but the supported workaround for allowing one file is to separate it from the blocked files. Since there is no “Allow” field in the described setup, the simplest approach is to put all files you want blocked into a separate directory, such as “stuff,” and keep the one file you want crawled in the directory above it. That avoids blocking the file while still preventing crawling of the rest of the folder.

To prevent robots from crawling or indexing, the standard approach is robots.txt, which asks robots not to crawl or index certain pages on your site.

If you’re trying to use a Robots META tag, it belongs in the head of the document, not inside a div in the body. Putting something like `NAME="ROBOTS" CONTENT="NOINDEX, NOFOLLOW"` inside a div will not be interpreted as a robots instruction and will also invalidate your HTML.

URLs beginning with “www2” are usually just subdomains, like “www1.” They often exist because the site uses wildcard DNS, so many subdomains can point to the same service. In older setups, “www1,” “www2,” etc. were also used for simple load balancing, with different subdomains mapping to different physical servers. This is less common now, but it still appears on some sites.

If URLs begin with www2, they’re usually treated as a separate subdomain. The closest guidance here is to redirect them to your main domain if you don’t use those subdomains. For Apache, the example shown is:

RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^(www2|2|anothersite.com)\.(.+)$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://%2/$1 [R=301,L]

This helps send traffic and backlinks from www2.example.com to example.com. The evidence also says Google may index them even if they return 5xx errors. If you actually have content on such subdomains, you could run into duplicate-content issues.

New HTML5 elements themselves don’t automatically improve search ranking. The useful part is that they can make content easier for a search engine to understand if the engine supports those semantics.

Switching from valid HTML 4.01 to valid HTML5 should not change rankings by itself. If both versions are properly marked up and the links aren’t broken, there’s no expected ranking impact from the markup change alone.

So a complete update is more likely to be neutral or slightly helpful, not harmful, provided it’s done cleanly.

- In that view, add a Custom Filter to Exclude Mobile? traffic
- Add another Custom Filter to Exclude Tablet? traffic

A likely explanation is that some of the “visits” are bots or very short hits. Also, Google Analytics counts returning visitors within 30 minutes as the same visitor, so visitor counts can look lower than expected. Checking Traffic Sources may help identify suspicious sources generating those visits.

Use mod_rewrite on domain.com. The example given is:

RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://example.com/subfolder/index.php [L,QSA]

This matches any request on domain.com and sends it to example.com/subfolder/index.php. L stops further rewriting, and QSA preserves the query string, so something like domain.com?id=cow keeps the ?id=cow part.

The practical difference is that a dedicated server gives you exclusive use of the hardware, while a VPS gives you root access on a shared physical machine.

So from your point of view:
- Dedicated: all CPU, memory, and disk I/O are yours.
- VPS: those resources may be shared with other customers, and performance can vary depending on overselling and host quality.

VPSes are often cheaper because providers can pack multiple virtual machines onto one server, assuming not everyone uses full resources at once.

If your workload is not heavy on disk I/O, a VPS can be perfectly fine. Quality VPS providers that limit overselling cost more, but can perform more consistently.

A hosting package gives you basic site features like uploading files, creating databases, and installing common software, but you share disk and CPU with others and can’t freely change the server software.

A virtual private server behaves like its own server, but it shares the physical machine with other VPSs. It has limits on memory and CPU, and you can install and configure software much more freely.

A managed dedicated server is a real server used only by you.

For ASP.net and MS SQL Server, the choice depends on how much control and resources you need. If you need more control over ASP and SQL Server, a VPS or dedicated server fits better than a basic hosting package.

No—by default, SSL certificate verification covers only the name it was issued for. If your certificate is for www.mydomain.com, users going to mydomain.com will get a mismatch warning.

The standard fix is to redirect http://mydomain.com to https://www.mydomain.com, so everyone uses one canonical host. It’s also possible to get a certificate that covers more than one name, and that is supported in modern browsers.

There’s no difference between `http://example.com/` and `http://example.com` for a homepage URL. The trailing slash does matter in some cases for links into a directory, but for the root homepage these two forms are equivalent. There’s no specific rule that says you must always add or avoid the final `/`; the main advice is to be consistent in your own URLs.

A trailing slash historically suggested a directory, while no slash suggested a file. Today it’s mostly obsolete.

For SEO, the main point is consistency: use either the slash version or the non-slash version everywhere. Mixing both can make the same page look like duplicate content.

So the difference is mostly URL structure, not SEO ranking. Keep internal links consistent, and avoid linking to both `http://example.com/page/` and `http://example.com/page`.

From the provided answer, the main point is that an international domain itself may not make much difference to rankings. Search engines are said to care more about actual page content and social presence than the domain name.

So a likely pitfall is assuming that simply changing to an international domain, like .es, will automatically improve SEO worldwide. The strongest guidance here is to focus on content relevance and social presence rather than relying on the domain extension alone.

A main pitfall is assuming duplicate content across regions will automatically hurt SEO. The guidance here says duplicate content is not a problem for multiple geo-targets using the same language.

If you use subfolders for different geo-targets, add each subfolder in Google Webmaster Tools and specify targeting there. You can also use `<html lang="...">` and `hreflang` links to indicate language versions, but those are for language, not geo-targeting with the same language.

So the key SEO risk is poor international setup: not telling Google which folders target which regions/languages.

The evidence doesn’t cover internationalizing a website or SEO pitfalls specific to that. It only suggests a general SEO consideration: guest blogging may provide backlinks and some reputation, but the benefit depends on the host site’s rules and traffic, and you should be clear about your goal. If your aim is backlinks, other link-building methods may be just as effective; if it’s exposure or feedback, a highly trafficked site may help.

Use Google Webmaster Tools’ “Fetch as Googlebot” feature. That lets you test whether Google can reach the pages from its own servers and with the Googlebot user agent, which can reveal if the issue is connectivity or user-agent related rather than a general site outage. If your pages load for you but still get reported as 404s and won’t index, this is the closest supported next step from the evidence.

Use Google Webmaster Tools’ Health > Fetch as Google on one of the URLs marked “Access Denied.” If it fetches successfully and returns 200 OK, Google should re-visit the page and the URL can be submitted to the index. If it still returns 403 only for Google, the issue is likely your server configuration, and you’ll need to find why it is denying Googlebot access.

If the 404s have already been fixed on your site, you need to mark those errors as fixed in Google Webmaster Tools. After that, Google will stop reporting them unless it finds the same 404s again. If they keep appearing in Webmaster Tools, it means Google is still detecting those errors somewhere on the site.

If those old URLs now return a 4xx/5xx status, Google may keep trying them for months, and Search Console can keep updating the “Detected” date even after the bug is fixed. The documented guidance here is that 400 and 405 are generally treated like other 4xx errors, and a 401 Unauthorized may be more appropriate for pages only visible to signed-in users.

So, if the URLs are truly obsolete or should not be accessible, using the correct status code matters more than removing the error entries. I can’t confirm from this alone whether “safe to remove” applies to your specific 404s, but Google’s crawl-error list can lag behind reality.

Yes, if those old URLs are no longer meant to exist, you can remove them or leave them as 404s. The guidance here is to either 301 redirect them to the relevant new page, or to the home page if there’s no close match.

The main point is that crawlers will eventually stop requesting the old pages. You should be more concerned with human visitors hitting broken links.

If there’s a chance you may need some of those URLs later, that’s not a problem by itself; just don’t reuse them casually if they now return something different.

If those old URLs truly no longer exist and there isn’t a relevant replacement, yes, a 404 is acceptable and they should eventually drop out of the index faster than blocked pages. Use 301 redirects for any pages that have a clear new equivalent or you can meaningfully preserve. A custom 404 page is also recommended for user experience. If you can, keep a useful redirect for every page you can save; otherwise let the obsolete ones return 404.

A domain that only redirects is not the best way to get it indexed. The guidance here says it’s better not to redirect the old domain until the new site is ready. Keep the old domain active while you build the new one, then use a 301 redirect from old-domain.com to new-domain.com when the new site is ready. If you redirect to a temporary folder first, search engines may index that folder and you’ll have to clean up that traffic later.

If a new domain just 301 redirects to the main site, it generally won’t appear separately in search results. A 301 tells Google the page has permanently moved, so the redirected URL is expected to drop from the SERPs. The destination page should not be harmed if the new domain has no bad history.

A 302 may keep the old URL in the SERPs, but the evidence says you’d first need to put content on that domain and get it indexed, and it’s not recommended. So the closest supported answer is: no, a new domain that only redirects is not likely to be indexed as its own result.

Yes, search engines can still index the main domain or specific URLs if only the homepage is being redirected.

The redirect rule shown only matches the home page (`/`), so deeper URLs on the main domain can still be crawled and indexed. To redirect the whole domain to the new site, the rule should redirect all paths, not just the root.

A pattern like this is supported by the evidence:
`RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://subdomain.website.com$1 [R=301,L]`

So if a new domain just redirects to the main site, indexing depends on whether all URLs are redirected or only the homepage.

A 301 permanent redirect to a different domain works like other 301s: search engines associate the old URL with the new one, pass links and PageRank to the new URLs with a small loss, and eventually replace the old URLs in search results.

So if every page on the old domain is mapped to the corresponding page under the new domain/subdirectory, the SEO should generally carry over in the same way.

A 301 redirect passes most SEO value, but each extra 301 can lose a small amount of trust and authority. So if you’re redirecting to a different site/domain, the best practice is a direct one-to-one 301 from the old URL to the final destination, with no extra redirect steps.

Google should still index the new destination over time, but chaining redirects is slightly suboptimal. It’s worth checking the final response to make sure only one 301 is happening.

A 301 redirect is the right approach. Redirect each old URL to the matching page on the new domain, and search engines should treat the new URL as the permanent one and transfer incoming links to it.

This can help SEO because consolidating content under one domain creates a stronger internal linking structure and clearer site hierarchy. What it covers is moving pages from one domain to another in a way that preserves as much search value as possible.

Use headings to describe each page’s actual content. The main heading should generally contain the page’s main theme, which can be the page title or a variation of it. If a static H1 is relevant to every page and users can add H2 subheadings for the specific content, that may be enough, but that’s unlikely for every page. In general, changing the H1 based on what’s on the page is the better approach for SEO.

Heading tags like `<h1>` and `<h2>` do matter for SEO, but they do not make a “big” difference by themselves. They are a ranking factor, and they should be used properly.

Best practice:
- Use only one `<h1>` per page
- Follow with `<h2>` and `<h3>` as needed
- Treat them like a table of contents for the page

Used correctly, they help both users and search engines understand what your content is about.

A keyword in the domain name has only minor significance for SEO. Based on the answer provided, the other site is likely ranking ahead for other reasons, such as the number and quality of backlinks pointing to it. Having 30 backlinks is not necessarily enough, especially if they are low-quality or not indexed by Google. One strong backlink from an important site can be worth more than many weak links.

Changing your page URL or creating a subdomain would not be expected to solve the issue by itself. The evidence supports focusing on improving backlink quality and overall SEO rather than relying on the domain name.

Yes. A page on winecorp.com.au can outrank a keyword domain like perthwinefactory.com.au for the same keyword. Domain keywords are only one ranking factor, and they do not guarantee top placement. Rankings depend on many other factors, and if the keyword is competitive, a year may still not be long enough to see major changes. The practical guidance is to keep improving your optimization and be patient.

The thread doesn’t provide an answer. It only describes a need: a tool or service where you enter a domain and see which keywords it ranks for in Google SERPs, including positions. Based on that, the closest guidance is to use an SEO rank-tracking or keyword research tool that supports domain-based organic keyword discovery. Based on the provided answer, having different domains does not seem to make much of a difference for rankings, especially if they simply redirect to your main site. The guidance given is that search engines care more about actual page content and social presence than the domain name itself.

It doesn’t directly address multiple redirecting domains specifically, but the closest supported conclusion is that the impact on search rankings is likely minimal compared with content quality and presence.

Yes, multiple redirects can have an impact. The guidance here says Google has confirmed a small amount of trust and authority is lost for every 301 redirect. One redirect is usually fine, two is only slightly suboptimal, but three or more can become risky. If possible, set up a direct one-to-one 301 redirect from each old domain/page to the final main domain URL rather than chaining redirects.

Yes, it can have an impact. The provided guidance says that serving the same content on multiple domains can hurt SEO because Google may treat it as duplicate content and choose one site as the authoritative version. It also recommends using 301 permanent redirects so Google understands the content has moved. If the domains are only redirecting to your main domain, that’s the safer setup than letting multiple domains serve the same content directly.

If the exact domain is taken, the suggested SEO-friendly alternatives are to add a secondary keyword, use a synonym, add an “s” or other applicable suffix, add “the” or another applicable prefix, use an alternate TLD like .net or .co, or use a dash if the domain has two words.

If you mean an add-on domain specifically for better SEO, this evidence doesn’t address that directly; it only gives naming alternatives when your preferred domain is unavailable.

Use a 301 redirect from the add-on/short domain to the main domain. That sends users to the main site and tells search engines to index only the main URL, so the second domain won’t show up in search results.

You need both.

A CNAME is the DNS record that makes www.example.com resolve to your server, so browsers can find it. A rewrite or redirect rule on the server tells visitors who use example.com to go to www.example.com instead.

For standalone WordPress, the closest guidance supported here is to use DNS for the www host and a server-side redirect so one canonical domain is used.

A 301 redirect from an old domain to a new one may temporarily pass some value like indexed age or “link juice,” but Google is expected to treat this as manipulation if it’s just link spamming. The benefit is likely to fade as the new site is evaluated on its own merits.

So buying abandoned domains mainly to gain link juice is not a reliable long-term technique. If the old domains have real traffic, redirecting them could help that traffic. For lasting results, the supported guidance is to improve content quality and earn links from authoritative, related sites.

It may not be a good technique if your goal is link juice/PageRank. The best-supported guidance here is that expired domains may not produce the effect you expect, especially if they were previously penalized. Since you often can’t tell how they were used before, they can be difficult to get indexed and ranking well.

The closest supported approach is to buy domains you know have real traffic and use 301 redirects to your main domain, which may preserve traffic more reliably than relying on the old domain’s backlinks alone.

Not really as a “good technique” for fast, reliable link juice. The evidence says Google prefers 301 redirects for passing value, and cross-domain canonical tags are tricky and not something to rely on. Canonicals are mainly for fixing duplicate-content issues, not as a solid way to move authority between domains.

So if your goal is to get the new domain to rank well, the closest supported guidance is to use 301 redirects rather than trying to buy abandoned domains just for juice.

The best approach is to use one main domain and have all the other domains permanently redirect to it with a 301 redirect. That’s the best choice from both users’ and Google’s point of view.

If you absolutely need to keep multiple domains live, the closest supported alternative is to make each secondary domain a small, individualized landing page and then link to the primary domain.

The evidence does not support relying on duplicate content across several domains for SEO gains, nor does it confirm any “exact match” bonus from redirects or canonicals.

The best-supported approach is not to keep identical sites on multiple city domains. Redirected domains won’t rank highly, so they usually won’t drive much traffic to the main site.

A better option is to use one main domain and create separate location landing pages, like mycompany.com/my-company-cleveland and mycompany.com/my-company-columbus, with content specific to each location.

If you actually have branches in those cities, setting up location pages in Google Places/Business Profile can help those locations rank well. If you do not have real locations there, city-specific pages may be seen as spammy.

Google Analytics will report for the page inside the iframe, not for the site/page that hosts the iframe. So if the snippet is only in the iframe, it won’t track the embedding domain itself.

If you want to know which website is hosting the iframe, you’d need to capture that separately outside of Google Analytics.

If you’re running Apache on the server, use name-based virtual hosting so multiple domains can share the same IP and server. This is the standard approach for hosting several WordPress sites on one machine. You’d configure a separate virtual host for each domain in Apache and point each domain to the same server IP. The Apache documentation on Name-Based Virtual Hosting has the setup details.

example1.mysite.com and example2.mysite.com are subdomains of mysite.com.

“Multi-domain” means a site can be accessed by more than one domain name, such as two different domains both showing the same website. That is not the same as subdomains, so they are not interchangeable.

If you mean the names like example1.mysite.com, the proper term is subdomains.

Forwarding multiple TLDs to one domain is not inherently bad for SEO, but the type of forwarding matters. The evidence says registrar “domain forwarding” like framed forwarding is unlikely to provide any SEO benefit. A 301 redirect can pass some SEO value only if the forwarded domain already had its own history, indexing, and backlinks. If the domains are just newly registered, forwarding them won’t help SEO.

Forwarding multiple top-level domains to one domain is generally risky for SEO. The guidance here says redirects from one domain to another usually give poor results, and rankings can drop or disappear, at least in the short term. It may recover later as organic use and backlinks build again, but the old domains themselves won’t help and can even hurt. If the domains are meant to stay separate, a better SEO approach would be to keep the domain content as it was rather than merge them all into one.

Forwarding multiple top-level domains to one domain is not directly covered by this evidence. It does support the general idea that Google cares little for exact-match domains and does not reward keyword-heavy domains or subdomains much, so using extra domains mainly for keywords is unlikely to help SEO. Based on that, forwarding several domains to one site should not be expected to improve SEO, and it may be pointless if the domains are only keyword variants.

A 301 redirect can be used for moving from one domain to another, including from a country-specific domain to a different domain. The evidence only covers a case where `.do` was redirected to `.co`, and it says Google may take about 30 days for full recrawling and indexing to catch up.

So if you’ve just set up the redirect, it may simply be too soon to expect search results to update. If the issue persists after about a month, the evidence suggests checking your redirect setup/options.

I can only confirm that the domain extension is considered a matter for SEO in the referenced discussion, but there’s no recorded answer about redirecting from .com or .org to a country-code domain like .am.

Closest guidance supported here: the thread treats domain extension as SEO-relevant, so choosing the domain you want to rank with matters. It does not say whether a redirect is recommended or how it would affect SEO.

If you want, I can help with general best practices for redirecting between TLDs.

It depends on the country extension. Some country domains have restrictions, such as requiring you to be a resident or a business in that country. For .be, there are no restrictions.

This evidence does not cover redirects from .com or .org to a country domain like .am. The closest guidance it supports is that you should check the rules for the specific country extension you want to use.

No. If the forwarded-to domain is just a new domain, forwarding/redirection won’t give the old domain SEO benefit or make it rank better for the keyword in the domain name.

The only supported case here is a 301 redirect from an established, already indexed domain with backlinks to another domain; that can pass some SEO benefit. The registrar forwarding shown is likely framed forwarding, which is unlikely to help SEO.

The evidence says subdomains are treated as their own entity, but Alexa consolidates subdomains under the primary domain for traffic rank.

It does not specifically mention forwarded domains. So based on this, a forwarded domain isn’t addressed directly. The closest guidance is that ranking is generally computed at the domain level, and subdomains may be counted together with the primary domain.

If both domains point to the same website and the pages are the same, search engines usually choose one set of title/meta snippets based on the page they index. You generally cannot force different SERP titles/descriptions for the exact same content just by using two domains.

If you want different titles/descriptions in search results, the supported approach is to have different pages or different page content per domain, or use proper canonical/hreflang setup depending on your goal. Changing title/description frequently is possible, but there is no recommended minimum or maximum rate, and frequent changes may affect rankings or snippet stability.

Use a 301 redirect from the parked/old domain to the main domain. That tells search engines which domain is canonical and helps reduce duplicate-content issues, so SERPs should consolidate over time.

RewriteEngine On
