Because Google can’t fetch the redirected content, it shows the “description not available because of this site’s robots.txt” message.

The likely fix is to stop redirecting public visitors/search bots from the homepage to the login page, or make sure the public page is accessible without that redirect. Once Google can crawl a public page directly, indexing/snippet generation should improve.

Use HTML5 if you want; it is not harmful to mobile SEO and is generally fine for both mobile and regular websites. In fact, HTML5 semantic markup can help search engines understand your content better. The provided information does not cover broader SEO support steps, but it does support using HTML5 as part of your website’s SEO setup.

Support SEO by starting with keyword research, then organizing your site around themes and related subtopics. Use important keywords in page titles, meta descriptions, URLs, headings, the first paragraph, and early content. Keep each page focused on its own keyword set, with some overlap allowed.

A practical sequence is:
1. Find target keywords using tools like Google Trends and search suggestions.
2. Structure content into theme-based directories/pages.
3. Optimize each page’s title, description, h1/h2, and body content.
4. Keep a keyword reference list for your pages.

The thread also suggests tools like Noble Samurai and Link Assistant. It does not fully cover link buying/renting or a complete SEO workflow.

To support your website’s SEO, use analysis tools to check SEO score and related factors that affect search visibility. The evidence specifically mentions these tools: YSlow, SEO Doctor, Google Webmaster Tools, and Google Page Speed. It also notes that browser add-ons for Google Chrome or Mozilla can be useful.

Based on this, start by auditing your site with these tools, then use the results to improve performance and SEO-related issues they identify. The provided information does not explain the full SEO process, but it does support using these tools to analyze and promote your website in search engines.

You can’t directly choose which pages Google shows there. Google selects those sitelinks automatically. The only control mentioned is to demote items so they may move lower in preference, and that demotion lasts 90 days. To do that, set up a Google Webmaster Tools account, then go to Site Configuration -> Sitelinks.

You can’t directly force Google to show site sections under a result description. The closest supported guidance here is to make sure your site and Google+ page are properly linked, and for business pages to create/verify the page as a local or non-local business page.

It also suggests using a Google+ badge/link between the site and the page, since Google refers to “linking for Google+ pages.”

If you mean the extra links under a search result, that’s controlled by Google’s search algorithms, not a setting you can turn on. The best supported steps are to ensure clear site structure and proper linking/verification.

You can’t directly make Google display your site sections under the description. Google decides whether to use your meta description, page text, or another snippet in search results.

To improve the chance of getting the right snippet:
- Use a unique meta description on each page.
- Make it accurately describe that page’s content.
- Include the section names and key terms you want surfaced.

If there’s no meta description, Google may pull text from the page instead. You can also prevent snippets entirely with `<meta name="robots" content="nosnippet">`, but that would hide the snippet altogether.

Googlebot can try URLs that aren’t linked, including odd parameter combinations. The closest guidance here is to make sure those requests are handled safely: verify they really come from Googlebot, check whether there’s an external referrer, and make your code return the right status codes for bad URLs (typically 404, sometimes 301 when appropriate) instead of throwing exceptions.

This doesn’t directly explain a brand-new site being ignored, but it does suggest fixing crawl errors and bad URL handling first. If Googlebot is hitting invalid URLs, that won’t help crawlability.

If the site is currently only showing a “coming soon” page, that can explain why Googlebot reports it can’t access the site. Removing the property from Webmaster Tools would not necessarily stop Google from trying to crawl the URL if it still exists publicly.

The closest guidance supported here is to make sure the site is actually reachable again, or expect those messages to continue while the placeholder page remains. If the site has moved, the practical path is to restore access or publish the new site content at that address.

Yes—search engines are fine with HTTPS.

If your HTTP site forwards to HTTPS, the new HTTPS page can be indexed and the old HTTP page can be removed from the index, as long as the content is the same and the HTTPS page does not point its canonical URL back to the HTTP version.

If Googlebot seems to be ignoring the new site, the main thing this supports is checking that the HTTPS version is accessible and that the canonical URL is set to the HTTPS page, not the old HTTP one.

This looks like a reporting mismatch in Webmaster Tools rather than a real indexing problem. The evidence says the index status report can be outdated or incorrect, while the Sitemaps report showing 492 of 493 indexed and a `site:` search returning 1,630 results suggest many pages are actually indexed.

It also supports the possibility that `www` and non-`www` are being treated separately, which can make the index status report show only part of the site. The closest guidance supported is to add both the `www` and non-`www` versions in Webmaster Tools and set a preferred domain.

Google Webmaster Tools does not use real-time data. Its index status can lag by a few days, and sometimes data may be missing for up to 2 weeks. If your site appears in Google search and the sitemap section shows indexed URLs, that indicates the pages are indexed even if the index status still shows 0. The same kind of delay can happen with traffic and keyword data.

If the site is in Google Webmaster Tools, that doesn’t guarantee it will immediately appear for a site: search or normal Google results. The only guidance supported here is that it can take time for Google to show the site. One suggestion given is to add the site to web directories with good page rank, but the main point is simply that indexing/visibility may not happen right away.

Set up Webmaster Tools for both domains and use the URL Removal feature on the google.com / sites.google.com content. The thread says this was the best available workaround for mapped Google Sites domains because there was no way to specify canonical links at the time.

As for “site:” search results, the evidence doesn’t give a direct fix for that specific symptom, but it does support treating both URLs as separate entries in Webmaster Tools and removing the unwanted Google Sites version.

If you type the full URL, www.caterboxgroup.co.uk, into Google search, and it returns results, that indicates the domain is indexed. The “site:” style search may not always behave as expected right away for a young site.

As for the “domain” and “registered” keywords in Webmaster Tools, Google can derive keywords from pages that link to your site, not only from words on your own pages.

The closest guidance supported here is: your site is young, so keep working on it and give it time.

To help individual blog posts rank above index pages, the guidance given is to strengthen the post pages themselves: get good links to the article pages, and make sure each new article is added to both the XML and HTML sitemap so search engines find it quickly. It also notes that post pages should usually be more relevant anyway because their titles, headings, and text differ from the index pages.

It does not recommend a “noindex, follow” solution as the best approach, though it says it likely wouldn’t cause immediate issues.

Not really. If a page is publicly indexed and it contains a word, you generally can’t make it searchable for one term but not another term that appears on the same page. The closest option supported here is to avoid publishing the unwanted term at all, or move that content to a private section of the site.

If you can identify the pages as a sequence, use pagination markup with rel="next" and rel="prev" in the head. That helps search engines treat the set as one sequence instead of indexing each page separately.

If the pages are random and hard to sequence, parameter filters in Google/Bing Webmaster Tools may be a better fit.

If you must use noindex, use noindex without nofollow, so bots can still follow links on those pages.

Google may be indexing the other pages but not the home page because it can drop a page from the index if it sees duplicate content, thin content, long-term inaccessibility (like 404s), robots.txt blocking, .htaccess blocking/410 responses, or a penalty/blacklist from spam or bad backlinks.

The closest guidance here is to check whether the home page is returning a different status than the others, is blocked by robots.txt or .htaccess, or has content that looks duplicated or too thin. If none of those apply, a penalty or blacklist is another possibility.

Google can’t crawl your database directly. It only indexes pages it can reach by following normal links on your site.

In your setup, Google should be able to find articles like `display.php?id=1` and `display.php?id=2` if those links are on crawlable pages such as `/articles.php` and not only behind JavaScript actions.

If only the home page is showing up, it usually means the other pages aren’t being discovered or aren’t reachable through normal links. Google does not care whether the content comes from one PHP script or many separate files, as long as each article has a public URL it can crawl.

Google’s `site:` query doesn’t reliably show every indexed page, so the home page may still be indexed even if it doesn’t appear in that list. The evidence says the home page is indexed and cached by Google and can appear in search results. It also says the order in `site:` results does not reflect a page’s importance. So the most supported answer is: all pages aren’t necessarily “turning up” except the home page; `site:` is just an imperfect check. If you want to verify the home page, search for a unique text string from it rather than relying on `site:`.

One way supported here is to tag paid traffic with a parameter, so it won’t be mistaken for organic visits. For example, set your ad URL to something.php?source=cpc. You can also use bit.ly links. This helps differentiate paid-for visitors from real organic visitors in Google Analytics.

If you mean generally increasing organic traffic, this evidence doesn’t cover that directly.

The evidence doesn’t really address how to generate organic traffic; it mainly covers how to handle a traffic spike after organic traffic has already increased.

The closest guidance it supports is to make your site faster and easier to serve:
- figure out the bottleneck
- make static content where possible
- use a CDN for scripts and popular images
- reduce page requests with image sprites
- cache rendered pages and smaller page fragments

If you want, I can also help with general organic traffic ideas, but that isn’t covered here.

The evidence doesn’t really explain the best ways to generate organic traffic. It only suggests using Moz’s Open Site Explorer to inspect a competitor’s link data, see where they’re earning press/attention, and compare link metrics across sites to understand competition and difficulty.

Closest guidance supported here: analyze competitors’ backlinks and link metrics to reverse engineer what’s driving their visibility. If you want, I can help turn that into a practical organic-traffic research process.

Google may be choosing the index page because that page contained the content when it was crawled. To improve this, you can:

- Put a no-index directive on the blog/gallery index page, though that’s a drastic step and may make sense for a gallery.
- Show excerpts on the index page instead of the full post content.
- Get deep links to the individual post pages from other sites.

These steps can help Google surface the proper individual pages more often.

You can’t directly control how many preview lines Google shows for your result. What you can do is improve the information Google may choose to display about your site. Helpful items include:

- location/business info through Google Places
- meta information like ratings, price, and author details
- event information

These can make your listing more prominent and better differentiated in search results, even though Google still decides what appears.

A Google+ Page is the business’s social page, like a Facebook Page. If the business has a physical location, it can create and verify a Local Google+ Page, which merges the listing with the social page into one verified page.

To get the local-style display in Google results, the key step covered here is verifying the Local Google+ Page. Google sends a postcard with a PIN to the business address, and the PIN must be entered before it expires.

This does not fully explain search ranking or exact display differences, but it supports creating/verifying the Local page and merging it with the existing listing.

The site is actually indexed fine. The suggested checks were to sign up for Google Webmaster Tools and to search Google with `site:recordhuy.be` to confirm indexing. In the thread, the update says the site is indexed just fine, so the issue is likely not missing from Google but possibly low visibility or poor SEO.

It may have been removed for duplicate content, weak content, copyright concerns, outside spam links, non-family-friendly content, deceptive ad placement, or even without an obvious reason. The suggested next step is to check Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console stats and compare sitemap pages vs. indexed pages over time.

If you can’t find a clear cause, the only guidance here is to move on and recreate the page in a different form.

It may not be immediate. The only guidance here is to first check whether the problem happens in all browsers, since browser-specific issues can affect ad display. The answer also suggests that ads can lag because advertisers take time to catch up to changes in ad-blocking code. Since it’s been only 12 hours, that timing could still be part of the issue, but this does not confirm that the redirect itself will automatically restore the ads.

A good first SEO step is to correctly fill the title tag and use H1 tags properly. The answer also suggests getting links from other websites with good anchor text. If you’re starting with SEO activity, these are the main actions supported here. It also mentions that a good domain name and server location can help, but the core first priorities are title tags, H1 tags, and quality backlinks with relevant anchor text.

The first step in SEO activity isn’t explained here. The only thing covered is that “low/medium/high activity” in website stats likely refers to how many pages a visitor browses in a session, possibly with time spent on pages also factored in.

If you mean SEO work, the closest guidance supported here is to start by understanding your website statistics and how visitors behave, then look into the software or company generating the stats for exact definitions before acting on them.

First, do keyword research. The answer says to start by using Google search suggestions and Google Trends, then organize the site’s content into themes and assign keywords to each page. After that, optimize page titles, descriptions, headings, URLs, and early content. It also mentions planning the site structure and naming directories/pages around the most important keywords.

If you mean the very first activity, it’s keyword research.

Yes, this can be normal. The indexed count in Google Webmaster Tools can be very slow to update, especially for sites with few backlinks or that aren’t crawled often. Since your sitemap report already shows 46 of 250 URLs indexed, Google has found and indexed some pages; the “Total Indexed” number may just not have caught up yet. Give it more time and keep monitoring. If it stays at zero for a long period, the next thing to check is whether the site is being crawled regularly.

After a 301 redirect, it can be expected for the old site’s Webmaster Tools data to start reflecting the new site, while the new site may still show zero indexed pages for a while.

The guidance supported here is:
- Use the Change of Address form in Webmaster Tools.
- Resubmit the sitemap for the old site so Google can follow the 301s.
- Submit the sitemap for the new site too.
- Check visibility with a `site:` search, since Webmaster Tools may lag or not match what’s actually indexed.

If the new site still shows zero after that, the evidence doesn’t say more about the cause.

If Google search can find the pages, then the index is probably fine. The most likely issue is with the sitemap or a temporary Google Webmaster Tools reporting glitch.

Check whether:
- the sitemap shows an error in the Issues column
- Test Sitemap passes
- the sitemap loads in a browser
- the URLs in the sitemap exactly match the live pages
- Health > Index Status shows anything unusual

If none of that shows a problem, it may just be a temporary blip in Google Webmaster Tools and could correct itself within 24 hours.

Google’s grid/summary-style result is a rich snippet type of display, and Google has been rolling out support for it for some time. The closest guidance here is to use the markup Google provides to signal paginated or catalog-like content, as seen on real estate and product sites. It’s not something you can force with a single meta tag, and eligibility depends on Google’s support for that content type. The referenced guidance points to Google’s own blog post and video on how to signal this kind of content.

I can’t help with getting a special “grid view” appearance in Google results like Twitter’s, because the provided material only discusses SEO-friendly URL choices for “c#” and says Google ranking depends on many factors, not just the URL.

Closest guidance supported here:
- Keywords in URLs can help, but they are not the only ranking signal.
- A clean, human-friendly structure is recommended, like:
  /csharp/
  /csharp/programming-concepts/
- Using %23 may be technically more exact, but it could confuse users.
- Focus on page content and structure for your audience rather than trying to force the search result format.

You can’t reliably force or directly obtain that kind of special grid-style presence from Google based on the information here. The closest guidance is to use Google Webmaster Tools (Search Console) to see your top search queries and average ranking position.

If you want to know whether your site appears for a keyword or phrase and where, Search Console is the supported way to check. Automated ranking tools exist, but they may violate Google’s terms of service.

A Yahoo Directory listing is not a likely explanation for low SERP visibility of specific site sections. The supported guidance here is that Yahoo Directory no longer delivers meaningful traffic and is generally considered not worth the $299 annual fee. So if sections of your site are appearing poorly in search results, this evidence does not point to Yahoo Directory as the fix.

The closest supported conclusion is that directory submission is unlikely to significantly improve SERP appearance. If you want, I can help you think through more likely causes of section-specific indexing or visibility issues.

The likely cause is Internet Explorer compatibility mode on the intranet/live site, not IIS 5 vs IIS 6. Even if the page asks for IE=edge, IE can still render intranet sites in compatibility mode by default, which can change list bullets, table borders, and image sizing enough to break the layout. Firefox may display both correctly because it doesn’t use that IE compatibility behavior. The closest fix supported here is to change IE’s view/compatibility settings so the live site renders in the same mode as staging/dev.

The evidence only supports this much: hidden divs and JavaScript can make content harder for some crawlers to see, and search engines may treat very different bot-visible content as cloaking. It does not confirm that your specific login/signup hidden divs are causing low appearance in SERPs.

Closest guidance: if the hidden sections are the same for bots and users, they’re less likely to be a cloaking issue, but JavaScript/hidden content can still complicate crawling. The safe approach is to make sure your important content is visible in a text browser and not dependent on JS to be discovered.

If the URLs change, 301 redirect every changed URL, including images. The guidance here is that redirects can pass most, but not all, value, so keeping existing page URLs is best if they’re already good. Also rebuild the site with proper headings, alt text, meta data, and a sitemap. If you’re only replacing tables with divs and the page URLs stay the same, no redirects are needed for those pages.

After replacing the tables with divs, the main next step is to map all old URLs to the new ones and make sure you preserve content and structure during the migration. If the site is static and the pages are irregular, you’ll likely need either a script to extract and import the content into the CMS or manual data entry. For bulk content, exporting to CSV and loading it into the new system is the closest supported approach. Then back up the old site, move the CMS files/database, and test everything after migration.

After replacing the content tables with divs, the next step supported here is to change the module overrides as well. The accepted answer suggests copying all the content from the beez template’s html folder, then updating the module overrides so modules on the right side also render without tables.

Google decides what rich previews appear in search results. The supported guidance here is to use schema.org markup on your site to help Google understand your content and improve the chance it appears more accurately in SERPs. For blog content, adding relevant schema markup and making sure your pages are crawlable is the closest supported approach. Even then, Google may still choose whether or not to show images or other preview elements.

Google can detect a blog from more signals than a checker like WooRank. If your site has Atom or RSS feeds in meta tags, that helps. Google also uses its own bots and other signals to recognize blog content, so if Search Console/Webmaster tools show no issues, you likely don’t need to worry about another site’s report.

If you want your blog content to appear in Google Search, make sure the blog is on your own website and is crawlable, with feeds and normal indexable pages. A Blogspot page isn’t required based on this guidance.

Google doesn’t treat blog posts and HTML pages fundamentally differently. A new blog post can appear quickly if Google crawled it soon after publishing, especially if the page was linked internally, fresh, and your site is already well established. It may also have been discovered through a blog-related ping or sitemap update. Static HTML pages can take longer if they’re found less quickly or updated less often.

You can’t force immediate indexing, but you can help by:
- submitting an XML sitemap
- linking to the page from other pages on your site
- making sure the page is crawlable and returns a normal 200 response
- using Google Search Console to request indexing if needed

It’s still ultimately up to Google’s crawl and index timing.

The Google tool you’re likely looking for is Data Highlighter in Google Webmaster Tools (now Google Search Console). It lets you mark up parts of a page like product price, photo, and description so Google can better understand and display the page. It does not generate visible HTML for the page itself; it’s a way to tell Google about page elements.

If your goal is SEO for OpenCart product pages, this is the closest match from the evidence.

If you have a manageable number of products, an XML sitemap of all products may be enough, and the extra crawlable links are not strictly necessary, though simpler navigation is better. If you have a very large catalog, you need crawlable navigation in addition to sitemaps.

For structure, the main point is to give Googlebot a crawlable path into the catalog, like type, size, brand, accessories, etc. The exact order matters less than making the sections easy to drill into.

For indexing, the guidance here is to index all products you can. If Google and other bots can’t find them, they’re effectively invisible.

Use clean, indexable URL paths for product pages, like /products/brand/short-description, and keep pagination in the same structure. Add breadcrumbs so search engines and users can move through Brand > Product pages easily. A separate static category/product browser can help SEO if it creates useful, unique pages.

Canonical URLs are mainly for duplicate or very similar pages, not for pages with different content. Filter values are less clear from the evidence, but the supported idea is to expose them as readable URL segments rather than query strings or POST if you want them crawlable.

For OpenCart specifically, the evidence doesn’t cover implementation details, but the closest guidance is to create SEO-friendly, unique product and category URLs, with breadcrumbs and sensible pagination.

The best way to get backlinks is to publish high-quality content on your website so other webmasters want to link to it naturally.

If you want more links, the weaker methods mentioned were forum signatures, directory submissions, link exchanges, blog comments, and article directories, but these are low quality and usually help less than links from established, relevant sites.

Also, make sure links are not marked “nofollow,” since those are essentially worthless for SEO. Avoid spamming other websites.

If your sitemap URL stays the same and it updates dynamically, you usually do not need to resubmit it every day. Search engines can revisit the sitemap on their own. Since this is a news portal adding new pages daily, the closest supported guidance is to keep the sitemap accessible and updated, and let Google recrawl it. Resubmitting is only needed if the sitemap location changes or you want to manually prompt Google after major changes.

No, this would not help your Google ranking from an SEO standpoint. The accepted answer says Facebook app pages can’t be indexed or crawled by search engines because users must be logged in to see them, so links from the app to your website would have no SEO value. The evidence does not confirm whether the links are specifically marked nofollow, but it does support that they won’t benefit SEO much, if at all.

Having a Facebook page can help drive traffic if people like content on your site, because that activity may show up in their friends’ news feeds with a link back to the specific page they liked. The strongest guidance here is to put the Like button on the actual page the user is viewing, so the share points to that exact result page rather than just the root site.

The evidence does not confirm that Facebook likes directly improve Google rankings. It only supports using Facebook to increase visibility and referral traffic.

The report is counting Facebook likes/shares for the website URL, not likes on your Facebook Page.

So your page’s 21 likes won’t appear there unless the URL itself has been liked/shared on Facebook. The tool is checking social engagement for the analyzed web address, and in the example given that URL has no Facebook shares or likes.

If you want a higher count in that report, it would need likes/shares on the specific website URL, not just on the Facebook page.

This can happen after a 301 redirect. The guidance here is to use Google Webmaster Tools’ Change of Address form, resubmit the sitemap from the old site so Google can pick up the 301 redirects, and then submit the sitemap for the new site.

Also check visibility directly in Google with a site: search, like site:www.google.com, to see whether the new site is indexed even if Webmaster Tools shows 0 pages.

If your new WordPress site has 0 indexed pages, Google may simply not have discovered or chosen to index them yet. Google can still find pages through links or a submitted sitemap, and it may index them unless you prevent it.

To stop a page from being indexed, use:
<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">

and block it in robots.txt, for example:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /the-page

If the site is new, also make sure pages are linked internally or included in a sitemap so Google can find them.

0 indexed doesn’t necessarily mean nothing is being found. In the thread, the site was already indexed, but Google was indexing the www version, while the bare domain was not the one referenced in Google Webmaster Tools.

“Not selected” can mean Google is seeing duplicate URLs or alternate versions of the same page. In that example, both holiday-home.uk.com and www.holiday-home.uk.com returned the same content, and www/.../index.html was also another URL for the same page. Google may choose only one version to index.

The closest fix supported there is to use one preferred version of the site, set a 301 redirect from the other version, and make sure your sitemap and links use the same canonical URL format.

The evidence only covers a multilingual WordPress multisite setup with subdomains/mapped domains, and the advice given is to use hreflang tags to point Google to the Italian, German, and English versions. It does not explain why a site won’t index.

Closest guidance supported here: make sure each language version is linked with `rel="alternate" hreflang="..."` and submit the relevant subdomains/mapped domains so Google can discover them. If you want, I can help you check common indexation blockers based on this setup.

The site likely isn’t indexing well because it’s new and many pages look low-quality or unoriginal: for most pages, the only unique text is a title and one-line description. Googlebot may treat a brand-new site with thousands of similar pages as suspicious or spammy.

Closest fixes supported here:
- Create an XML sitemap.
- Check the site in Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console.
- Try increasing the crawl rate there.
- Improve page quality and uniqueness; starting with a smaller set of hand-picked, more substantial pages may help.

Google may be crawling the site, but it won’t index or rank pages if it sees the site as low-quality or spammy. In the thread, the main issue was that the site was filled with unrelated links, which made it look like spam to search engines. New sites can also take time to build reputation and links from other sites.

So the closest guidance is: remove unrelated/spammy links, improve the site’s relevance and content, and be patient while Google reassesses it. Having keywords and descriptions alone won’t guarantee indexing or search visibility.

Yes, it can be normal. Googlebot doesn’t index on a fixed schedule, so a page may be found quickly or may take hours, days, or longer. The guidance here says you can’t predict when Googlebot will visit.

To improve the chance of faster indexing, the closest suggestions are:
- add crawlable links to your site or new page
- publish content regularly
- submit new URLs in your sitemap via Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console
- ping Google for the new URL

If you want, I can also help you check for common reasons a page stays unindexed.

It isn’t normal to assume Google stops indexing just because a site is being worked on a lot. The guidance here says the opposite: Google tends to like frequently updated sites and may crawl them more because they seem “alive.” It does not support the idea that Google suspends crawling/indexing until a site stabilizes.

If you’re not indexed after a month, this answer doesn’t explain why, only that frequent changes alone are not a known reason.

It’s normal for some URLs not to be indexed after a month, but not for a large share of submitted URLs to remain unindexed. In the example, 2,521 sitemap URLs were submitted and only 548 indexed, with none of 1,256 mobile URLs indexed, which suggests a possible site issue rather than just normal delay.

The suggested checks are: confirm sitemap URLs are valid, review Google Search Console index status for “not selected” or “blocked by robots,” look for duplicate content, and check for any Google messages about suspicious links or other problems. If mobile URLs are all unindexed, that points to a more serious configuration issue.

The safest directories mentioned are business.com, Yahoo Directory, and DMOZ. The guidance given was that beyond those three, the responder would not pay for directory listings, because paid directory links may not help and Google may give very low PageRank to links from sites known to be paid directories.

So, if your goal is more traffic and better search rankings, the supported advice here is to focus only on those established directories and avoid paid directory schemes.

To prepare for higher traffic, the advice here is to test your site’s performance before the spike. Run benchmark tools such as Google Page Speed and YSlow to find inexpensive performance improvements. You can also do preemptive load and performance tests with free tools before and after any changes to measure whether they help. This covers preparation for handling traffic more effectively, though it doesn’t discuss broader traffic-growth tactics.

Having video alone won’t increase traffic quality. The guidance here is that “quality” users come from quality content, and video helps only if it’s genuinely useful or entertaining for your audience. Good videos can give visitors a reason to stay longer and return; poor videos may drive them away. So if your goal is better traffic, focus on producing content your users value, whether that’s video or another format.

It isn’t something you can force. Google decides which sites get preview images or embedded video results in search. The closest guidance supported here is to make sure your pages use schema.org markup for videos, because that’s the kind of structured data Google would likely rely on if it supports this beyond YouTube.

Even with markup, there’s no guarantee Google will show your site that way.

Google doesn’t guarantee that a search box will appear in search results. The closest supported guidance is that if you want Google to understand your site’s internal search, you should provide structured data for a sitelinks search box and have a site search function that Google can crawl and understand.

Even then, Google decides whether to show it. There isn’t a manual way to force it to appear in results.

If you want, I can also explain the typical requirements for sitelinks search box markup.

You generally don’t need to do anything special for a site logo or header image. Sitemaps are for pages, not the individual layout pieces that make them up, and the image sitemap tags are mainly for important content images, not decoration.

If you want Google to associate an image with your site, the closest supported approach is to include it on the homepage or on a page specifically for brand/press assets, and list it there. I would not add it to every page just because it appears everywhere.

I’m not aware of an official, widely supported way to tell Google to show that exact logo image in search results.

Bingbot crawling your sitemap but not showing pages in results can still happen if indexing is blocked or inconsistent between protocols. The provided guidance says robots.txt can’t disallow only HTTPS when served over HTTP. If you want different rules for HTTPS, you’d need to serve a separate robots.txt for HTTPS, for example by rewriting https://example.com/robots.txt to a deny-all file. That would block crawling over HTTPS, but not HTTP. If your pages are being crawled and still not appearing, this evidence only supports checking whether HTTPS is being blocked differently from HTTP; it doesn’t explain other ranking/indexing causes.

A sitemap alone doesn’t guarantee indexing. The issue may be that Bing can crawl the sitemap, but many listed URLs are returning 404 or 500 errors, so only the homepage is getting indexed.

The closest guidance supported here is:
- Check that new URLs return 200 OK.
- Check that old URLs return 301 redirects to the new pages.
- Make sure the redirected-to pages do not themselves return 404.
- Crawl the site with a tool like Screaming Frog or Xenu to find bad URLs and response codes.

It also sounds possible that Bing is still seeing the old sitemap entries or cached URLs, but the main evidence points to URL/redirect/server errors preventing indexing.

If Bing is crawling your sitemap but pages don’t appear in results, the closest guidance here is that search console/index reports can lag behind actual indexing by days or even up to 2 weeks. So a sitemap being crawled or showing indexed URLs doesn’t always mean the index report is current. If the pages are showing in search for site: queries, that suggests they are indexed and the reporting is just delayed. If they still don’t appear in normal searches, you may need to wait for updates and keep checking the index/status data over time.

If Google is crawling but not indexing yet, the likely issue here is timing and robots.txt handling. An empty robots.txt can sometimes be treated cautiously, so it’s better to explicitly allow all pages:

User-agent: *
Disallow: 

After that, Google may still take at least a week and sometimes up to a month to index the site. It can index pages as it crawls them, even before finishing the whole crawl.

To help speed things up, the supported guidance here is to improve the site’s reputation with more high-quality inbound links. Crawl rate is mainly governed by PageRank.

Google may crawl those pages but still choose not to index them if they look duplicate or near-duplicate. In that case, manual submission usually won’t help much. The guidance here is to use canonical tags where possible for duplicate content, and improve signals that help indexing: make the content more unique, increase its perceived value, and get more quality backlinks/traffic. Also check for any common technical issues that might be blocking indexing.

Google can crawl a site without ranking it well. In this case, the site was described as having lots of unrelated links, which made it look like spam. Search results depend partly on page content and links from other sites, so a new site may take time to build trust. The closest guidance supported here is to improve the site’s relevance and remove spam-like or unrelated links; otherwise it may not appear in keyword searches even if `site:ecservice.ro` shows pages.

Google can index pages before it finishes crawling the whole site, so a crawl rate of 25 pages per day doesn’t by itself explain the lack of indexing.

The answer supports two likely reasons:
- If your robots.txt was recently removed or left empty, Google may treat that change cautiously and not honor it immediately.
- Indexing can take time anyway: usually at least a week, sometimes up to a month.

It also says the safest robots.txt is one that explicitly allows everything:
User-agent: *
Disallow: 

If you want faster crawling, the guidance given is to improve the site’s reputation with more high-quality inbound links.

If Googlebot is crawling your site but pages still aren’t indexed, the evidence points to a robots.txt issue. The site’s robots.txt contains:

User-agent: *
Disallow:

That can block crawling/indexing behavior. The suggested fix is to remove that disallow rule. This evidence doesn’t say whether that is the only cause, but it directly identifies robots.txt as the problem shown in the thread.

Seeing Googlebot crawl 25 pages per day does not guarantee your site will be indexed. The only guidance here is that you can check which pages are indexed by searching:

site:mydomain.com

in Google. That will show the pages currently indexed. If a page was added to the sitemap 2 weeks ago and still doesn’t appear, this method can help confirm whether it’s indexed, but it doesn’t explain why it isn’t indexed.

A zero PageRank update doesn’t necessarily mean your site is penalized. The PageRank metric has not been updated for a long time, so it may no longer reflect your site’s real standing. In the case described, the site was not penalized.

If your rankings are low, the best supported guidance here is to stop relying on PageRank as the measure of success. Focus instead on other factors that affect ranking and visibility, since PageRank is outdated and not accurate anymore.

If the site was defaced, the main concerns are whether it was fully cleaned up, whether Google has issued any warnings, and whether harmful backlinks were created. Check the site with a security scanner, review Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console for hacking or malware messages, and inspect the backlink profile with a tool like Ahrefs. Also confirm the site is still indexed using a search like site:domain.com.

If those checks are clean, the site can still improve. The next step is to create strong, useful content and ensure the website is well structured and built correctly so Google re-crawls it and can rank it better over time.

This sounds like a DNS cache issue. In the resolved thread, the behavior cleared up when tested from a different computer, which suggested the old DNS entry was still being cached locally. The closest guidance supported here is to try another machine or browser/network to confirm, then wait for DNS propagation or clear local DNS cache before assuming WordPress is misconfigured.

It’s likely a server-side PHP/Apache configuration issue rather than a WordPress problem. Since it affected all WordPress sites on the shared host but not static sites, PHP handling was probably broken temporarily, causing the server to send the index.php file instead of executing it.

The accepted answer suggests it was occasional and temporary, possibly from an imperfect Apache configuration update. It doesn’t point specifically to PHP memory limits. It also says this is not common on professional hosting and isn’t necessarily a reason to worry unless it keeps happening.

This likely isn’t caused by WordPress itself. The more likely problem is DNS: your domain may no longer resolve publicly, even though the site works locally on your Raspberry Pi.

Check whether the domain is still registered and not expired or transferred. If it is still yours, verify your DNS settings and make sure the records point to the correct server/IP.

In short: the site appears unreachable to others because the domain name is not being found or resolved correctly.

Search engines treat different domains as separate for SEO, even if they are similar in name, belong to the same owner, or have a similar theme. So if your clothing website’s tags are on a different domain from another site and you do not use duplicate content, there is no reason one should negatively affect the other’s SEO.

This does not specifically cover SEO tags themselves, but the closest guidance supported here is that similar domains are not a problem by themselves; duplicate content is what you should avoid.

If you’re using a plain HTML/CSS site, the supported guidance here is to add SEO labels/tags yourself rather than rely on a script. The answer says a tagging script wouldn’t really help, because SEO is about optimizing your content, and manually tagging your pages is likely as good as or better than using an automated tool.

For a clothing site, that means using descriptive page titles, headings, and tags/labels you choose yourself for products and categories. If you want automation, this evidence doesn’t recommend a specific script or confirm that one would improve SEO.

No — links in heading tags don’t get extra SEO weight or passed value compared with links in normal text. The only effect described is semantic: a link’s context and closeness to heading/title text may help search engines understand the page topic, but that is not a boost for the link itself.

So for a clothing website, adding tags or links in headings won’t improve rankings just by being in a header. Use headings for clear structure and relevant content instead.

If your traffic has suddenly increased from Google domains, the likely explanation is that you’re ranking higher for certain search terms and getting more organic search traffic.

To find out what’s driving it, check Google Analytics:
Traffic Sources → Sources → Search → Organic

Then compare this month with last month using the date range selector. That should show which search terms contributed most to the increase.

If you’re expecting a traffic spike, the advice here is to improve site performance before the surge rather than just adding hardware. Run your site through benchmark tools like Google PageSpeed and YSlow to find simple, low-cost performance improvements. Also do preemptive load and performance testing with free tools before and after changes so you can measure any gains.

Yes. The evidence describes a site that is crawled and indexed but still ranks very low. The suggested explanation is that ranking can lag even when indexing is fine, especially if the site is new or faces competitors. The closest guidance supported here is to wait, keep working on SEO, and build legitimate visibility and backlinks over time.

Yes. The thread says the site was not penalized or indexed poorly; it was just young, with few backlinks, so ranking and PageRank were low. It suggests being patient, continuing SEO/SEM work, publishing content, getting more good backlinks, and submitting a sitemap to Google Webmaster Tools.

Yes—this can happen even when indexing is fine. In the example, Google is showing another URL with the site’s title and description, and that other site redirects back to the original site. The suggested fix is to identify the other site’s IP and block it via .htaccess so it can’t scrape content, and to add canonical URLs so Google knows the original source.

You can’t force Google to give you the visitor’s search keywords by indexing your site with only HTTPS. The closest guidance here is that Google Webmasters/Search Console provides search traffic information, but after Google Secure Search the referrer data became more opaque, so you cannot get keywords as before.

What you may still see are some referral parameters like `ved` and `cd`, which can indicate the search result vertical and position, but not the actual keywords entered by the visitor.

There isn’t a way to directly tell Google to index specific keywords. The closest guidance here is to make the keywords clearly present in your pages, keep an up-to-date sitemap.xml in Google Webmaster Tools, and use “Fetch as Google” after major changes so Google can recrawl the site. The answer also says to place the keywords in bold throughout the text, but it does not guarantee rankings or indexing for those exact terms.

Using the same key phrase in the URL, title, and H1 can still help, but it won’t have the same weight it used to. Exact-match domains are not as strong as before, and Google prefers a good brand/business name over keyword-stuffed domains.

A better approach is to use a solid brand domain and put the relevant keywords in the URL path, for example:
businessname.com/cars-for-sale-in-melbourne

The evidence also suggests that rankings can depend on age, authority, and backlinks, so a keyword-rich domain alone isn’t enough. It doesn’t clearly say whether changing “Car Sales Melbourne” to “Sales Car Melbourne” with a different location would work equally well.

For a WordPress blog, the suggested basics are:

- Install WordPress SEO by Yoast for on-page optimization help for target keywords.
- Install Google Analytics by Yoast and set it up properly.
- Submit the XML sitemap generated by the SEO plugin to Google Webmaster Tools and Bing Webmaster Tools.
- If you use images or videos, add separate image and video sitemap plugins.

These are the main tips covered. If you want more advanced SEO advice, I’d need more specific guidance or a review of your blog’s content and structure.

For a blog, the closest guidance here is basic SEO setup: do keyword research first, then organize your content by themes, and use your main keywords in the title tag, description meta tag, URL, H1/H2 tags, and early in the content. Keep each page focused on its own keywords, even if some overlap.

It also suggests using Google Trends and Google search suggestions for keyword ideas.

This does not cover broader blog-specific tactics like posting frequency, internal linking, or social promotion, but it does support starting with keyword research and on-page optimization for each post.

If your blog posts are mostly unrelated to your shareware, it supports hosting the blog on a separate domain. That gives you flexibility to keep the blog broader while still letting the shareware site surface only the relevant posts.

A practical approach is to tag posts about the shareware and use a tag RSS feed to pull those into a news section on the shareware site. That way, users who care about the software can see the related updates, while others can visit the full blog separately.

The thread only explains how to get a Google Map/business location to show in search results, not a menu.

For the map/location result, it says to:
- register your business with Google/Google Places
- make sure your NAP (name, address, phone) is consistent everywhere
- add citations on local directories and sites like Facebook, Twitter, Yelp, etc.

It also says this can take 7–21 days and is not guaranteed.

If you meant a site menu or sitelinks in Google search results, this evidence doesn’t cover that.

The provided material doesn’t explain how to add a menu to Google search results, and the thread has no answer on record.

It only shows someone asking how to make a search box appear in Google search results. The closest guidance supported here is that you may be referring to Google’s search box in search results, but no procedure is given.

If you mean adding sitelinks or a search box for your own website in Google results, you’d need guidance from Google’s structured data or search appearance documentation.

Google generally does not want site search results pages indexed, and those pages often don’t add value for users. The closest guidance here is to avoid exposing your internal search results to Google and to use robots.txt to prevent crawling of search results pages or other auto-generated pages that don’t add much value.

Adding all those local search links to a sitemap is not supported by this guidance as a way to make Google show them in search. If your goal is visibility, it’s better to create normal, indexable pages for the people/names rather than trying to index `mysite.com/?q=david+jones` search-result URLs.

Don’t trade links. The guidance here is that traded links have little value and can even put your site at risk if you link to a bad neighborhood.

Instead, earn quality links and use strong page titles to help influence anchor text naturally, since you won’t have direct control over how others link to you.

For a new site, focus first on easier, less competitive keywords. That can help you rank sooner, bring in very targeted traffic, and build momentum toward broader terms. Also, targeting those easier phrases helps you cover more general keywords naturally through your content.

The keyword tool is mainly for AdWords research, not a direct SEO difficulty score. A “very low” competition rating there only means fewer advertisers are bidding on the term; it does not mean the keyword is easy to rank for in search.

It may still be useful for SEO because search volume matters, but you should not choose `mario` just because AdWords competition is low. The best next step is to use SEO-focused competitive research tools that measure how hard it is to rank against the current top pages.

Yes — the evidence points to Webmasters Stack Exchange as a free Q&A site with many SEO questions and answers. You can browse the SEO tag here: https://webmasters.stackexchange.com/questions/tagged/seo

A likely cause is that the pages may still be indexed but not ranking well right now. The guidance given is to check whether they’re still indexed by searching with site:yourdomain.com. A similar case mentioned that after about 2 weeks, rankings returned to normal, with some pages moving up or down a few places.

So, if your pages disappeared from search results, first verify whether they’re still in the index. If they are, it may be a temporary ranking fluctuation rather than full deindexing.

The likely reason is that Google may be recognizing the cross-linking pattern across many sites you own, which can reduce or prevent indexing of those link pages. The evidence also suggests .info domains may be affected if they’re young, since they were associated with spam and may not appear in results for up to 6 months.

Adding more non-link content might help make the pages less thin, but the support here only clearly points to site-wide linking patterns and possible domain-extension/age issues.

Submitting URLs in a sitemap does not guarantee they’ll be indexed. Google can know about the pages and still choose not to index many of them. The guidance supported here is to get more links to the pages, especially the ones not indexed yet, so Google can discover and prioritize them more effectively.

Since your site is a single-page Ajax app, the sitemap can help Google find content, but it still doesn’t ensure indexing of every URL.

You can’t guarantee the top position, but you can improve your ranking by making pages unique and relevant, using a unique title and meta description on each page, using proper HTML and schema.org where applicable, getting quality links from relevant sites, keeping outgoing links relevant, adding a sitemap in Google Search Console, using keywords naturally in URLs, and making the site fast, HTTPS-secured, and mobile-friendly. Avoid keyword spamming or repeated content, since that can hurt rankings.

You can’t force a website into the top position of Google. The only supported guidance here is that the “average position” shown in Google Webmaster Tools may not match what you see if you’re looking at only web search, because the position can also apply to other search types, such as image search. In the example, the site’s position of 1.0 was confirmed in image search, while the user had mistakenly restricted results to web search.

So the closest practical advice is to check whether you’re comparing the same search type and remember that the reported position is an average, not a guaranteed fixed ranking in a specific search view.

To check your website’s real position, use Chrome private/incognito mode, Google Webmaster Tools, or an external rank-tracking tool like Rankerizer or Serpbook. If your goal is to appear in the top position on Google, this doesn’t provide a way to force that. It only covers how to view rankings more accurately.

Google can make pages appear and disappear for several reasons, including duplicate content, weak content, copyright issues, outside spam links, non-family-friendly content, deceptive ad placement, or sometimes for no clear reason. The suggested first step is to check Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console and compare sitemap pages versus indexed pages over time.

If you can’t find a specific issue, the only guidance given is that there may not be much to do after the fact other than recreate the page in a different form.

Google can change how it shows your result if it thinks your page titles aren’t strong enough. In the example, the word “logo” was likely taken from an image alt tag and added to the SERP title.

Closest guidance:
- Check for an image alt text like “logo”
- Use more descriptive alt text, such as “Logo [yourName]”
- Improve your page titles
- Wait for Google to recrawl and update the results

If your site is appearing and disappearing, the same general issue may apply: Google may be re-evaluating how it represents your pages in search.

If your site appears and disappears from Google results, the most supported explanation here is a Google algorithm change rather than a technical indexing error. Since pages still show up at times, it’s less likely to be a robots.txt mistake.

The advice supported by the thread is to review whether your site has:
- high-quality content
- enough site authority
- older, established content
- quality backlinks from sites not affected by recent Google updates

Also check whether your site may have been affected by updates like Penguin. If you can, compare your site against those factors and look for patterns in when the drops happen.

There’s no set maximum length for an alt value or a title attribute. For alt text, the usual guidance is to keep it under about 125 characters for usability, especially for visually impaired users. For a title attribute, similar usability concerns apply, and tooltips may get cut off in some browsers.

If you mean the title element for SEO, search engines may truncate it or replace it, so keeping it under about 70 characters is commonly advised.

Swapping synonyms on every page visit would be counter-productive. Once you remove one word and replace it with another, you stop ranking better for the original word and start ranking better for the new one. That means each term gets shown less consistently, which can hurt rather than help.

The safest guidance is to pick the word that is most appropriate for the page and use it consistently. If several terms are truly suitable, choose the one with the highest search volume and focus on that.

Meta keywords have zero effect on rankings in Google and most major search engines. So changing them dynamically, or worrying about how often they change, isn’t something that would help SEO. The closest guidance supported here is that it’s not worth spending time on meta keywords at all.

The evidence doesn’t give a definitive cause. It does show a mismatch between the sitemap report and the Index Status report: one can show 6 submitted URLs and only 1 or 0 indexed there, while Index Status shows 11 indexed pages overall. That means the sitemap view is only comparing submitted URLs against that sitemap, not necessarily all indexed pages on your site.

So the closest supported guidance is: the pages may still be indexed, and the sitemap tab can lag or reflect only URLs it recognizes from the submitted sitemap. If the pages appear in Google search, that supports that they are indexed even if the sitemap count says otherwise.

Google Webmaster Tools doesn’t always show real-time data. The index status can lag behind actual indexing by a few days, and sometimes up to 2 weeks, so it may show 0 even though your sitemap and Google search results already show indexed pages. There’s usually nothing to worry about; the tool is just behind.

There’s no recorded answer here. Based on what’s provided, the only supported guidance is that content can be changed at any frequency. The evidence does not give a real fact, minimum, or maximum rate for changing `<title>`, description meta tag, or keywords meta tag, and it does not say whether daily changes affect ranking.

So the closest supported answer is: no specific frequency limit is provided, and the question about ranking impact is unanswered in the material shown.

A very broad, low-competition-looking phrase like “why does the” usually isn’t useful by itself. The answer says you probably can’t do much with it unless your site has lots of content about “why” questions, because visitors may land on your site and not find what they want, causing a high bounce rate.

It also says the 1% competition figure is misleading: even if no one targets that exact phrase, many sites may target longer phrases containing it and still rank well for those searches.

Best practical guidance supported here: focus on specific, related long-tail phrases and build content around them rather than trying to rank for the broad starter phrase.

There’s no recorded answer in the thread. The only guidance available is that the question asks for a paid or free tool to find keywords/phrases that return fewer than 100 or no results, without doing it manually.

So, based on this, the closest supported advice is: you’d need a tool or search-engine query data source that reports query frequency or result counts; the thread does not identify one.

Based on the answer provided, the main SEO items to use are: correctly fill the title tag, use H1 tags, get links from other websites with good anchor text, choose a good domain name, and consider server location.

If you mean what else to use beyond those, the evidence doesn’t specify more SEO tactics. It only supports these basics.

Use keyword research first, then organize your site by themes. Put your most important keywords in page titles, meta descriptions, headings, first paragraph, URL structure, and early content. Each page should target its own keyword set.

The answer also mentions using Google Trends and tools like Noble Samurai and Link Assistant, plus structuring content into “theme pyramids” and naming directories/pages with relevant keywords.

It does not really cover other SEO methods beyond on-page keyword use and site organization, so if you mean backlinks, social, technical SEO, or content strategy, this only gives limited guidance.

Use the schema.org format for structured data. It’s meant to help search engines understand your page and can improve how results are displayed. Google, Microsoft, and Yahoo have agreed to use the formats listed there. If you’re choosing between microdata and RDFa, the best guidance here is to follow schema.org’s specified format.

If your homepage has more backlinks, it often ranks better, but Google ranks pages individually. An internal page can outrank the homepage if it’s better optimized and more relevant.

You don’t need to move the better business page to the homepage just to rank better. If you want the homepage to rank, optimize the homepage for SEO. Otherwise, it’s fine for the internal page to rank above it.

You can’t reliably measure home page on-page SEO “before and after” in a controlled way, because search engines keep re-evaluating rankings while they crawl and index changes. You can compare keyword positions before and after, but there’s no guarantee any change was caused by your optimization.

So the closest supported approach is to benchmark current rankings for your target keywords, make your on-page changes, then compare later—but treat any difference as suggestive, not conclusive.

Based on the evidence, the safest guidance is to leave your current meta tags/keywords alone and not replace “balloon decorations” with only “Boston balloon” or “Boston balloon decorations.” The answer suggests keeping the current tags, adding location names in the footer, and also hinting at location in the main body text.

It does not say whether this will preserve your first-page ranking, or how likely a new Boston landing page is to rank quickly. It only implies that adding a landing page may be less effective than making the homepage location-aware and linking to city pages from it.

If you want, I can help draft location-friendly meta tag text that still keeps the main keyword.

The meta keywords tag has no SEO effect, so optimizing it for a keyword won’t help rankings. There’s also no official maximum length. A common guideline is to keep it somewhere around 100 to 255 characters, but the main point is simply to use words that match your page content. If you’re focusing on SEO, it’s better to spend effort on other meta tags and on-page content instead.

Yes—based on the example, include the specific keyword plus “wallpaper” and a general “wallpaper” term in the meta keywords. For an Iron Man image, something like:

<meta name="keywords" content="iron man, iron man wallpaper, wallpaper" />

That’s the closest guidance supported here. It suggests combining the subject term with the content type, rather than listing only the character names.

Using `rel="canonical"` on those language-specific pages is the recommended method, and it’s sufficient for telling Google that they should be treated as the same as `www.site.com/aslgm`.

If you already have:

`<link rel="canonical" href="http://www.site.com/aslgm" />`

on those pages, that is the closest guidance supported here.

Google’s `link:` search is not reliable for finding all backlinks. It may show only a small, changing subset of links, and its results can contradict Google Webmaster Tools. In this case, the closest guidance is to use a backlink tool such as MajesticSEO for more accurate results.

The thread does not answer how to make Google show all links, and it does not mention any way to close the question for more comments or answers.

Google Sitelinks generally require a site with quite a bit of traffic, and there’s no easy public algorithm to force them. The best guidance here is to keep creating great content and make your navigation easy for Google to understand with semantic HTML, using a nav element or an id like nav/navigation for the menu.

Avoid JavaScript for links and menus. Sitelinks are rare and may change over time, so give it time.

If you already have sitelinks, Google Webmaster Tools may let you control which links appear.

The evidence suggests it may simply take time for Bing/Yahoo to refresh and reindex the site, especially after earlier duplicate content. It also notes that Bing and Yahoo can differ from Google, so being visible in Google does not guarantee Bing/Yahoo ranking.

A useful check is to search Bing with site:yoursite.com to see whether the pages are indexed at all. If they are not indexed, the issue is more likely reindexing/refresh delay. If they are indexed but still not ranking, then it may be a ranking issue rather than a complete omission.

If Google/Bing are still finding old URLs from the previous adult site, the guidance here is to keep those old pages returning 404 and let them fall out of the index. Do not 301 redirect them to a replacement page, because that can cause search engines to keep treating the old URLs as valid.

It can take quite a while for them to disappear. The only additional step suggested is trying to get the old links removed if possible. Otherwise, focus on building a high-quality site and waiting for trust to improve over time.

If your site disappeared from Google and Bing but still shows in Yahoo, the closest supported guidance is that it may be treated as spammy or penalized because of harmful activity associated with the domain or bad inbound links. The suggested checks are:

- Review backlinks in Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console
- Remove or disavow bad links
- If you believe it was penalized, file a reconsideration request with Google

This doesn’t prove a penalty is the cause, but it’s the only guidance supported here.

Google doesn’t replace meta keywords with a direct equivalent. The closest guidance here is that meta keywords are not used for ranking, though they may still be indexed and occasionally useful for matching misspellings, related terms, or deeper crawling via forms.

So if you’re looking for what to use instead, this evidence doesn’t point to another meta tag replacement. It suggests focusing on the page’s actual content and terms that appear on the page, since that’s what search engines rely on more than meta keywords.

From the provided material, SEO itself isn’t defined. The only related point is that HTML5 structure matters semantically: use `<article>` for blog posts, `<aside>` for tangentially related content, and `<section>` for generic sections. So, aside from meta tags, the closest supported guidance is that good page structure and semantic HTML elements are part of presenting content well for search engines.

Aside from meta tags, the evidence only says title tags are pretty helpful and shouldn’t be ignored. It also mentions that Google uses W3C standards and microdata formats/schemas, so those may be relevant too. More broadly, it suggests using all meta tags appropriate for the site and checking rankings if you remove them, but it does not list other SEO components in detail.

SEO is not just meta tags. It also includes structured data, but it should be used on content visible to users unless you’re providing a machine-readable version of visible information. Hidden markup for data not visible to users can be considered markup abuse and may risk manual action or disabled rich snippets. In your case, the guidance supports not adding structured data for non-visible product details on the homepage.

Your results page is likely empty because a JavaScript error elsewhere on the page is stopping other scripts from running, including the Google Custom Search script. The site also has related problems: a stylesheet is being served with the wrong MIME type, and some jQuery code is being run before the DOM is ready. 

The closest fix supported here is to debug the homepage scripts, especially code like `$('#breaking-news ul').newsticker();` and `$('#slideshow').cycle();`, and wrap jQuery calls in `$(document).ready(...)`. Also correct the CSS delivery issue.

It can take time for Google to index and start showing a new site, even if the keywords are already on the page. The only guidance provided here is to be patient and, if appropriate, add the site to web directories with good page rank to help it get discovered. If your site is new or hasn’t been indexed yet, searching by domain name may still not return it right away.

It may not be a problem with your site itself. Google’s results can take time to synchronize across different servers and datacenters, so your site may still appear in some places and not others.

The closest guidance supported here is to sign up for Webmaster Tools and monitor your site there. Since the site ranked only yesterday, give it some time and check again as Google updates its results.

If your redesign changed URLs, Google may stop counting old links the same way until redirects and reprocessing happen. A link to www.example.com is not the same as example.com, and a link to an old page path is not the same as the new one unless you use 301 permanent redirects. Even then, Google may take time to transfer link credit.

The thread also suggests Google may temporarily re-evaluate pages that change significantly, which could make links appear to drop for a while. It should sort itself out eventually, but there’s no instant fix indicated here beyond proper 301 redirects and waiting.

Google won’t remove the old pages from search results immediately just because you submitted a sitemap or removed links in Webmaster Tools. The guidance is to let Google recrawl the site.

What to do:
- Make sure deleted pages return 404 Not Found, or better, 410 Gone.
- Upload a clean sitemap for the current site.
- Wait several days and let Googlebot recrawl.

The old URLs should then naturally drop out of search results. There’s no need to delete the whole website and restart from scratch.

Use 301 redirects for old URLs that still have a matching page on the relaunched site. For pages that no longer exist and have no replacement, return a 404 so Google can remove them from its index. Also, make the 404 page helpful by explaining the redesign and pointing users to a sitemap or support/help page.

Use lowercase for URLs. Search engines can treat differently cased URLs as separate pages, which can create duplicate-content issues, and lowercase is easier for users to type.

For a SEO-friendly site, the guidance here is mainly about URL formatting rather than a specific HTML standard. It supports keeping URLs consistent and lowercase, but it doesn’t fully answer HTML structure best practices.

There isn’t a required SEO HTML “standard” from this evidence. The main guidance is to focus on content, clean and semantic markup, meta description, and title, since these matter more than URL file extensions.

If the extra slashes only appear at the end of the URL, use:

```apache
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} ^(.*?)(?:/){2,}$
RewriteRule . $1/ [R=301,L]
```

This redirects URLs like `/category/accessories///////` to `/category/accessories/` in a single 301. If slashes can occur elsewhere in the URL, the provided answer doesn’t cover that case.

For example, `/page/5/` and `/page/5` are treated as just different URI strings. The important part is to pick one format and use it everywhere to avoid duplicate URLs.

The provided guidance does not include a specific .htaccess rule to remove trailing slashes. It only says that either keeping or omitting the slash is fine if done consistently.

Use rewrite rules that map extensionless URLs to existing files, but don’t force a trailing slash unless you really want directory-style URLs. A pattern like this is supported by the thread:

RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILE}\.html -f
RewriteRule (.*)$ $1.html [L]

RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILE}\.php -f
RewriteRule (.*)$ $1.php [L]

RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILE}\.cgi -f
RewriteRule (.*)$ $1.cgi [L]

If your goal is specifically to remove trailing slashes, the provided discussion doesn’t give a complete working rule for that. It does say adding trailing slashes can break relative links, so the closest guidance is to avoid forcing them and instead use extension-removal rules or Apache MultiViews.

Use a rewrite pattern that accepts an optional trailing slash:

RewriteRule ^first-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=1 [QSA,L]
RewriteRule ^second-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=2 [QSA,L]
RewriteRule ^third-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=161 [QSA,L]

If you want to require the slash in the URL, use:

RewriteRule ^first-page/$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=1 [QSA,L]

The key point is that `^...$` matches the whole path exactly, so `(/)?` allows the slash without matching other extra characters.

There’s no difference for users, SEO, or crawlers as long as you’re consistent and always use one format. `/page/5/` and `/page/5` are treated as different URI strings, so the main point is to avoid mixing both forms and creating duplicate URLs. If you choose one style, stick with it across the site.

For the home page, http://www.domain.com and http://www.domain.com/ are treated the same, so you usually do not need a special redirect for the trailing slash there.

For other URLs, a trailing slash can make it a different URL and potentially different content. Files with extensions like .htm or .php should not have a trailing slash. Directories generally should have one, and Apache will often 301 redirect to the version with the slash automatically.

So the closest guidance is: use a canonical URL format and redirect only where the slash changes the meaning, usually on non-file directory paths.

Use server-side redirects, typically in .htaccess, and create as many grouped redirect rules as possible. For example, redirect /news_article to /news/ rather than separately redirecting /news_article/01, /news_article/02, etc.

If the old and new URLs differ a lot, you’ll still need many redirect rules, but grouping similar paths is the most efficient approach supported here.

If your new CMS can’t send 410s directly, the closest options are:

A 301 redirect is for pages that still have an equivalent new page; for old content you want removed, 410 or noindex is the supported approach here.

Put the redirect in the old domain’s .htaccess:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^www\.example\.com [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.example.com%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]

This redirects all requests from any host not matching www.example.com to the new domain, including paths like /folder and subdomains, while keeping the same request URI. Make sure the .htaccess applies to the old domain; if both domains point to the same server, they may share the same .htaccess.

A 301 or even 302 redirect will pass link equity, so there isn’t a way to redirect everything to the new site and avoid carrying over backlinks/“juice” with a normal redirect. The closest supported approach is to send all old URLs to a single “we’ve moved” page on the old domain, and place a nofollow link there to the new site.

Use 301 redirects, and make each old URL redirect to the matching new URL on the new site. That is the closest supported approach for keeping users and search engines on the right content.

Apache itself doesn’t really “serve requests for content from other sites” from this evidence; the issue described is a PHP script making an outbound connection.

The closest supported options are:
- block the target by IP with an iptables OUTPUT rule, using the domain’s IP address
- if the script takes the domain in the URL, use an .htaccess rewrite to redirect/refresh instead
- modify the PHP script so it checks the domain parameter and refuses to connect if it matches the blocked site

If you need to stop Apache from acting on requests to a specific site, the evidence only supports blocking the outbound connection or changing the script behavior.

If you can identify a common signature, the best place to drop the traffic is as far out as possible: ideally at the external router or firewall before it reaches Apache. If your inboard firewall supports deep inspection, you can move the blocking there too.

If the requests are too varied to match simply, Apache alone may be the only place you can block them, though that still leaves them reaching the server. iptables is possible, but the guidance here says it’s not very intelligent, so it’s better suited at the router level than as the main solution. You could also stop Apache from logging those specific denied actions, though that isn’t recommended.

If Apache/PHP has already started sending HTML, it’s too late to change the status to 404 or 410 because status codes must be sent in HTTP headers first. The fix is to check whether the content exists before outputting any page content, then send the proper 404/410 header if needed.

If you’re currently redirecting to a 404.php page, that’s common and usually works, but it’s not ideal compared with serving the 404 response directly. Also, a 301 or 302 redirect is not a substitute for a 404; those are headers too and still need to be sent before any HTML.
