Use a 301 redirect. That will make requests to the old URL path display the target page, such as `moved.html`, regardless of which URI under that virtual folder was requested. The example answer points to an HTTP redirection page for this setup.

Using visibility: hidden by itself isn’t the issue; the key point is intent. If the fonts/content are being hidden to manipulate search rankings, that would be considered cloaking and against search engine rules, regardless of whether it’s done with CSS or JavaScript.

This evidence doesn’t specifically address preloading web fonts, but it does support the general guidance that hiding content for SEO manipulation is risky. If the hidden fonts are purely for rendering/performance and not to affect rankings, this answer doesn’t say that would be penalized.

Loading fonts from Google or another remote source can be slower than using local fonts, but it lets you use a specific font across systems. The supported guidance here is to prefer local/system fonts when you can, and use a font API if you absolutely need a particular font.

This doesn’t say anything about SEO or using visibility:hidden. Based on the available info, the closest advice is that hidden/remote-font techniques may affect load speed, but there’s no evidence here that they are bad for SEO.

Using visibility:hidden to preload fonts isn’t directly addressed here, but the general SEO point is that content hidden behind JavaScript or click-to-reveal isn’t automatically bad for SEO if search engines can process the page and the content is still accessible.

The guidance here is to avoid relying entirely on JavaScript with no fallback. If text or navigation is hidden, provide a no-JS fallback or a server-rendered/default visible version for users and bots. For fonts specifically, hiding them with CSS for preload is a performance technique, but this evidence doesn’t say it hurts SEO. The closest supported advice is: make sure important text and links are still available without JS.

Yes—based on the answer here, Google can understand content hidden with display:none and take it into account for rankings. So preloading both sections and toggling one visible at a time should be fine SEO-wise, as long as the content is available in the page and your JavaScript shows it gracefully on click.

The evidence does not specifically address hiding all other content except the clicked jump-linked section, but it supports the general approach of using hidden content and toggling visibility. If you can, also make sure the content remains accessible when JavaScript is disabled.

Use jump links that call JavaScript to change the media time. The supported pattern here is:

`oAudio.currentTime = time;`

So for a one-page site, you can make each link run a function like `ChangeTime(time)` that pauses the player, sets `currentTime`, then plays.

This does not cover hiding/showing page sections, but the closest supported approach is to use the clicked jump link to control what is displayed with JavaScript, while the audio/video time is changed through `currentTime`. If you want, I can help adapt this into a one-page jump-link layout.

If your goal is to make a one-page site where only the section for the clicked jump link is shown, the provided material doesn’t cover that behavior. It only shows that an overlapping container can block clicks on navigation links, even when the visible content seems not to overlap.

Closest guidance supported here: make sure no element, such as a wide container like `#right`, overlaps the jump links and intercepts clicks. If links still aren’t clickable, inspect the layout for hidden or transparent overlapping elements.

The provided thread does not include an answer, so it doesn’t establish whether Google always downranks pages with hidden text.

What it does cover is the concern that hidden text can be used for spam, while an FAQ with collapsed answers is also a common user interface pattern. Based on that, the safest supported guidance is: don’t assume all hidden text is treated the same, and if you use hidden FAQ answers, make sure they are for user convenience rather than to stuff keywords or mislead search engines.

A hidden or 1px iframe should not lower your page rank. The concern in the answer is SEO-related: if search engines crawl content inside an iframe, they may associate that content with the iframe’s own page rather than your hosting page. So it’s not ideal for important site content, but it isn’t described as a ranking penalty. If you can avoid iframes, that’s better; if not, using one is sometimes the only practical option.

Google and other search engines can understand JavaScript to some extent, so click-to-show content is not automatically bad for SEO. But it’s still best to make sure the page can be viewed in some form without JavaScript, especially navigation.

A common safe approach is to use a no-JS fallback, such as Modernizr’s .no-js class. Then you can show the menu and other text content by default when JavaScript isn’t available, while keeping the interactive version for users with JavaScript.

So the closest guidance is: keep the design if you want, but provide fallback content that search engines and non-JavaScript users can access.

Google’s guidance here is about text that’s hidden from visitors but shown to search engines. If the text is genuinely part of the page and still presented to users, that’s less likely to be an issue.

The example answer suggests not using display:none for the heading text, and instead using CSS to present the text visually while keeping it visible to users. It also says the concern is hidden text “solely for search engines rather than visitors.”

I can’t confirm a specific Google penalty for overflow:hidden from the evidence alone. The closest supported guidance is: avoid hiding text from visitors; present it in a way users can still see it.

Based on this, using overflow:auto would not affect rankings or get you penalized, because it isn’t considered manipulation. The same guidance would most likely apply to overflow:hidden if it’s just a layout choice and not used to hide keyword text for ranking purposes. If you’re using it to conceal keyword-rich content, that could be a different situation, but that isn’t covered here.

Based on the thread, using hidden text for a CSS sprite/button fallback should be fine and not penalized, as long as it isn’t done to manipulate search rankings. The key distinction is intent: hidden text used for usability or fallback is generally acceptable. The evidence doesn’t specifically mention `overflow: hidden`, but it supports the broader idea that hiding text for UI purposes is not the kind of hidden text that triggers penalties.

Yes, both visibility:hidden and display:none can affect SEO if they’re used to hide keyword-rich content for ranking manipulation. The key issue is the intent: hiding content to deceive search engines is considered cloaking and can violate search engine rules, regardless of whether you use CSS, JavaScript, or text-indent:-9999px.

If content is hidden for normal UX reasons, the technique itself isn’t the main problem. The evidence here only supports that using these methods to manipulate rankings is risky and can get you penalized.

Yes, hiding content with CSS or JavaScript can affect SEO if keyword-rich text is hidden from users on page load. Google expects users to be able to find the text they searched for without needing to uncover it first.

That said, there is no absolute ban on hidden content. Common patterns like dropdown menus, tooltips, and tabs that reveal content through user interaction are generally fine.

So:
- `visibility:hidden` / `display:none` can be a problem if they hide important keyword text initially.
- If the content is meant for UI behavior and is later revealed to the user, it’s generally acceptable.
- The main risk is hidden text used to manipulate rankings.

No. `rel="nofollow"` won’t help here. Search engines don’t request hash links or `javascript:` links from your server, so adding `nofollow` won’t change how they’re processed. These links also aren’t passing PageRank to anything else, so there’s no need to use `nofollow` to block that.

If anything, adding `nofollow` could be ignored or, in the worst case, waste PageRank. For offscreen sliding content, this answer only supports that `nofollow` is not the solution for SEO concerns around those menu links.

Use a URL scheme that changes with each view, such as hashbang URLs like `#!/subpage`, and make your server return the matching content when bots request the escaped-fragment version, like `?_escaped_fragment_=subpage`. That lets JavaScript users get the sliding/offscreen effect, while bots and non-JS users still receive crawlable content from normal server responses.

So the basic approach is:
- update the URL for each page/state
- serve equivalent content without JavaScript
- have JavaScript enhance the transition/animation only

This is the closest supported guidance for keeping AJAX-style sliding content search-bot friendly.

If you want offscreen or hidden content without hurting SEO, the closest supported guidance here is to keep the content on the page and use proper URL handling rather than moving everything to one homepage or duplicating pages. For a site merge, preserve each existing page’s content by redirecting each old URL to the most relevant new URL with a 301 redirect. Don’t send everything to the new homepage. If multiple old pages map to one new page, redirect them all there.

Yes, but only a little. The answer says you want your text content as close to the top of the source as possible, so having lots of structural HTML before the main content is not ideal. However, it also says this is not a huge factor and you should not worry too much or make extreme changes just for this. More important SEO factors exist.

CSS positioning/formatting itself does not directly affect SEO rankings. It mainly changes how the page looks to users, not how bots or crawlers read it.

That said, better design and usability can indirectly help SEO if it leads to more users staying, returning, linking, or sharing the page. So the CSS isn’t a ranking factor by itself, but the user experience it creates can have indirect effects.

CSS positioning itself is probably not a direct SEO ranking factor. The guidance here says valid HTML and/or CSS likely doesn’t affect rankings directly, but clean, valid code is recommended because it helps search engines crawl and index content properly. If positioning causes invalid or hard-to-interpret markup, that could indirectly hurt SEO by making crawling/indexing harder.

Changing only the IP address by moving your domain to another server is not documented here as having a specific SEO effect. The available evidence only says the thread asked whether changing servers (and thus the IP address) would affect SEO, but it contains no answer.

Closest guidance supported by the evidence: you are not changing the domain name, only the server/IP. If you want the safest migration, keep the site content and URLs unchanged while switching servers.

If the image has changed enough that you want search engines to treat it as a different image, it’s reasonable to version the filename so the new version gets picked up. That suggests the filename can reflect the update rather than staying identical.

Some CDNs also support query strings on image URLs to indicate an updated asset.

What this covers: versioning image filenames/URLs can help signal a changed image. It does not say there’s a specific SEO keyword format you must use.

For SEO benefit, image filenames should include short, concise keywords. The image URL/path can also include keywords and that can help, but it’s less important than the filename itself. So a descriptive filename like keyword.jpg is the key part, and adding relevant keywords in the folder path may provide some additional benefit.

For SEO benefit, the filenames should be descriptive, and the URLs should be structured logically. The answer specifically advises using descriptive filenames for SEO.

It also suggests organizing images in a centralized directory structure, with general-purpose images in one folder and object-specific images in subdirectories, often using IDs rather than product or category names. It doesn’t prove this is best for SEO, but says it’s a practical, extensible approach.

So the closest guidance supported is: use descriptive image filenames, and keep URLs/paths organized and logical rather than relying on category or product names in directory structure.

Using IP-based geolocation for regular users is not, by itself, an SEO problem. Search engines generally won’t dislike the content if they’re seeing the same kind of content a normal visitor would.

The main limitation is that crawlers may only see one location-specific version, so it’s harder to target multiple regions. A practical fix is to let users manually change their region, such as with a link or form. That also helps when IP geolocation is wrong and lets you create region-specific URLs that can be indexed, for example by submitting them in an XML sitemap.

Blocking a specific geolocation can be done with geolocation scripts/services, including PHP options. The main SEO risk is blocking search engines by mistake. The guidance here is to check the visitor’s user agent for known bots like “Googlebot” or “Baidu” first, and only apply the geolocation block to non-search-engine traffic.

That said, if a scraper spoofs a user agent, this method can be bypassed. Also, search engines may have limited presence from certain regions, so blocking by geography can affect crawling if you’re not careful.

No, there’s no intrinsic SEO advantage to www over non-www, or http over https. The main issue is duplicate access: if both versions of the same site are reachable, search engines may index both, splitting links and value.

A 301 permanent redirect is the usual fix. It tells search engines the move is permanent and helps transfer value to the preferred, canonical version.

Best practice is to choose one version (www or non-www, and one protocol such as https) and use it consistently, including internal links. If possible, links on your site should point directly to the preferred version so redirects aren’t needed as often.

No—www is not better than non-www for SEO. The important part is consistency: pick one version and use it for all URLs. A 301 redirect from the version you don’t use to the one you do is a good practice, and setting your preferred domain in Google Webmaster Tools can help.

Backlinks not showing in Google doesn’t necessarily mean they aren’t there. The thread only shows that the site had been optimized and that Bing/Yahoo returned many backlinks, but it doesn’t include a recorded answer explaining Google’s behavior.

The closest guidance supported is that Google may simply not display backlink data the same way, or not show all links via a link: query. So even with good SEO, daily social updates, directories, redirects, and schema in place, Google may still not report backlinks in a visible way.

If you want to verify backlinks, use other tools or Search Console rather than relying on Google’s link: operator.

“Login Only” usually means you’re only able to log in, not bypass the site’s database restrictions. For a WordPress database backup, the closest supported options are:

- Ask the hosting company’s tech support for a backup; they may provide a one-click backup or SQL dump.
- If you have SSH access, use `mysqldump`.
- If you don’t have SSH, use a MySQL client on your computer, but you’ll need the host to allow remote DB access. In that case, `localhost` must be replaced with the server’s IP address and port 3306 must be open.
- If you have a control panel, use its backup feature to generate an SQL file.

A “Login Only” rejection usually means the server/firewall is seeing repeated failed SMTP AUTH logins and is treating them as suspicious, often as brute-force attempts. The likely fix is to identify the source IP or host from the logs and block that specific IP with your firewall/iptables or similar protection.

If the source is a domain name, resolve it first with nslookup example.com. Be careful: if it’s a shared or pooled host, blocking it may also block valid users from that network. Also, if the attempts are coming from changing IPs, the same pattern may keep reappearing from other addresses.

Create the user/grants for `something`@`localhost`, not only `something`@`%`.

MySQL treats `localhost` as a different host from `%`, so when you connect locally it looks for `something`@`localhost` and rejects `something`@`%`.

Add a matching account and privileges, for example:

`CREATE USER 'something'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';`
`GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON something.* TO 'something'@'localhost';`

Then reconnect.

Having a “Home” link on the home page is generally not negative for SEO. The provided answer doesn’t mention any SEO penalty from a home navigation item.

What it does say is that shared pages like “About us” or “Vacancies” should be managed in one place instead of duplicated, and that two separate WordPress installs add admin and maintenance overhead. So based on this, the concern is more about site structure and duplication than a “Home” menu item hurting SEO.

No. Based on the provided guidance, having an explicit “home” link is not described as negative for SEO. The answer says there’s “no harm” in having a home link unless the navigation is already crowded. It also suggests keeping the logo linked to the home page too. So the main consideration is usability and navigation space, not SEO harm.

No. The evidence suggests the bigger SEO concern is lack of internal click navigation, not having a “home” item on the home page. Internal links help SEO, and a sitemap can help search engines find and index content even if users can’t click to it. So a home navigation item is not shown to be negative here; the closest supported guidance is that more internal linking is generally beneficial.

Use a condition on HTTPS and the host, then redirect to the non-www version:

RewriteCond %{HTTPS} ^on$
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www\.x\.co\.uk$
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://x\.co\.uk$1 [L,R=301]

This redirects only https://www.x.co.uk to https://x.co.uk, and leaves non-HTTPS requests unchanged.

Yes. A 301 permanent redirect is the usual way to send non-www to www while preserving the protocol, and it tells search engines the move is permanent so value can be transferred.

The key is to redirect to the canonical version you want, so:
- http://example.com → http://www.example.com
- https://example.com → https://www.example.com

Also make internal links use the preferred address so redirects are rarely needed. If the site is accessible on both http and https, that should be handled too, since duplication is the underlying SEO issue.

If your domain is using nameservers not controlled by the registrar, you must add the DNS record at the company that controls those nameservers, not at the registrar.

For routing host.com to www.host.com, you’d typically create the needed DNS entry in the DNS panel for the domain, usually at the nameserver provider. The evidence specifically covers TXT/SPF records, but the same idea applies: DNS changes must be made where the nameservers are hosted.

Check which nameservers your domain is using, then add the record there. If you’re using a “panel” in .NET or cPanel, look for DNS Zone / DNS Management for that domain.

DNS can point host.com and www.host.com to different places, but if both are ending up on the same IP, the likely issue is how the records are set in your DNS/panel, or that your provider is automatically aliasing www to the root domain.

What the evidence supports is that separate A records can be used for each name:
- host.com → your home IP
- www.host.com → your webhosting IP

If DNS alone won’t keep them separate, the closest supported alternative is using a reverse proxy to serve one site at www.host.com and another at host.com.

If you want, I can help you map the exact DNS records to create in your .NET panel.

To make host.com go to www.host.com, set the root domain to redirect to www rather than trying to use a wildcard host. An A record points to an IP address, so if you only have a CNAME for www, you’d need either:

- an A record for host.com pointing to your server’s IP, then configure a redirect from host.com to www.host.com, or
- a redirect service if your host doesn’t give you a fixed IP.

The site should be accessible from one version only, and the other should redirect to it. If your panel route supports redirects, set the non-www domain to redirect permanently to www.host.com.

Yes, but only a little. The answer says keywords in the image URL/folder path can help, especially if they’re short and concise, but the filename is the more important part for SEO. So between /foobar/images/keyword.jpg and /keyword/images/keyword.jpg, the second is likely slightly better, but the main benefit comes from the image filename itself.

It doesn’t really matter for SEO between a folder-style URL and a file-style URL. The key point is that URLs aren’t required to map directly to real files or folders, and many sites use rewrites so the visible URL is just for users.

The best guidance supported here is to make URLs short, descriptive, and user-friendly. So a clean, readable URL is preferable, but the choice of folder vs. filename itself isn’t the important SEO factor.

If the old URLs all start with /cdn/, you don’t need to match each nested folder level. A single rule can remove that part and keep the rest of the path:

RedirectMatch 301 ^/cdn/(.*) /$1

So /cdn/folder/folder/file.html would redirect to /folder/folder/file.html.

Changing from .html to no extension is not inherently better for SEO. The key issue is that changing URL structure can make pages look new to search engines, lose links temporarily, and cause 404s for users until search engines re-index.

If you do change extensions or remove them, use 301 redirects from the old URLs to the new ones so search engines and browsers know the pages moved. If the file names stay the same, a redirect pattern can handle it.

If you’re deciding whether to use .html at all, the evidence only supports that changing extensions on a live site has SEO and usability consequences; it doesn’t show that one extension ranks better than another.

There’s no SEO benefit to removing the filetype extension. Keeping “.html” mainly helps with consistency if you already have many URLs and want to avoid unnecessary 301 redirects. Removing it can give more flexibility if you later change technologies like .php or .aspx, and it makes URLs slightly shorter and less intimidating, but that’s about it.

From the evidence, the file type itself doesn’t improve SEO. WordPress or PHP mainly make managing pages easier and can help you create SEO-friendly URLs. You can achieve the same SEO results with static HTML if the content and structure are equivalent.

So the choice is mostly about maintenance:
- .html: simple static pages
- .php/templates: easier to reuse header/sidebar/footer across many pages
- “nothing” isn’t really a separate SEO advantage

If your goal is SEO, focus on content, site structure, and URLs rather than whether the extension is .html or .php.

There’s no simple “.html, .php or nothing” SEO rule here. An almost empty homepage isn’t automatically bad for SEO. What matters is whether the homepage has a purpose and whether it needs to rank for non-branded keywords.

If your important content is on inner pages, those pages can still rank even if the homepage is minimal. Also, if the content is loaded with JavaScript, search engines may still be able to crawl and index it depending on how it’s implemented.

So the closest guidance is: make the homepage useful to visitors, and only worry about adding more content there if you want the homepage itself to rank.

If you’re changing from .html to .php, use 301 redirects from every old URL to the new one. That’s the supported way to preserve SEO as much as possible.

If you can avoid extensions entirely, that’s considered a good option too because the URLs are more user-friendly.

So, best choices:
- .php: fine, but 301-redirect old .html URLs
- nothing: also fine, often preferred for clean URLs
- don’t leave both versions accessible without redirects, or you may split SEO value

Google generally does not care whether a page is .html or .php. What matters is the content returned and the HTTP headers/status.

The closest guidance here is that browsers render based on the response content type, not the filename extension, and search engines should be told about redirects with a 301 if you move from one URL to another. So if .html and .php pages serve the same content, Google would not treat them differently just because of the extension.

No clear difference is indicated. The answer says Google indexes pages with query strings fine, and that if you keep the same URLs, users and search engines will see them the same, so you don’t have to worry about pages being reindexed just because of the extension. It also says SSI can be done in PHP without needing query strings. So based on this, .html, .shtml, and .php pages are not treated differently by Google just because of the file extension; the URL and content matter more.

No. Based on the evidence, there’s no SEO benefit to keeping or removing the .html extension.

Keeping it only helps with consistency if you already have many existing URLs and want to avoid adding 301 redirects. Removing it can give you more flexibility if you later change technologies, and it makes URLs a bit shorter and less intimidating, but that’s not an SEO advantage.

No. The accepted guidance says adding .html does not provide SEO benefit and can even add unnecessary processing if you need rewriting. If your pages are generated dynamically, keeping clean URLs like /answer/my-question-no-1 is fine. Changing them to /answer/my-question-no-1.html would not improve rankings, and may introduce drawbacks.

The evidence only addresses top-level domains and regional targeting, not www vs. non-www.

What it does support is that domain choice can matter for country-specific searches, and that using separate regional paths like /us/ and /ca/ is a valid approach. It does not say whether www.foo.com or foo.com is better.

Closest guidance: pick one version and use it consistently, and if you have separate regional audiences, use clear region-specific structure or country-specific domains.

Use both, for different purposes. The CNAME is for DNS so www.example.com resolves to your server. The server-side rewrite/redirect is for making example.com send visitors to www.example.com.

So the usual setup is:
- point www to your server with a CNAME
- redirect the non-www version to the www version

If you’re asking which is “better” to use as the main public address, this answer doesn’t choose between them; it only supports using one canonical version and redirecting the other.

Use the version without the question mark in the middle of the path. It’s treated as a real path, so the hierarchy is clearer and easier for search engines and people to understand. The version with the question mark is treated as query arguments after the main document, not as part of the path.

For www vs non-www specifically, this evidence doesn’t compare those two directly. The closest guidance it supports is to pick one consistent URL format and use it everywhere.

Chrome usually decides a page’s language from things like the site’s content, headers, or the user’s browser settings. The evidence here only supports the general guidance that you should not try to force users to use a specific browser; instead, fix the site so it works correctly across browsers. If Chrome is showing Serbian unexpectedly, the closest supported advice is to check your app’s language/content and browser compatibility rather than trying to force Chrome itself.

You can’t force Chrome to treat a site as English just with a meta tag. The evidence says Google/Chrome use the visible content of the page to determine language, not code-level tags like `meta name="language"` or `lang` attributes.

So if Chrome is identifying it as Serbian, the closest fix supported here is to make the visible page content English. If the content is actually English but still misdetected, the provided evidence only shows that language tags won’t override that detection.

Chrome usually decides a site’s language from the page content and tags like `<html lang="...">`, not from a manual “force English” switch for the site itself.

The closest guidance supported here is to make sure your English version is clearly marked, for example:
- `<html lang="en">` on the English pages
- correct `hreflang="en"` / `hreflang="sr"` links between versions

If Chrome is still showing Serbian, the issue is likely that the page content or language tags are making it look Serbian. There’s no evidence here of a Chrome setting that forces a website to English.

The answer covers cost and setup tradeoffs, but not SEO directly. It suggests choosing a CDN if you need to handle traffic spikes or variable demand, and using your own server may be more cost-effective for steady, high traffic. It also notes that CDN integration depends on the provider, and for your own static server, rsync over SSH is a common way to move files.

For SEO impact, this thread does not say whether moving media files to a CDN helps or hurts rankings. The closest guidance it supports is to focus on reliability and performance: if the CDN improves speed and availability, that may be beneficial, but the SEO effect is not addressed here.

If you set up a proper redirect from the old image URLs to the new CDN URLs, the SEO impact should settle back to normal after about a month. You may see some ranking fluctuations during that period. The guidance here favors moving to the CDN if it improves page speed, since faster loading is generally beneficial for search engines.

Hosting images on a CDN can impact SEO if those images are currently helping your rankings. The main point is that image SEO depends on things like good alt text and relevant surrounding content. If you move images to a CDN, using a CNAME to keep the URL on your domain is suggested as a way to avoid affecting rankings. If images are not contributing much to SEO, the impact may be minimal.

Hosting images on a CDN is described as a way to serve static content, including images, CSS, JavaScript, and videos. The answer does not say that using a CDN hurts SEO. It says a CDN should be used when it improves speed for most users and is financially viable. So, based on this, hosting images on a CDN is not shown to negatively impact SEO; the closest supported guidance is to use it when it makes the site faster.

The provided material doesn’t give a browser-specific rule of thumb. It only supports the general idea that reducing file size and enabling gzip help with bandwidth and page load time, especially for first-time visitors who won’t have cached assets yet.

So the closest guidance is to optimize for faster loading overall rather than any particular browser. If you want, I can help draft a practical browser support strategy from general best practices.

A general rule of thumb isn’t given for browsers in the provided text. It only says that, for media, you should host everything you can and delegate when you can’t, with the choice depending on control, cost, latency, and bandwidth. It also suggests most sites host their own data except for large, high-bandwidth media like large images and videos. If you’re asking about browsers specifically, this doesn’t cover that directly. The closest guidance would be to prioritize the environments most of your users use and optimize based on practical limits like compatibility, performance, and user share.

There isn’t a single universal rule of thumb in the provided guidance. The closest advice is to base your target on current usage statistics and choose the minimum browsers/resolutions that cover most users.

For screen resolution, the cited figures suggest 1024x768 as an effective minimum, while noting that many users don’t browse fullscreen.

For browsers, the guidance suggests checking browser statistics and that Firefox/Chrome users often run recent versions due to auto-updates. It also recommends consulting multiple statistics sources to get a broader picture before deciding.

The evidence doesn’t provide an answer. It only shows that someone asked whether WordPress sites get indexed quicker than regular sites and mentions opinions suggesting WordPress may help with SEO or meta configuration, but there’s no recorded answer or confirmation.

So, based on this evidence, I can’t say that WordPress websites are indexed quicker. The closest supported guidance is that some people believe WordPress helps with SEO setup, especially meta configuration, but the thread itself does not verify that search engines index WordPress sites faster.

Use the keyword that matches what each page actually says, and optimize page by page rather than the site overall. The keyword list only shows what Google recognizes for your site; it does not mean you will rank for those terms.

So if your content uses “colors,” target “colors.” If it uses “colours,” target “colours.” If your audience searches both spellings, it can make sense to include both naturally on the relevant page, but don’t rely on combining keywords just to get results.

If the site is new, it may also take months before pages perform for those terms.

If you mean HTML meta keywords, the evidence says major search engines do not use the meta keywords tag, so it doesn’t matter much whether you use colors, colours, or both for SEO.

If you still want to include keywords for some other reason, the closest guidance supported here is to use the terms that match your content. But for search engines like Google, the meta keywords tag is not used.

Use one keyword consistently rather than splitting it up. The closest guidance here is to keep the company name as a single word in the text, then apply styling separately with CSS or JavaScript. If you need both spellings, use them only where they naturally fit in normal text; don’t break the word into pieces for SEO.

What you showed would not be keyword stuffing, because the phrase isn’t being repeated excessively. The accepted guidance says repeating the same word more than 2 times is where it becomes a concern, and gave an example like “purchase glasses, Purchase glass” with repeated words in title and alt as keyword stuffing.

So, using “purchase glasses” once in the title and alt, and “purchase socks” once for another product, is described as reasonable.

Repeating content that helps users is not necessarily keyword stuffing, as long as it’s not just stuffing keywords related to your site. The guidance here suggests that repeated help text across pages is better moved to a separate help page and linked from each page to avoid duplicate content concerns.

For titles, repeating something like “Download PDF” can be acceptable if it’s relevant to each page and each title is still unique, such as “Download PDF: Article one,” “Download PDF: Article two,” and so on. It does not say this would be spam. It also does not claim it will improve Google traffic; only that relevance and uniqueness matter.

Alexa rank is based on visits from users in Alexa’s system, not on backlinks, so it won’t show “many back links” the way a backlink checker would. The evidence says Alexa ranking can be improved by increasing Alexa-tracked traffic, for example by installing the Alexa toolbar or adding an Alexa widget to your site. That widget tracks visitors with Alexa, but it may slow the page down. If you want to understand backlinks specifically, Alexa rank is not the right metric.

Alexa’s backlink count can differ a lot from Google Webmaster Tools and Ahrefs because each uses a different crawler, and they don’t crawl the web in the same way, at the same volume, or at the same rate. So Alexa may not show many of your back links even if other tools do. The evidence only supports that the difference comes from differing crawl methods, not which tool is best for every use case.

Alexa rank is a traffic score, not a backlink count, so it won’t show many of your backlinks. The evidence only indicates that different URLs can have the same Alexa rank if they have the same score or similar traffic. So if you’re using Alexa rank for a tool, it’s measuring ranking based on traffic, not how many links point to a page. If you need backlink information, you’ll need a backlink-specific source rather than Alexa rank.

Alexa’s meta tag is only for proving site ownership; it does not track visitors. If it’s loaded once on your site, that’s enough.

Alexa ranking is based on pageviews/visits from people who have the Alexa toolbar installed. With infinite scroll, the page will probably count as only one view, so it may not help your Alexa rank much.

If your site isn’t ranking well on Alexa, this is likely because Alexa rank depends on toolbar users and pageviews, not on the meta tag itself. Alexa rank can also be misleading and may change without any real improvement.

Alexa rank is based on Alexa’s count of unique visitors. The thread suggests that, rather than focusing on Alexa, you shouldn’t worry about it because it’s described as a useless metric. One answer says installing the Alexa toolbar and visiting your site daily would increase the rank, but that’s not a meaningful measure of site quality. The closest guidance supported here is: don’t prioritize Alexa ranking; focus on real traffic and engagement instead.

Alexa ranks are often unreliable, and new sites may not get a rank quickly, especially without much traffic. The best-supported advice here is to make sure Alexa can index the site, then drive real traffic to it. Things that may help include installing the Alexa toolbar, getting users who have the toolbar to visit, and attracting traffic from blogs, forums, Twitter, and email newsletters. Even then, the accuracy may still be poor, and very low-traffic sites may not get a meaningful Alexa rank.

Yes, you can send content via RSS Feed, and if other sites republish it, that is duplicate content. The guidance here says the republishing sites are the ones that would be hit with duplicate-content penalties, not your site. It also says Google has improved its algorithm to credit the original publisher, though it’s not perfect.

To help reduce issues, include a hard link to the original article in your RSS feed so republished copies show you as the original author.

If you mean sending your content out through RSS for others to display, the guidance here is that excerpts are generally seen as more acceptable, while republishing the full content is more likely to cross a line unless the other site explicitly allows it. If it’s your own content and you permit republishing, that’s the clearest path. For anything business-related or legally sensitive, you should check with a lawyer.

It’s likely referer spam. The HTTP referer field can be faked, so strange incoming links in your stats may not be real visitors from that site. A good check is to compare the request IPs with the domain shown in the referrer logs. If they don’t match, the traffic likely came from somewhere else, possibly a server trying to promote that site.

No. `nofollow` is for links you don’t want to endorse or pass ranking influence to, typically when you don’t have editorial control over the link. `rel="canonical"` is for duplicate or equivalent pages and tells search engines which URL is the primary one. If a page is non-canonical because it’s a duplicate, the right fix is to use a canonical URL, not `nofollow` on links to it.

No. The guidance here says rel="nofollow" is not an acceptable way to handle internal links just because they are not part of your keyword strategy or because they point to non-relevant pages. Nofollow is meant for links you don’t have editorial control over, not for manipulating how Google crawls or interprets your own site.

For internal links, the better approach is to change the anchor text if needed. If you can’t, leave the links alone.

The evidence doesn’t say that shared or reseller webhosting accounts let customers install and run their own web servers like Node.js. It only covers that reseller hosting may have different resource limits, that customers may expect support, and that the author prefers using a VPS with tools like Webmin/Virtualmin for managing multiple customers.

So the closest guidance supported here is: if you need customers to run more advanced server software, a VPS may be a better fit than shared hosting or a typical reseller account.

It depends on the hosting type.

On shared hosting, you usually can’t run customized programs continuously in the back end or have full control like installing and running your own webserver/node.js setup. On a dedicated server, you usually can do those things.

CPU/memory limits still apply based on the hardware or resources assigned, and you typically would not get sudo on shared hosting. CRON jobs may be allowed on both, and can sometimes be used as a workaround.

Not from this evidence. It only shows that you can buy multiple hosting accounts and use their DNS servers for redundancy, plus set up separate email accounts. It does not say whether webhosting accounts let customers install or run application servers like Node.js. The closest supported guidance is that the question is more complex than simple DNS tricks and may need a different solution than standard web hosting.

Based on this, the claimed SEO benefit is that shorter URLs are considered better for SEO. It also says removing “/category/” makes URLs easier to remember for users and avoids using an English word in the URL, which may help if the site is in another language.

It does not provide any other SEO-specific advantage or a disadvantage for keeping “/category/”.

The supported guidance is that your current structure is already considered very good for users and SEO. Changing it to add extra qualifiers like /cat-land or /prod-details is not recommended because longer URLs are generally less user-friendly and can slightly dilute keyword value. If you want a change, the only safe improvement mentioned is adding trailing slashes consistently:

www.example.com/category1/
www.example.com/category1/sub-category/
www.example.com/category1/sub-category/product-name/

So for SEO, the evidence supports keeping the URLs short and simple rather than adding more path segments.

Using a URL like www.example.com/category/subcategory/ can help a little because Google may consider the URL text as a relevance signal. In the example, putting “subcategory” closer to the end of the URL may improve the keyword match slightly.

But the main SEO factors are page content and domain, so changing URL format alone should not usually cause a big ranking shift if the content stays the same. A proper 301 redirect, updated canonical, sitemap, and resubmission are the right steps.

If rankings still don’t move, it may be because Google hasn’t fully refreshed its index yet, or the redirect/status handling isn’t correct.

If a site is hosted in the USA and accessed from the UK to Australia, the main issue is usually distance/latency, which can make it feel slow.

The supported ways to improve it are:
- move static files like images, CSS, and JavaScript closer to users
- use a CDN with a presence in Australia (or nearby for the users)
- if needed, host files in a local data center and route users with Anycast DNS
- if it is still slow, the heavier option is to replicate the whole app in that region, which is more complex and expensive

So, for faster UK-to-Australia access, the closest guidance is to serve static content from a nearby region/CDN and keep the main app in the USA if possible.

A UK-to-Australia connection mainly affects latency, not raw throughput. For website visitors, a faster server link only helps if your server is actually hitting its bandwidth limit; otherwise the long distance is usually the bigger factor in perceived speed.

To estimate what you need, multiply expected concurrent users by average data per user. For example, 100 simultaneous users on 200 KB pages could need about 20 MB of bandwidth.

Sites with lots of media or high user counts need more bandwidth; small text-heavy sites usually need much less.

A sign you need to upgrade is that your server’s network usage is consistently near the limit. On Windows Server, check Network Interface bytes sent/sec in Performance Monitor.

There isn’t an answer in the thread confirming that Google Analytics lets you save a custom default date range as a personal preference. The only thing shown is that the current default display is “last one month,” and the user wants “last 3 days” instead.

So, based on this, I can’t confirm that the default date range can be changed and saved once. The closest guidance supported here is that you may need to change the range manually each time.

If the domains are for different brands or products, it can make sense to register them to protect the names and keep competitors from taking them. But registering extra keyword-rich domains just for SEO is not recommended; that can be penalized. The guidance here leans toward using one main domain for your site and investing in it, while buying only the domains you actually need.

If you do use multiple domains, a 301 redirect to the single main domain is supported by the example, but the evidence doesn’t fully cover sitemap setup or Google Webmaster Tools details.

It’s generally not a good idea to have multiple domains serving the same content, because search engines may treat it as duplicate content. The guidance here says Google can penalize this and may not know which domain is authoritative.

If you need to move to a new domain, the supported approach is to use 301 permanent redirects so search engines understand the content has migrated. If the second domain is only temporary, it still recommends redirecting rather than serving the same site on both domains.

Registering multiple domains is not inherently a bad idea, but spreading them across different registrars is generally a bad idea. The guidance here says major registrars are extremely unlikely to steal your domains, and many loss stories come from people missing renewal emails. It also says using different providers for each domain is an administrative nightmare.

So if your goal is just safety, this supports keeping domains in one place rather than splitting them up. It doesn’t directly address pointing multiple domains to a single website, but it does support that registering many domains separately is usually not worth the management burden.

A good place mentioned is themeforest.com. It’s described as having very high-quality templates for many kinds of sites, including plain HTML, Facebook, and WordPress. If you want more creative options than the standard template sites, that’s the strongest recommendation supported here.

Yes. Links or sitemap entries using https can cause Google to index https versions of a site that is otherwise HTTP.

The supported fix is to:
- replace any internal https links with http
- check sitemap files for https URLs
- add a 301 redirect from all https URLs to the matching http URLs

A canonical tag was suggested in the question, but the guidance provided here specifically recommends correcting links/sitemaps and using 301 redirects. Google may take some days or longer to recrawl and replace the https URLs with http ones.

If your HTTPS page is showing a Google custom search request to http://www.google.com/cse, that’s a mixed-content issue. The supported guidance here says Google later added HTTPS support for JavaScript custom search, and you can switch the Google script host from http:// to https:// to avoid insecure-item warnings.

The evidence doesn’t directly explain why Google search results might appear for a purely HTTP site, but it does show that if your site is HTTPS and you’re using Google custom search, the Google code should be loaded over HTTPS. If you’re still seeing an http:// Google URL, the closest supported fix is to replace it with the HTTPS version where possible.

If Google is showing a page that should be HTTP-only or is appending a query string, robots.txt won’t remove it from the index; it only blocks crawling. If the URL is linked internally or externally, Google can still index it.

The closest fixes supported here are:
- use a canonical tag on the page pointing to your preferred URL
- if HTTP is the preferred protocol, normalize with a 301 redirect
- optionally set URL Parameter Filters in Google Webmaster Tools for the query string

For a purely http:// site, make sure the canonical points to the http:// version, not https://.

For paginated product listings, the evidence supports using rel="canonical" to point duplicate or equivalent URLs to the preferred URL, especially for page 1. It also suggests not using rel="next" on the base page when there are multiple paginated sets on the same page, because multiple rel="next" targets would be problematic.

So, the closest guidance here is: use canonical for the preferred version, preserve query strings in canonicals for page 2+ if they represent the same content, and do not rely on rel="next" on the base page in this mixed-pagination setup. If you can configure query string parameters in webmaster tools, that may also help.

If the paginated pages are just different views of the same product list, use rel="canonical" only when there is a single non-paginated “all products” page that is a true superset of the paginated pages.

If you don’t have such a page, don’t use rel="canonical" for the pagination. The guidance here does not support using rel-prev-next instead, so the safest answer from this is: use canonical to the all-products page if it exists; otherwise do nothing.

For paginated product listing pages, the supported guidance here is to use rel="prev" and rel="next" for the pagination. That’s the closest match to the thread’s recommendation for listing pages spread across multiple pages.

The evidence does not support using canonical instead of pagination tags for this case, and it does not suggest doing nothing if the pages are a paginated series.

So: use rel="prev" and rel="next".

The most efficient approach described is to add redirect rules in your .htaccess file and group old URLs where possible, so many old links can point to a new section with one rule instead of one rule per page. For example, an old `/news_article/...` folder can be redirected to `/news/`. If your old and new URLs don’t share a common pattern, you’ll still need a long list of redirects for the specific pages and images you want to preserve.

You can’t see a complete list of those “not selected” URLs in Google’s tools. The closest guidance is to identify likely duplicates or redirects yourself by checking common causes such as www/non-www, http/https, URL parameters, and by using a crawling tool to map redirects and duplicate pages on your site.

Google no longer seems to treat a rewritten URL like test_param_1.html as inherently better for indexing than a URL with parameters like index.php?module=test&param=1. So URL rewriting is not the only way to get pages indexed or cached by Google.

What matters more is whether the pages are similar. If they are, use rel="canonical" to tell Google which page is the main one, so ranking signals are not split.

The evidence doesn’t show a reliable way to identify a site’s development language. It only says the site described is “100% home-cooked code” and not built with a framework like WordPress or Drupal.

So, from this, the closest supported guidance is:
- You can’t determine the development language from the URL/language-switching behavior alone.
- You’d need to inspect the site’s source code, files, or server-side hints to know the language.

If you mean the website’s development language, the evidence doesn’t give a direct method. It only covers language detection for multilingual sites.

Closest guidance: you can inspect cues like the Accept-Language header or Geo-IP, but that tells you the user’s language, not the site’s development language. For a specific website, you’d typically need server-side access, which hosted CMSs usually don’t allow. The evidence also suggests using separate language subdomains and behavior-based selection rather than forcing automatic detection.

If you want, I can help with practical ways to infer a site’s tech stack from its source, but that isn’t covered here.

You can’t determine a website’s development language from the provided information. It only covers how to handle multi-country, multilingual sites: use geographic targeting, avoid canonicalizing different country sites to each other, and add hreflang links between translated pages. If you want the development language, you’d need other clues such as page source, response headers, file extensions, or server-side scripts—not something this evidence addresses.

To show different content based on where a visitor is, use IP geolocation. With plain HTML, you’d need to do it in the browser, typically via JavaScript plus a geolocation service/API.

Search for “IP geolocation javascript” to find providers. Some free services exist, but reliability can vary, and they may sometimes detect the location incorrectly. It’s a good idea to include an override so users can manually choose the correct region, for example if they’re identified as being in the wrong country.

To view your website as if you were in a different city or country, use a VPN or a proxy. These change your IP location so the site appears to come from places like New York. Paid services are usually faster and less noticeable; free ones can be slow. VPNs are generally more secure than proxies because they use encryption.

To see how your site performs from different locations, the provided guidance recommends using Google and Bing webmaster tools rather than manually searching from various computers. After registering your site, these tools show metrics like average position, impressions, click-through rate, and keyword data. The linked services are:

Google Webmaster Tools: http://www.google.com/webmasters/tools/
Bing Webmaster Toolbox: http://www.bing.com/toolbox/webmaster/

This doesn’t specifically describe a location-by-location viewing tool, but it does cover the best supported way to check SEO performance without relying on personal searches.

Your pageviews themselves won’t affect your search ranking, but your search ranking can affect pageviews.

Launching a new site can change your search visibility, for better or worse, depending on how the relaunch is done. To help preserve ranking, keep URLs pointing to the updated content or set proper redirects from old URLs to new ones. Also make sure the new site is SEO-friendly, with clear URLs, good headlines, proper markup, and relevant keywords.

No. The hosting payment period itself does not affect search rankings. What matters is that your website stays online, has good content, and remains available for search engine crawlers. If the site goes offline, reindexing can start once crawlers encounter that change. So choosing yearly versus monthly hosting should not affect ranking, as long as the website stays up.

To help keep rankings during a redesign, the advice given is to use 301 redirects, time the migration away from domain expiry/renewal, update far-future HTTP expiry headers, migrate slowly with the old and new sites running in parallel where possible, and introduce the new structure early using sitemaps. If duplicate URLs appear, use the rel="canonical" HTTP header (or meta tag version) to point to the correct URL. If the linking structure or site position changes a lot, the key question is whether it’s in users’ best interest.

A redesign by itself doesn’t have to hurt your Google rank, especially if you keep the same URLs, title tags, meta descriptions, ALT tags, headings, images, and content. The key point is that changing the content can change rankings, since Google uses those signals to understand the page.

If the site already ranks well, it’s safer to make changes in small steps rather than all at once. Also make sure the new design is coded well and is fast. If you keep the content and core signals the same, the guidance suggests you’re less likely to lose positions, and you might even improve over time.

A major redesign can hurt rankings if it changes important SEO elements. The guidance here says to keep these unchanged: page titles, meta tags, heading tags, page content, URL structure, and Google verification code. It also says changes outside those areas should not affect ranking. If rankings do drop after a redesign, reverting to the old files would not be guaranteed to restore the old ranking, but that is not directly confirmed here.

There’s no maximum number stated here. Multiple A records can be used for one domain, and browsers usually receive the full list and try another if one fails. The practical guidance supported here is that this can work for fault tolerance, but it has caveats around browser, OS, proxy, and cache behavior.

The evidence suggests there’s no theoretical limit on the number of subdomains, so the practical answer is “effectively unlimited.” That said, it does not specifically state a maximum number of DNS A-records for one domain. Closest guidance: subdomains can be created in very large numbers, but any real limit would be practical rather than a fixed DNS limit.

The provided material doesn’t give a maximum number of DNS A-records you can use on one domain. It only says that a health-checking DNS service can return one A record when a server is online and fall back to an alternate server when it’s offline.

So, from this evidence, the closest supported guidance is: you can use multiple A records in a failover setup, but the exact maximum isn’t specified here.

The only concrete option mentioned is Twilio, which costs $0.01 per message, with non-US in private beta. For SMS ads, the suggestion is simply to search for “SMS adverts” and contact a few companies that sell advertising to ask whether they do SMS ad placements. It doesn’t name a specific SMS ad network or website that lets users interact via SMS for a charge.

A supported option is Clickatell. The cited answer says it has been used to send and receive SMS with PHP, and that its SMS Gateway page has details. This covers using an HTTP-to-SMS gateway so a website can interact with users by SMS, including incoming messages. It does not specify pricing, but it does fit the “at a charge” part as a gateway service.

The evidence says this isn’t possible in a useful way with YouTube’s embed player. It suggests that for a single video you could make the embed 1px by 1px and use autoplay, but it doesn’t say that’s an approved or policy-safe method. It also says you can’t really shrink it to show only the controls because YouTube content scales automatically with the player size.

So, based on this, there’s no support here for hiding the video display while keeping just the controls, and nothing here confirms whether that would be against YouTube’s terms of use.

The question appears to be about setting a default message for an AddThis “invite a friend” email button, including when users choose Gmail or Yahoo from the AddThis box.

The supported guidance shown here only says this is about dynamically changing the message sent through AddThis, and warns that doing so can create spam abuse risks. It does not provide a method for setting the default message.

So, based on this, there isn’t a confirmed answer here for how to configure that default message.

The redirection is now working again: googlepages URLs are being redirected to Google Sites once more. The only supported conclusion here is that the issue was fixed, but there’s no information on why it broke or what changed.

The issue is not about making the validator ignore the code. The fix is to replace unencoded ampersands in the script URL with `&`. That addresses the validator error and is the supported way to include the script. This will help the page validate better.

If your real concern is whether a redirect is transparent to Google and other search engines, this evidence does not cover that.

If your goal is to remove pages from Google’s index, the accepted guidance here says not to 301 everything to the homepage. A 301 means “moved,” so Google may keep the old URLs for a while.

The closest supported approach is to return 410 Gone for the pages you want removed, while leaving /index.html and static files like .gif, .jpg, .png, .css, and .js alone. The example rule set shown is:

ErrorDocument 410 /error-docs/e410.html

RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !^/error-docs/
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !=/index.html
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !\.(gif|jpe?g|png|css|js)$
RewriteRule . - [G]

This serves a custom 410 page instead of redirecting.

For a one-page web app, the usual SEO basics still apply per page: use a proper title tag, an H1, and other standard on-page signals.

The main limitation is that you won’t have internal links between pages, and those are valuable for SEO because they pass PageRank and anchor text relevance. With only one page, that advantage is missing.

The best way to compensate is to make the app genuinely useful so it can earn quality external links, which can help your SEO significantly.

If your app requires login to see the content, search engines won’t be able to get past the login form, so only the login page is likely to be indexed. That is already the most restrictive option.

For the GoDaddy placeholder showing in Google, the guidance is to make sure the domain and site are configured correctly, then wait for Google to crawl and index it. New sites with few or no backlinks can take time.

A practical next step is to register the site in Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console to check for indexing issues and basic SEO problems.

Google won’t index or rank parts of one page separately; it’s essentially all or nothing. Using crawlable Ajax can make content available as separate URLs, but the guidance here says that’s a bad idea for a one-page site because it’s not accessible, fails without JavaScript, and can block other search engines.

The recommended approach is to split the content into multiple pages, each with one purpose. If you use Ajax, make sure the same content is still available without JavaScript, following progressive enhancement.

Use a canonical tag, not noindex. If the six URLs show the same content, add rel="canonical" on the duplicate pages pointing to the preferred URL, for example the “all reviews” page or whichever version you want indexed. In the example given, the remaining 5 URLs would each point to www.mysite.com/Review/CODE/0.

If it looks bad to users, it’s bad from a developer perspective too, because many people won’t visit a site that triggers a warning. The answer also says it has never heard of a site being rated badly because of the registrar; that would not make much sense, especially with a well-known registrar like eNom. It suggests continuing to worry about it as long as you want visitors, since a warning acts like a big red flag and will likely make many users leave.

A binary upvote/downvote system, a 5-star scale, and an upvote-only system can all work if your goal is simply to have “good” content rise and “poor” content sink. If you want richer data, a point scale gives more detail than binary. If you care about easier collaborative filtering, binary is preferable.

A key caveat is calibration: star ratings can be skewed by extreme voters, so the scale should be adjusted to the actual distribution of ratings. A point scale can still be very useful if you account for its median and spread. An upvote-only system loses information about dislikes, so it’s less informative than the others.

For SEO, it doesn’t matter whether pages are static or generated from a database. What matters is that search engines can reach them by following links on your site.

More pages on one site are not automatically better; the key is having accessible, useful pages.

For helping crawlers index a large site, the supported guidance is to:
- link to your pages from other pages on your site
- add an HTML sitemap for important links
- add an XML sitemap at the root of your site, e.g. sitemap.xml

An XML sitemap lists URLs in a search-engine-friendly format and can help search engines find your pages.

A one-page site can work, but it usually makes SEO harder for individual topics because you only get one page title, one H1, and one main page focus. If the page covers several services, it’s less likely to rank strongly for any single service.

If you can, separate your services into multiple pages so each page can target one topic more clearly. Internal linking between those pages can also help a little through anchor text and page-to-page authority transfer.

For a one-page site, the best-supported guidance here is to keep the page tightly focused and use the single title/H1/meta description to reflect the main topic as clearly as possible.

The provided information only covers SEO for YouTube video content, not one-page websites.

The closest guidance it supports is that searchable text matters: if content is mainly audio or otherwise not directly readable by search engines, adding a transcription helps search engines understand and rank it. For a one-page website, the analogous best practice would be to ensure the page includes clear, indexable text that describes the content, rather than relying only on non-text elements.

“Fresh content” here means content that Googlebot finds when it crawls your site. “Content Keywords” are simply the words Googlebot found while crawling; they’re not something you need to optimize for and don’t appear to be tied to ranking relevance.

The evidence does not say whether Submit to Index updates previously indexed pages faster or only submits new URLs. It only supports that Submit to Index is not something you should use to optimize Content Keywords, and that Googlebot’s crawl is what determines what words are found.

There’s no way to guarantee that Google will index “fresh content” immediately. Google crawls when it chooses, and sites that update often and earn quality links are typically crawled more frequently.

If you add new pages, your sitemap should include them and grow with your site. But even with a sitemap, Google may not find or update changes quickly. The practical guidance is to keep adding content, make sure your sitemap reflects all pages you want crawled, and build links to help Google discover updates sooner.

If the changing portion is becoming completely different content with different markup and topic, you should expect it to behave like a new site section for SEO. The existing content and links will not carry much value if they no longer match the new pages.

So the closest guidance supported here is: treat the new eCommerce area as starting from scratch for rankings and organic traffic on those pages. If you remove the blog content entirely, expect the old rankings and visitors tied to that content to drop significantly.

If the changing part is a paginated archive, that’s generally fine for SEO. The key is to give each individual item its own URL, so Google and users can still access it directly even if it moves from page to page in the archive.

For the archive pages themselves, one suggestion is to let only page 1 be indexed and set later pages to noindex,follow so search engines don’t index lots of near-duplicate paginated pages, but still follow their links to the real item pages.

So the supported guidance is: dynamic content is okay, but make sure the individual content items are on stable URLs and link them from the archive pages.

Google hasn’t explicitly said you must translate URL paths, but keywords in URLs can help, and local-language keywords may be better than untranslated ones. It may also improve click-through because users can recognize URLs in their own language.

That said, the benefit is probably modest, so it’s reasonable to weigh it against the extra work and long-term maintenance of translating and managing URLs. If the cost is high, keeping a consistent non-translated path is still a defensible choice.

A “back link” is an inbound link from another site to your site.

Based on this, a sitewide keyword-rich backlink from a Blogspot page likely only passes weight from the most relevant instance of that link, not every repeated copy. Removing those links would most likely affect the specific keyword(s) tied to that anchor text, and even then the impact may be small. Overall, rankings depend on many factors, so the safest guidance is to review which backlinks are actually contributing to each search query before removing anything.

A “back link” here is a page link that uses JavaScript to send the user to the previous page in browser history, like the browser Back button.

It can help some users navigate, but it’s not always a good idea to hard-code it because:
- it won’t work if JavaScript is disabled
- if a new visitor clicks it, they may be taken off-site

The evidence does not say it affects search ranking. It only discusses usability and implementation.

A back link is a link from one site or page to another. Based on the guidance here, links themselves are important because search engines use them to understand what a site is about. The provided answer doesn’t explain “back link” specifically, but it does say that diluting a site’s focus could be risky for search ranking. So, if a backlink points to unrelated content, it may contribute to confusion about the site’s topic and could be risky.

No. The only guidance here says you should not host or keep copyrighted content once you receive notice that it’s copyrighted, and that a site should not encourage uploading copyrighted material. It does not say that missing copyright information or being unable to contact the author makes it legal to use the material. The closest supported advice is to assume it may still be protected and to remove it if you get a notice.

Not enough information here to say it’s legal. The only guidance supported is that uploading copyrighted music or movies for personal use can still be legally disputed, and movies may raise extra issues because DVD encryption can’t be circumvented under the DMCA, even for personal use.

If the material is copyrighted, the absence of copyright information or a way to contact the author does not by itself make it free to use. The closest supported answer is: you should not assume it’s allowed without permission or a license.

If you mean changing the IP address associated with a nameserver hostname, you update the nameserver host record at your domain registrar. If you mean replacing a static IP with a domain name for a host, the evidence only covers nameservers: it says the registrar stores both the hostname and IP for registered nameservers, and you change the IP through the registrar.

If you want a domain name to follow a changing IP, the DNS provider must update the A record automatically. The guidance here is to use a dynamic DNS provider that manages the A record for your root domain, then set www to point to that domain with a CNAME.

You can’t use a CNAME at the root domain. If you only have No-IP free service, it may not support what you need. If you need this setup, either use a paid dynamic DNS service or get a static IP from your provider.

This usually isn’t a DNS problem. It means the web server is only set up for the www version, and the non-www name isn’t being handled.

“www” is just a subdomain, so both addresses need to be configured to point to the same site, or one should redirect to the other.

The closest fix supported by the evidence is to add a redirect or virtual host so `example.com` goes to `www.example.com` or vice versa. With Apache, that can be done with a separate virtual host and a permanent redirect. If you’re using 123-reg hosting, you’d need to set the domain/website configuration so both names are recognized.

If your site only works with www and gives a 400 error without it, the fix shown is to redirect the non-www version to www using Apache mod_rewrite.

Create an .htaccess file in your site root and add:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^yourdomain\.com [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.yourdomain.com/$1 [R=301,NC,L]

Replace yourdomain.com with your real domain.

This applies if your hosting uses Apache and allows .htaccess.

If the site only works with www, the closest supported fix is to point both the @ and www A records to the hosting IP address, or use 301 redirects so the non-www version forwards to the www version.

What this does cover is that 123-reg hosting packages can’t have the associated domain changed after purchase, and 123-reg planned a domain mapping feature so any domain could be mapped to a package and pointed at the correct IP.

If you need a domain other than the one already associated with the hosting, the supported option was to buy a new hosting package for that domain.

If your goal is just to understand the protocol behavior, the closest supported guidance is that SSL/TLS is what makes an HTTPS connection secure; it isn’t something you can “turn on” for plain HTTP. It does not cover any workaround for expired certificates or redirecting requests in that situation.

You can’t make an expired SSL cert direct HTTPS to HTTP; once the cert expires, HTTPS will fail certificate validation. The supported guidance here is to let the certificates expire and remove DNS records like A/AAAA/MX/CNAME so users don’t hit the old site and get warnings. If you need the domain retired sooner and want to prevent misuse of old certs/keys, revoke the certificates before they expire. If the site must still be reachable, it would need a valid certificate for HTTPS, not an expired one.

You can’t avoid the certificate warning with a redirect alone. For an HTTPS request, the browser must complete the TLS handshake before any HTTP redirect is sent. So if the cert is expired or doesn’t match `www.domain.com`, the warning appears first.

To redirect `https://www.domain.com` to `https://domain.com` without warnings, the certificate must be valid for both names, typically by adding `www.domain.com` to the certificate’s subjectAltName or getting a new cert that covers both.

For pages that can be reached in both HTTP and HTTPS, use canonical tags to indicate the preferred version. For pages that should always be secure, use 301 redirects from HTTP to HTTPS.

Create separate profiles for each version you want to track, then add a hostname filter to each profile.

Admin -> Profiles -> Filters -> New Filter
- Filter Type: Predefined filter
- Include Only
- Traffic to the hostname
- that contain
- your hostname, such as http.example.com or https.example.com

Repeat for each profile. If you leave one main profile without a hostname filter, you can still see combined traffic there.

The guidance here is to keep `rel="nofollow"` on all user-generated outgoing links. domain.com -> dynamically updated A record
www.domain.com -> CNAME to domain.com

That avoids pointing records directly at your changing IP. The guidance does not cover changing the address of a non-root domain specifically, but it does indicate that www can be CNAME’d to the root, while the root itself needs an A record handled by the DNS provider.

A high number of nofollow links is not, by itself, a problem. Nofollow links cannot hurt the ranking of the site containing them. If a link on your site is nofollow, that specific target page won’t get ranking benefit from it; any “lost” value is effectively passed to other normal links instead.

The closest guidance supported here is to focus on making a consistent, user-friendly site rather than worrying about the nofollow/do-follow ratio.

- use a 301 redirect for permanent URL changes
- use either .htaccess or PHP depending on where it’s easiest to implement
