That rule should be placed in .htaccess, not in httpd.conf. Use:

RewriteEngine on
RewriteRule ^/site/(.*) /~username/site/$1 [PT]

If it’s in httpd.conf, Apache may be processing it in a different context and still looking under /var/www/site/. Moving it to .htaccess should address the redirect issue.

Your pattern is only matching one character because `(.)` means “exactly one character.” That’s why a URL like `/a3ff/ABC` would only keep `A`.

To match the rest of the path, use `(.*)` instead, for example:

RewriteRule ^a3ff/(.*) [DOMAINNAME]/$1 [R=301,QSA,L]

If you want specific pages redirected to the homepage, you may also need to use more exact patterns for those page names instead of broad matches.

Yes. Use the RewriteLog and RewriteLogLevel directives to log the rewrite activity. A higher RewriteLogLevel makes the output more verbose and detailed. You’ll likely need to restart IIS for it to take effect.

Be aware that on a busy site the log can grow very quickly, making it hard to trace a single request, so it’s best to test on a dev machine or when traffic is low.

Try adding a slash before the query string:

RewriteEngine on
RewriteRule ^([A-Za-z0-9-]+)$ /?site=$1

If that still doesn’t work, add [R] after the target so it becomes an external redirect and you can see where it’s going in the browser:

RewriteRule ^([A-Za-z0-9-]+)$ /?site=$1 [R]

Yes—use `/?$` to make the trailing slash optional and collapse each pair of rules into one:

RewriteRule ^([A-Za-z0-9_\-]+)/?$ /userviewproducts.php?category=$1 [L]
RewriteRule ^([A-Za-z0-9_\-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+)/?$ /userviewproducts.php?category=$1 [L]
RewriteRule ^([A-Za-z0-9_\-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+)/?$ /viewbuyproduct.php?1=$1 [L]

This keeps the same behavior for `/a`, `/a/`, `/a/a`, `/a/a/`, `/a/a/a`, and `/a/a/a/`.

To force the site to use www, the shown approach does the opposite: it redirects from `www.example.com` to `example.com`.

If you want `example.com` to redirect to `www.example.com`, use the same idea in reverse:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^example.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.example.com/$1 [R=301,L]

Place this in the root `.htaccess` file.

If you want to switch between www and non-www, the key is to use a 301 Moved Permanently redirect. That tells search engines the URL has permanently moved, helps avoid duplicate content, and should let the new version be indexed. The result described here says changing from www to non-www did not affect rankings when done with a 301 and the preferred version was updated in Webmaster Tools.

Use one rule that redirects if the host is example.com or the request is not HTTPS:

RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^example\.com$ [OR]
RewriteCond %{HTTPS} !on
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://www.example.com/$1 [R,L]

This will send http://example.com, http://www.example.com, and https://example.com to https://www.example.com in one step. If you have other subdomains, keep the host check as-is; otherwise you can also use a negative match against www.example.com.

A single old dynamic URL can only 301 to one destination. If one old URL now corresponds to multiple new static URLs, you can’t redirect it to all of them.

The closest workable approach is to keep product.php active and have it resolve the request to the correct product, while adding a rule to redirect the new-style URLs back to product.php with parameters. The other approach mentioned is to detect requests for /product.php in code and redirect them to one specific new URL.

If your old URLs are one-to-one with products, redirect each old URL to its matching new URL and keep the old URL active only for that redirect.

To make it a 301 redirect, the target must be a full URL with protocol and domain, not just a relative path.

So the rule would be:

RewriteRule ^(\S+)/directory/(\d+)/(\d+)/entry/(\d+)/?$ http://www.example.com/directories/index.cfm?sFuseAction=XXX.YYYY.ZZZZ&nDirectoryID=$2&nEntryID=$4&nCategoryID=$3&sDirectory=$1 [NC,L]

This covers the syntax needed for a 301 redirect.

Use a RewriteCond that matches the query string on the dynamic URL, then redirect the /dyn/ path to the new page:

RewriteCond %{QUERY_STRING} ^q=customer%20reference&f= [NC]
RewriteRule ^dyn/$ /customer-references/? [L,R=301]

This was the working solution. It handles the dynamic URL by checking the query string and sends /dyn/ to /customer-references/ with a 301 redirect.

Yes. You can 301-redirect an entire folder, not just a single page. The example given is:

Redirect permanent /OLD http://example.com/NEW

That will redirect every file under the old directory to the matching path under the new directory, such as:

/OLD/page_one.html -> /NEW/page_one.html

/OLD/page_two.html -> /NEW/page_two.html

This is specifically described for Apache’s mod_alias Redirect directive.

If your site serves the same content at both `mydomain.com` and `www.mydomain.com`, register both in Google Webmaster Tools and then set your preferred domain. If you can set a 301/permanent redirect from the non-canonical version to the canonical one, that’s the better option.

To use a www domain with Google Webmaster Tools, point `www.mydomain.com` to `ghs.google.com` as you’ve done, and set up a redirect from `mydomain.com` to `www.mydomain.com`. This is not a DNS change.

GoDaddy provides domain forwarding for this. Use their forwarding feature to redirect the non-www domain to the www version.

Yes. If the path stays the same and only the domain changes, add this to the .htaccess in the old site’s root:

Redirect 301 / http://www.someothersite.com/

This sends all requests to the new domain and preserves the rest of the URL and query string.

If WordPress rewrite rules are already in that .htaccess, they may run first, since RewriteRule has higher priority than Redirect. In that case, you may need to disable or adjust those rules so the 301 redirect happens first.

A 500 from .htaccess can mean one of the directives isn’t allowed. Try removing lines one at a time to find the culprit.

In particular, check whether mod_rewrite is enabled, and whether the server allows the Options directive. If AllowOverride doesn’t permit Options, `Options +FollowSymLinks` can trigger the error.

The redirect rule itself is:

`RewriteEngine on`
`RewriteRule (.*) http://www.blog.mysite.co.uk/$1 [R=301,L]`

If the error goes away when you remove `Options +FollowSymLinks`, that’s likely the issue.

Use a 301 redirect. The support in the evidence says 301 indicates the document has permanently moved, and it does not prevent a new document from later appearing at the old URI. If the old username URL becomes valid again in the future, Google can recrawl it and, when it returns 200, index it again.

The thread doesn’t contain a resolved answer, so I can’t say which option was chosen as best. The closest guidance supported here is that, for SEO, the question is about moving from an old domain/site to a new one while keeping the old site’s value. The options discussed are:

- 301 redirect the old domain to the new one
- 301 redirect each old page to its closest matching new page
- keep both sites and link from old pages to new ones

If your goal is preserving search value, the page-to-page 301 approach is the one most directly aligned with matching old URLs to relevant new URLs.

Search engines can still index a new site even before it gets visitors, but you may be buried by competition at first. The best approach is not to rely only on search engines: get other sites linking to the new site, publish good quality content, and use other marketing channels too.

If you mean redirecting existing users from an old site to a new one, the evidence here doesn’t cover the technical redirect method. The closest guidance it supports is to make the new site discoverable through links, content, and broader promotion rather than SEO alone.

Yes. For a search-engine-friendly permanent redirect, set GoDaddy to Redirect type: 301 (Permanent) and Forward settings: Forward only. “Forward with masking” uses a frame redirect, not a 301.

Based on the provided answer, folders are generally the simpler choice for tech/scale/admin reasons. Subdomains can be nicer to type and remember, but they add more complexity and maintenance. A suggested compromise is to use URL rewriting to make folder-style URLs behave like subdomains.

Subdomains are mainly recommended if you need separate servers under the same domain, or if your site is a portal/network for many separate sites or user sites. If that doesn’t describe your case, folders are likely the better fit.

Doing both is the best-supported approach here. A 301 redirect from `page.php` to `page` will send Google and users to the preferred URL, and the canonical tag on the page will reinforce that `page` is the correct version. Together, they should prevent Google from treating the two URLs as duplicates.

Google can crawl subdirectories from URLs it finds, so if you have links pointing to /content/foo/foo.html, it may also try /content/foo and /content. Blocking /content/ in robots.txt should not affect your current pages unless you have relevant pages under /content. If your real pages are outside /content, you should be fine.

You can’t submit a wildcard de-index request like `file.php*`. The removal tool is meant for emergencies, not bulk cleanup.

The supported approach is to tell Google those URLs are gone or changed, and let the crawler clean them up over time. If they should no longer exist, return a `410 Gone` response for them. If the issue is that the same content is reachable through multiple URLs, use canonicalization and/or redirects so Google learns the preferred URL.

Keywords in URLs can help a little, but only as a very small SEO factor. They also help users understand what a link is about. Great content, titles, and link text matter much more.

So they’re not useless, but they’re also not something to force. If you already have a working URL structure, changing it just to add keywords is debatable and may not be worth it. A natural, readable URL is the best approach supported here.

Repeating a thread title in a forum isn’t automatically keyword stuffing. The key point is whether the terms are used naturally and in context, not just how many times they appear. If a page is short and mostly made up of the same phrase, that could be a concern. But on forums, repeated titles in headers, meta titles, and posts are common, and Google is generally understood to handle that kind of structure. If it reads well and the keywords are part of normal discussion, it’s usually not treated as stuffing.

Including the same “ratings-reviews-prices” words in every product URL would probably be seen as spammy/keyword stuffing, especially since it would repeat across all pages without variation. If the pages really do contain prices, ratings, and reviews, you don’t need to force those words into the URL. A safer approach is to keep the URL focused on the unique product name and use those terms naturally in the page content, title, and description where relevant.

If the URL represents a real categorized page with enough different content for each result, it should be okay. The answer says Google can understand keywords in the URL and in a query string similarly, so switching to a query string does not remove the issue by itself.

For your case, those pages are treated as categorized pages, so that is acceptable. It also suggests you usually do not need lots of keywords in the URL; 3–4 are enough, and keywords can be put in metadata instead.

Google no longer supports Google Authorship, so there’s no need to add rel="author" for Google, including multiple rel="author" links. The closer guidance supported here is to use structured data instead. rel="author" may still exist as a microformat for other applications, but this doesn’t imply Google needs or uses multiple rel="author" links.

The evidence says rel=author is an HTML5 standard and doesn’t have to be tied to a Google profile. It doesn’t specifically address whether Google is OK with multiple rel="author" links. The closest supported guidance is that Google uses rel=author to identify authorship and may show a photo if it’s linked to a Google profile, but no restriction on multiple author links is mentioned here.

The evidence doesn’t show a clear Google rule against multiple rel="author" links. It says there wasn’t a canonical answer, and that technically you could add markup, but it might be viewed as odd. It also suggests Google would likely suppress brand profiles if it had a problem with them. So the safest supported guidance is: there’s no confirmed prohibition here, but this use wasn’t clearly intended and wasn’t well established.

PageRank is per page, not per website. The PR value you see is stale and reflects an older point in time, while Google updates PageRank internally daily or more often. So an observed PR increase is usually not the direct cause of a traffic jump; it’s more likely a reflection of changes that already happened, such as new links or other ranking factors. Also, PageRank now plays a very small role in rankings, so a 1-point change is unlikely to explain a 300% traffic increase.

Google doesn’t provide a history of PageRank for a specific site or page. The accepted answer says the only way to have historical values would have been to record them yourself over time.

It also says the toolbar PageRank data became stale, with Google not releasing data for pages created since December 2013, so “n/a” PageRank is not a reliable signal.

The closest guidance supported here is to focus on other indicators instead: how often Googlebot crawls the page, whether it’s indexed, whether it ranks for keywords, and whether it gets Google search referrals.

Generally, no. Search engines know that blogs often have category or tag pages that are mostly listings/excerpts, and that alone is not usually a problem. The guidance here says Google no longer recommends blocking crawler access to duplicate content with robots.txt, and duplicate content on a site is not grounds for action unless it’s deceptive or intended to manipulate results.

So indexing category pages is usually fine. If your concern is that a category page ranks ahead of the article itself, the closest supported guidance is that this isn’t necessarily harmful, but it may not be the result you want.

Based on this, indexing category/tag pages is not clearly “good” in general. The cited experience says that noindexing tag and category archives, along with improving pagination, increased traffic by 30% in two weeks.

So if your main goal is overall traffic, the closest guidance supported here is to consider noindexing category and tag pages rather than indexing them. It does not prove this is always best for every site, but it suggests indexing those pages may not help overall traffic as much as improving site structure and pagination.

Not just for increasing indexed pages. The guidance here says Google cares about quality, not quantity, so if a category/search results page doesn’t offer something special and useful for visitors, it should be removed or kept out of the index. If the page is genuinely helpful to users, then keep it. In short: index it only when it provides real value, not just to boost search engine coverage.

It may help a little, but the impact is likely small. Using link relationships like index, start, prev, and next can help associate related pages and improve navigation for users, and browsers may use them too. Based on this, it’s not something that would have a big SEO effect, but it can still be worth doing if it matches your site structure.

Yes, crawlable hierarchy can help SEO more than a sitemap alone, because actual links on pages are better for Google to discover and crawl content. A sitemap will help too, but not as much as links in the site itself.

If your current navigation is only a search form, adding some normal browse-able hierarchy could be beneficial, even if limited. Breadcrumbs are especially helpful if they can appear on all pages.

It’s not just for “spiders”; real internal links are the stronger signal here.

Yes, according to the provided thread, a flat navigation with many links on every page can hurt SEO because it dilutes topical focus. The suggested fix is to organize URLs into a directory-style hierarchy and only link/index top-level categories sitewide, so deeper pages are not repeated everywhere. That helps create clearer content silos. It also says hiding deeper links with JavaScript is preferable to using nofollow, though that last point is noted as not fully substantiated.

The evidence only supports that short, meaningful URLs are preferable, and that deeper slash-separated paths aren’t necessarily a problem by themselves. It doesn’t compare slashes versus hyphens directly.

Closest guidance: use URLs that are concise and meaningful. If slashes help show a clear hierarchy, that’s acceptable; avoid making URLs overly long or shallow but unclear.

For SEO, the guidance here favors hyphens in the path, but avoiding hyphens in the domain name itself. The answer says hyphens can be useful in a file or post path, yet add unnecessary noise in a domain. It also notes there can be exceptions where a hyphen improves readability. So if you mean URLs or page slugs, hyphens are preferred; if you mean the domain name, avoid them unless they prevent confusion.

Article submission directories can sometimes help rankings by providing backlinks, but the support here says they’re usually not worth much unless you’re targeting very uncompetitive keywords. Google’s Panda/Farmer update is thought to have reduced the value of links from article directories and other low-quality content farms. So they’re not necessarily useless, but they’re generally a weak SEO tactic compared with guest posts on respected, relevant blogs, which may add value and attract a real audience.

Article submission directories can help SEO only a little. They may provide weak backlinks that can slowly add up, and they can matter more for very niche markets or search terms. But most directories rank poorly and have few incoming links, so their SEO value is usually minimal, often close to zero. For broad keywords, you should not expect significant ranking gains from directory submissions alone.

If the requests are really coming from Googlebot, the only guidance here is to verify the source IPs. It’s easy to spoof the Googlebot User-Agent, so check whether the IPs making the requests are actually owned by Google. If they are not, then it may be spoofed traffic rather than real Googlebot.

The evidence doesn’t cover how to increase crawl rate for a huge site, only how to confirm whether the crawl spike is legitimate.

If you need to slow down a bot that’s only distinguishable by IP, the supported guidance here is to limit requests/traffic per IP at the web server level. The referenced approach points to Apache rate-limiting per IP, which is the closest fit for a shared host with .htaccess and limited server control. It does not specifically explain how to slow Googlebot, but it does cover throttling a generic bot by IP.

The evidence doesn’t define “linkbaiting.” It only discusses ecommerce expand/collapse behavior and says that if the first click expands a menu and also links to the first-level category page, that may be acceptable. If you mean “linkbaiting” in the sense of making a first click lead to content and a second click lead deeper, this evidence suggests that requiring two clicks can lower conversion. Register the custom domain, domain.com, especially if you want full control or may move away from WordPress.com later. In general, the safer choice is the domain you control: domain.com.

Yes. The closest guidance here is to prioritize visitor experience: if a subsection is large enough that it feels better as its own page, give it one. If it’s small, a slide-down/accordion style is fine. Both approaches are considered valid.

For SEO, the advice supports separating the content so larger sections can have their own URL, while smaller ones can remain on the main page. It also suggests using an aside-style area for these links/content and, if desired, Ajax/modal behavior so users see it inline while search engines can still rank a full separate page.

In short: use separate pages for substantial sections; use expandable content for smaller ones.

There isn’t a fixed “best” ratio for home, category, and detail pages. In general, many incoming links naturally go to the home page, but some sites get lots of links to specific pages if those pages are popular.

The most effective approach is to get links to the pages you want to rank. That could include category pages, but it’s often the home page and individual content pages that benefit most. So yes, linking to category pages can help if those are important pages, but there’s no golden proportion to follow.

Use one main page that lists the full set, and if needed offer paginated or “show all” versions for navigation. That keeps the main page strongest for SEO and user discovery.

Internal section links like “#toprated” are not separate URLs in Google’s sense; they’re just anchors within one URL. If you want separate indexed URLs for sections or categories, you’d need actual separate pages.

If you create duplicate pages for portions of the list, use canonical tags or robots rules so only one version is indexed. The closest supported guidance here is: main page for ranking, optional split pages for users and tracking, but avoid duplicate content competing in search.

Yes, it could. The guidance here says globally nofollowing all external links usually doesn’t help, and may even hurt. If every external link is nofollow, Google might interpret the site as mostly sponsored/affiliate-like. Also, nofollow no longer “hoards” PageRank for you; linking externally doesn’t seem to hurt rankings in itself.

The supported use cases for nofollow are sponsored links and unreviewed user-generated links. Outside those cases, relevant external links may actually be a positive sign of authority.

Yes, it’s possible to rank an English site for a non-English keyword, because a keyword does not have to appear in the site’s text for the site to rank on it.

For finding what keywords a site ranks for, the closest guidance here is to use a tool like SEMrush. It won’t give a fully comprehensive list, but it’s described as the most accurate and comprehensive option mentioned.

Adding Spanish/French content to an English site should not, by itself, hurt rankings for English terms. Each page is judged on its own merits using many factors, and keyword counts from Webmaster Tools are not a reliable measure of relevance.

If the non-English content is on the same site, it’s better to organize it so Google can index it correctly, especially for multi-regional/multilingual sites.

The Spanish keywords showing up in Webmaster Tools don’t necessarily mean Google ranks you for those searches. They may just reflect words crawled on your pages.

If your rankings dropped after the platform change, the cause could be that change, an algorithm update, competition, or indexing issues—not simply the added translations.

Spanish text at the bottom of an English page would not be expected to change your page’s ranking directly from this evidence. What it can affect is Google’s understanding of the page language and the sitelinks Google chooses. Google tends to use links near the top of the page and links users click most, so mixing Spanish and English links on English pages can confuse Google. Put language-switch links in the footer instead of near the top, keep language sections separated by folder, and register both language versions in Webmaster Tools so you can demote wrong sitelinks.

The evidence doesn’t say how Spanish text at the bottom of an English page would affect rankings. It only shows someone asking about creating separate language versions for Polish and English on different domains, so the closest supported guidance is that language-specific versions are commonly managed separately to target keywords in each language.

If you add Spanish text to an English page, it could confuse the page’s language signal, but that specific ranking effect is not covered here. The safest supported approach from the evidence is to keep language versions clearly separated and set the correct language for the intended domain/page.

If you put Spanish text at the bottom of an otherwise English page, it could signal to Google that the page is intended more for Spanish speakers. That may help Spanish-language queries, but it could slightly hurt English-language ranking in some cases, depending on factors like incoming links and page-specific language data.

If your main goal is English traffic, the safest guidance supported here is to keep the URL, metadata, and most of the content in English.

No, not really. Based on this, you can’t tell Google to ignore specific words or parts of a page while still indexing the rest of it. If you don’t want the page found for “unicorn,” the closest supported options are to avoid publishing content about unicorns on that page, or move that content to a private section of your website.

Put a robots.txt file in the root of the subdomain you want ignored. That can block web spiders, including Googlebot, from crawling everything on that subdomain.

If you want to stop Google from accessing all of static.example.com, place robots.txt at the root of static.example.com and configure it to disallow crawling there. The robots.txt format and setup are described at robotstxt.org.

A free, user-friendly alternative mentioned here is the honeypot method. It adds a hidden field in the form, then checks server-side: if the field is empty, the visitor is likely human; if it’s filled, it’s likely a bot. This avoids CAPTCHA and is described as having better UX. The thread doesn’t mention a specific free spam blocker service, only this free technique.

The answer given was to rename common phpBB files so they’re harder for spammers to target. The files mentioned were memberlist.php, viewtopic.php, viewforum.php, ucp.php, and viewonline.php.

It was described as a temporary workaround, not a real fix: if attackers learn the changes or specifically target the site, the problem could return.

No other prevention method was confirmed in the thread beyond that workaround.

The guidance here is to promote the site rather than use spam. Suggested tactics were regular press releases, participating in related forums while spreading the word, and building a community to keep visitors involved. If you want more targeted advice, the question would need to be more specific about the kind of visibility you want to grow.

To reduce spam while keeping a visible email and contact form, the supported measures are:

- Obfuscate the email address by encoding it and decoding it with JavaScript after the page loads.
- Show the email as an image instead of plain text.
- Add a CAPTCHA to the contact form, or use a similar anti-bot challenge.

These approaches are meant to make it harder for spammers to harvest the address and submit the form automatically.

A good lower-friction alternative is the honeypot method. You add a hidden input field in the HTML, hide it with JavaScript, and check server-side whether it was filled in. If it stays empty, the visitor is likely human; if it’s filled, it’s likely a bot.

The suggested reason it works is that spambots often skip parsing JavaScript because it’s more expensive, while CSS-hidden fields may be detected by some bots. This is described as having very strong success in protecting sign-up forms.

Spam comments can hurt your blog’s ranking by creating low-quality or unnatural links, especially when comments include keyword-stuffed names or links to poor-quality sites. The evidence does not mention any specific PHP software for detecting spam.

If you want the closest guidance supported here, focus on preventing comment spam, filtering dangerous keywords, and blocking unnatural links so your site does not accumulate low-quality outbound links.

The closest guidance here is to rename files you think are frequently targeted. The suggested files were memberlist.php, viewtopic.php, viewforum.php, ucp.php, and viewonline.php. The idea was that changing these paths temporarily stopped spam registrations.

This does not describe a PHP spam-detection tool, and it’s only a temporary workaround. It may help if bots are hitting predictable phpBB endpoints, but it won’t fully prevent a focused attack.

If you’re using Wikipedia content, the key is to follow the license: attribute it with a link, and if you create derivatives, license them under the same terms. A specific deep link to the original source is also good for SEO and is less likely to trigger duplicate-content issues.

If you want to avoid any indexing concern, you can stop Google from indexing those pages by either blocking Googlebot in robots.txt or adding a meta robots noindex tag.

What this does not cover is a special “tell Google I gave credit” tag for non-news sites; the guidance here only mentions attribution, deep linking, and noindex/robots.txt.

Negative SEO appears to be possible, but it’s not proven to work reliably in every case. The material includes reported cases where bad links seemed to harm sites, and also cases where they did not. It also notes that some “victims” may actually have created the links themselves and blamed negative SEO, or that stories may be exaggerated. So the closest supported answer is: it’s not fiction, but its real-world effectiveness is uncertain and inconsistent.

They may be putting the spam link in the author field rather than the comment body. A lot of blog spam uses an innocuous-looking comment with the link hidden in the author name/info.

If it’s a non-standard comment form, bots may also be finding the form but not filling the fields correctly, for example because an input ID/name is different from what they expect.

The guidance here is to check whether the comment links use nofollow. If they do, search engine rankings should not be affected by those spam links. If they do not, then that is the concern. The evidence does not show a way to completely remove the comment so nobody, including friends, can see it. It only supports checking the link attribute and relying on nofollow to avoid ranking impact.

One effective approach is to add a honeypot field to your forms. This is an extra input that real users won’t notice, but many bots will fill in. For example, add a hidden text field and hide it with CSS. If the form is submitted with anything in that field, treat it as spam and discard it.

This works well to stop most automated spam, though it is not completely foolproof.

If the spam is manual, it’s hard to eliminate completely. Basic validation, CAPTCHA, and server-side checks may still be bypassed by a person submitting forms.

The strongest approach mentioned is a client-side timer script that prevents submission until the visitor has been on the page for a while, such as 1 minute. That can help block quick cut-and-paste and semi-automated submissions.

It also helps to assume the spammer may be hiring people to submit forms, so no single filter will stop everything. A layered approach is best, but the supported suggestion here is the timer-based client-side delay.

If a spam domain is pointing at your site/IP and showing a copy of your content, the closest practical steps are to set up a servlet or JSP redirect for the offending URL/domain, since Tomcat 7 doesn’t have the same easy virtual-host controls as Apache. Also contact your hosting company and ask whether they can help block or route it differently, and trace the spam domain to its registrar to request technical assistance.

To encourage better comments, ask readers direct questions at the end of your post, such as “What do you think?” or “Did I miss anything?” Invite opinions, other perspectives, and alternatives. The thread doesn’t provide a public IP list for comment spammers. It only suggests using Akismet for spam filtering, noting it has an API you can use even if you’re not on WordPress. It also mentions pricing, including a free option up to 10,000 pageviews a month and paid plans if you want to use additional options. If you’re dealing with Magento blog comment spam, this is the closest guidance given: use Akismet or a similar spam-filtering service rather than relying on a public IP blacklist.

The supported automated fix mentioned is to use a plugin like Cyb that blocks users from posting links until they meet a post-count requirement. The answer also suggests restricting profile permissions so users with fewer than 5 posts can’t use URLs in their profiles.

If spam still gets through, another option is a maximum posts-per-day limit set just below the level needed to start posting links.

The evidence doesn’t mention moderator-specific tools or a way for a moderator with no admin powers to fix the issue directly. It only supports tightening anti-spam rules like post counts, waiting periods, and URL restrictions.

If the bot is only identifiable by IP, the supported approach here is to rate-limit traffic per IP rather than “fix” the bot itself. The guidance points to Apache request/traffic limiting per IP, which can slow it down without outright blocking it.

Since you don’t have direct webserver control, the practical path is to ask the host to add/configure the relevant Apache module and apply per-IP limits in vhost or .htaccess, if allowed. If the traffic is tied to a known search engine and you want to preserve useful crawling, this is the closest option supported by the answer.

Generally, spam bots do not load the DOM or run JavaScript. Some tools can run a browser and execute JS, but those are usually slower and less common than bots that just scrape HTML and send direct POST requests.

So a jQuery checker may help against simpler bots, but it won’t stop all spam. If you can’t change the server-side code, you may be out of luck on the form itself. If submissions go to your email, improving your email spam filtering may be the best workaround.

I don’t have evidence about Pligg or the best way to stop spam sign-ups. The only supported guidance here is unrelated: Google may penalize pages with too many ads above the fold, and mobile search rankings can be hurt by intrusive pop-ups. If your concern is spam, I can’t confirm a specific Pligg fix from this material.

I don’t see anything specific about Pligg, but the closest guidance here is to require more effort before users can post links: a post-count quota, restricted profile URL permissions for users with fewer than 5 posts, and possibly a maximum number of posts per day set below the link-posting threshold. The answer also says email verification plus a three-day waiting period and minimum of five prior posts to post links reduced spam a lot on one forum. Spammers tend to give up when posting feels like work.

To reduce common spam on a WordPress blog, stop spammy comments from creating low-quality or unnatural links on your site. The evidence says spam often includes dangerous keywords like casinos, poker, gambling, and viagra, or uses keywords instead of real names to place target links.

The closest guidance supported here is to:
- watch for comments using suspicious keywords
- block or remove comments that contain unnatural or low-quality links
- avoid letting keyword-filled names or spammy link patterns stay on the blog

This helps prevent your site from being associated with low-quality or unnatural links, which can hurt rankings.

The main motivation is SEO: spammers want to get links to their sites.

For human spammers, a comment is often a test to see whether your site auto-approves comments; if it does, they may return. For bot spam, automated tools spray generic comments across many URLs and rely on volume. Even if most are blocked, they can still succeed on some sites, so the tactic is worth it to them.

To reduce this kind of spam, use anti-spam plugins like Akismet and make sure comments aren’t auto-approved.

To reduce spam on a WordPress blog, keep the email visible but make it harder for bots to scrape by encoding it and decoding it with JavaScript after page load, or by showing it as an image. For the contact form, add a CAPTCHA or a similar anti-bot challenge. These measures are meant to block automated spam while still keeping both a visible email address and a contact form.

Yes. The closest supported approach is to let the community police itself: allow and encourage users to flag spam, and use moderation to remove it quickly.

Other supported controls:
- Require new users to make multiple posts before they can add links or links in profiles
- Limit how many links new users can post in a day

The evidence says automated defenses are best for bots, but for human spam, community moderation is the most effective tool.

Yes. The guidance here is to use automated limits like requiring a minimum post count before users can post links, and possibly a waiting period or daily post cap. Also restrict profile permissions so new users can’t add URLs. This can significantly reduce spam even without full moderation, because spammers usually won’t bother with multiple required steps.

Not directly from this evidence. It only says that having abuse@ and postmaster@ addresses may help email not be treated as spam.

It does not address controlling spam on a site that allows user contributions without accounts. For that situation, the closest supported guidance is that spam control may involve email-related setup, but this evidence doesn’t give methods for site moderation or anti-spam protections.

Without investigating the site, it’s hard to tell exactly which one is happening.

The main motivation is SEO: spammers try to get links to their sites from yours.

For human spammers, they may be testing whether your site auto-approves comments or whether a link can slip through.

For bots, the spammer uses software to post the same comment across many found URLs. Even if most get blocked, a few may get published, and that can still make the effort worthwhile.

So they don’t need every spam comment to succeed; they rely on volume and the chance that some will get through.

No. In the robots.txt shown, only Baiduspider is blocked from the whole site:

User-agent: Baiduspider
Disallow: /

The rule for all other search engines is only:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /templates_c/

So `Disallow: /` affects only the user-agent it is under. If it were under `User-agent: *`, then the whole site would be blocked for all crawlers.

The most likely fix is to open IIS Manager, select the specific site/folder, and check Request Filtering there. Make sure the file extension you want to serve is allowed under the File Name Extensions tab. Also check the Hidden Segments and HTTP Verbs tabs in case the folder or a verb is being blocked.

If one folder works and another doesn’t, the blocking is probably set at the site/folder level rather than globally. The evidence also suggests a previously installed Request Filtering component or earlier configuration may be affecting only the newer folder.

The evidence does not fully answer whether a site with no backlinks would ever get listed in Google.

It does show that links from many networking sites may be marked nofollow, so they may not help search rankings. It also says those links are mainly useful for referral traffic and lead generation, not necessarily SEO benefit.

So the closest supported guidance is: backlinks from some sites may not help Google ranking, but the evidence does not say that a site with no backlinks can never be listed.

Yes, it can still be listed, but backlinks are not required for a page to appear in Google. The evidence only says Google can take backlinks into account when they exist and are not 404s, and that 410 or 301 handling affects whether those links help SEO. It does not say a site needs backlinks to be indexed. So a site with no backlinks may still get listed if Google discovers it another way, though the evidence does not cover how likely that is.

Yes, it can still be listed. The thread says a young site with few or no backlinks is not necessarily penalized; it may just take time for Google to crawl, index, and assign PageRank. It also suggests submitting a sitemap to Google Webmaster Tools and building more good backlinks over time. So the closest guidance is: lack of backlinks doesn’t mean “never listed,” but it may be indexed slowly and rank poorly until the site gains authority.

The page may already be indexed, and the “fetch as Google” problem could be temporary on Google’s side. The response suggests the redesigned site’s JavaScript may be interfering, so check that important content is visible without scripts. It also recommends adding a sitemap.xml and Google Analytics alongside Webmaster Tools to help Google discover and process the site. When checking indexing, use an incognito Chrome session to avoid localized results. If the fetch failures continue, the closest guidance supported here is to review JavaScript behavior and try again later in case Google’s fetch tools are having issues.

Use 301 redirects from the old URLs to the new ones. That helps search engines understand the pages permanently moved and points Google to the new locations, especially if other sites still link to the old URLs.

If your site uses Apache, you can set redirects in a .htaccess file, one line per old page, or use mod_rewrite for pattern-based redirects. Also, set up Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console to see what URLs Google is finding and how your site is ranking.

This doesn’t directly explain why the new pages are delayed, but it supports that redirects are the recommended fix for getting Google to recognize the new structure.

If your new pages aren’t indexing, the issue here was that the sitemap contained URLs that 301 redirected to other URLs. Google was indexing the destination URLs instead, so the sitemap appeared to have very few indexed pages.

The fix is to rebuild the sitemap with only live, final URLs, not redirected ones.

There was also a robots.txt problem: the user agent was missing. It should be:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /store-o

Sitemap: http://www.proboxinggear.com/store/sitemaps.xml

The provided information only shows that a page can be crawled and its links followed while still not being shown in search results by using `noindex, follow`. It does not say whether Google can discover a website that is not linked anywhere.

Closest guidance supported here: if Google can crawl a page, it can use that page’s links. But this does not answer discovery of a completely unlinked website.

Yes, but the provided answer says the Facebook profiles in question were not truly unlinked. They were discoverable because Facebook had crawlable links to a full directory from its homepage, and that directory only included public search listings.

So the supported guidance is: if a site has crawlable links to those pages, Google can discover them. The evidence does not show that Google can find a completely unlinked website on its own.

Yes, Google can discover some pages even if they are not linked from anywhere, but not reliably from the evidence here.

What the evidence does support is that Google’s `link:domain.com` can show many, but not all, backlinks to a site. It does not say whether Google can find a completely unlinked website.

So the closest supported answer is: Google may find pages through means other than visible backlinks, but this evidence only confirms partial backlink discovery, not full discovery of an isolated site.

Changing hosting itself should not hurt SEO ranking. The key is to keep the move seamless and minimize downtime. A fast, reliable host is fine; only very poor performance or very slow page loads could affect rankings, and that usually applies only in extreme cases.

Changing the host can affect SEO if the move changes what search engines see, so it’s safer to test on a development subdomain first and keep the live site unchanged. The guidance here is to back up the current site, use a live domain and a dev domain on the same server if possible, test changes on dev, then move changes gradually to production. If something hurts rankings, revert to the backup.

The provided thread does not include an answer, so it doesn’t confirm whether changing only the server location or IP will affect SEO.

Based on the question itself, the change described is a server move without changing the domain name. The evidence only supports that the domain stays the same and only the IP address changes.

If you want, I can help you with general SEO guidance for server migrations, but I can’t confirm the SEO impact from the material provided.

Changing server location or IP usually won’t affect SEO by itself. Search engines follow your domain and links, not the IP.

Possible exceptions: if the new IP is blacklisted, or if the new server is in a different country/region. In those cases, rankings could be affected, especially for search engines that use locality more heavily.

So if you’re only changing servers within the same region and the IP is clean, it should be fine.

A 2-week gap during the move could affect search results, mainly because Google may encounter 404s or no content during that time. The guidance here is to avoid that by keeping the transition smooth: use 301 redirects from old pages to the best matching new pages, watch for 404s in the first hours/days/weeks, and make sure the new site has a sitemap.xml. It also says hiding the new site isn’t strictly necessary, and Google recommends migrating section by section rather than leaving the domain effectively offline.

Yes, the provided answer suggests that being down for two weeks is preferable to starting over with a brand new domain because a new site would need fresh SEM and SEO optimization. So a 2-week outage may be less harmful to search performance than moving to a completely new domain. It doesn’t say exactly how much rankings would be affected, only that a new domain is the bigger SEO risk.

If Googlebot stops crawling the old URLs, pages can take a few weeks to drop out of the index. A 2-week gap during a hosting transition could matter mainly because those pages may not be crawled or updated during that time. The closest guidance supported here is that crawling should stop within a few days after the change, but it may still take a few weeks for the indexed results to disappear. If the site was offline, that could delay things until Google can crawl it again.

Those pages should still return a 200 OK response. To keep search engines from crawling and indexing them, serve a noindex, nofollow meta tag on those pages. If you want users who really want to view the content, you can keep a nofollow link that reveals it.

The closest supported approach is to make the content crawlable for search bots and search visitors while blocking logged-out users otherwise. One suggested method is Google’s first click free policy: let search bots through based on user agent, and let visitors coming from search through based on referrer, without requiring login.

That said, this does mean some users who haven’t explicitly opted in could still reach the page if they arrive from search. If your requirement is to keep logged-out users from viewing it entirely, the evidence doesn’t provide a way to do both that and full crawlability for all bots.

The evidence doesn’t say how to block page views from an adult site specifically. It does suggest focusing on attracting and retaining relevant traffic rather than relying on ads alone. It recommends linking your blogs together to keep visitors within your network, and using related affiliate links instead of unrelated ads.

For your situation, the closest guidance is to review where your traffic comes from and avoid placing ads or links that lead visitors away unless they’re useful and relevant. It also says there’s no specific threshold for when to add ads, but regular monthly traffic matters more than a fixed view count.

It could affect Google Image search if those images are currently helping your rankings. The guidance says the impact depends on whether the images benefit your ranking now. If you use good SEO practices like relevant alt text matching the surrounding content, images can still be indexed well. Using a CNAME is suggested as a good idea to avoid affecting rankings as much, especially if the images are already contributing to traffic.

Moving images to a CDN should not, by itself, hurt Google Image Search. In the evidence, a CDN-hosted image still indexed and ranked well.

What can change image preview behavior is how Google can fetch the image. If Google uses its own cached thumbnail in the preview, the clearer live image may not swap in. That can happen when Google can’t access the image directly or sees redirects/hotlink protection-like behavior.

The main benefit of a date in URL segments is that it matches a hierarchical structure. For example, /date/2010/02 can naturally be an index for that month, /date/2010 for a year, and /date/ for all years. That makes the URL schema more elegant and usable for navigation.

For an unordered set of parameters, key=value&key2=value2 is a better fit. So /date/2010-02-02 is not inherently “better” than ?date=2010-02-02; it depends on whether the information is really hierarchical or just a parameter.

The closest guidance is that moving content from one domain to another with 301 redirects usually gives poor SEO results, especially in the short term. To move a single page, the supported approach here would be:

2. Set up a 301 redirect from the old page URL to the matching new page URL.
3. Submit the new page/domain in Google Webmaster Tools and a sitemap.

It also warns that rankings may drop after the move and recover only gradually as new links and organic use build up.

The key is to 301-redirect the old page URL to the corresponding page on the new domain. If you’re moving only one page, make sure that exact old URL goes to the exact new URL, preserving the path and query string if needed. Also update any external links you control so they point directly to the new domain. You can notify Google through Webmaster Tools, but the essential part is the 301 redirect.

To move pages to a new domain, use 301 permanent redirects. The guidance here says search engines will notice the 301 and start indexing the new domain, and Google will know you’ve moved.

It also says the answer referenced would redirect all pages in one go, rather than setting up each page separately. So for a single page, the closest supported approach is to make that page return a 301 redirect to its new location on the new domain.

If you’re moving more than one page, the same idea applies: redirect each old URL to its corresponding new URL so search engines can follow the move.

The naked domain is treated as a rollup of all subdomains, so it can show the same Webmaster Tools data as the www version even if you use a 301 redirect. In other words, adding the naked domain doesn’t necessarily give you separate data just for that host.

It can be done on the IIS web server. The suggested approach is to use a rewrite/redirect rule in web.config so that requests for the naked domain are redirected to the www version.

Example:

<rewrite>
  <rules>
    <rule name="Redirect domain.com to www" patternSyntax="Wildcard" stopProcessing="true">
      <match url="*" />
      <conditions>
        <add input="{HTTP_HOST}" pattern="domain.com" />
      </conditions>
      <action type="Redirect" url="http://www.domain.com/{R:0}" />
    </rule>
  </rules>
</rewrite>

A regular-expression version is also shown in the evidence. This does not describe a DNS-only solution.

Best guidance supported here: keep real 404 pages, make sure they return an actual 404 server status, and avoid creating internal links to pages that don’t exist. Redirecting every 404 isn’t necessary; only use redirects where there is a relevant existing page.

The guidance here says duplicate content and a poor link profile can lead to lost rankings, and that publishing duplicate content just for links “will no longer help in organic search.”

If someone is copying your blog, the closest supported advice is to avoid duplicating your own content on other sites, use cross-domain canonicalization where possible, and focus on original, well-formatted content.

If someone else copies your blog content, Google usually doesn’t “penalize” you just for that. It may choose only one version to show in search results, based on factors like which site it found first and which site is stronger overall.

So the main effect is that your page may not get credit for that content if Google sees duplicates elsewhere. It can still help if users spend time on your site, but duplicated content itself doesn’t give you extra ranking value.

If the copying is happening through partner sites with permission, the same duplicate-content behavior still applies.

Yes, duplicate content can be an SEO issue, but the guidance here is that canonical URLs are used to tell Google which site/page is the original source. If someone is reposting your blog post verbatim, using a canonical URL on the copied page pointing to your original page is the closest supported way to signal that your page is the authoritative one. A short note saying it was copied may help readers, but the evidence only supports canonical URLs as the SEO solution.

The information provided only covers how to check whether an image or logo has been copied, not what to do after finding plagiarism.

The closest guidance it supports is using TinEye: upload your file or provide its URL, and it can find where the image came from, where it is being used, whether modified versions exist, and whether a higher-resolution version exists.

If your goal is to respond to a plagiarizing site, this evidence does not give removal, reporting, or legal steps.

If a site has copied a significant portion of your content, especially if it’s monetizing your content with ads or other revenue, you can file a DMCA takedown. It also matters what country you’re in and what country the mirror site is in, since the process can vary. If it’s only a small amount copied, the guidance here doesn’t fully cover what to do next.

If another site has copied your content, Google’s guidance says that scraping/republishing it is unlikely to hurt your site’s ranking. Google mainly uses duplicate-content handling to avoid showing the same content multiple times in results.

A 21% similarity level also doesn’t sound like the kind of copy that would normally cause SEO problems. A recent ranking drop on your site could be due to many other factors, so it would be risky to assume the competitor’s copying is the direct cause.

If the content was copied without permission, it may be a copyright issue, and the suggested first step would be to contact their ISP and be able to prove you created the original content.

Copying the same text content to a mobile version is not shown here to have a negative SEO impact by itself. The top answer says they usually put the same content on both the main and mobile site, with the mobile version being lighter, and use switchboard tags to avoid duplicate-content issues or other problems.

So the closest guidance supported here is: using the same content on both versions is a common practice, and proper tagging/canonical-style setup is suggested to help prevent duplicate content concerns.

The best-supported choice here is to keep it all on one domain, with sections or subcategories under it. The answer says it’s related content and that, personally, it would be kept on one domain.

More generally, the guidance is to choose the structure that is best for users and easiest to maintain, rather than splitting domains just for SEO. A single domain can also help consolidate links and avoid the overhead of managing multiple sites.

For SEO, a subfolder is suggested rather than a subdomain. The answer says subdomains are treated separately from the main domain and can cause a big page-rank hit, while a subfolder is preferred to help keep page-rank. It also notes you can 301 redirect from a subdomain to a subfolder if needed.

So either `forum.example.com` or `example.com/forum/` is fine; choose based on what’s easier for your site and users.

Yes, spaces are fine in the alt attribute; it should be human-readable text. The alt attribute is mainly for people using screen readers or when images don’t load, not specifically for improving search rankings.

For your transparent images that act as links, use descriptive alt text like “post new classified” rather than empty or space-only text.

As for JavaScript-rich content, search engines won’t penalize a page just for using JavaScript, but content hidden with display:none and later shown via JavaScript may be ignored, and deceptive hidden keyword stuffing or transparent links can cause problems.

Yes, it could be a problem if the category page is crawlable and every thumbnail uses the same repeated keywords in its alt text. It’s better to write alt text that describes each image specifically rather than repeating “unique” and “pen” on every item.

For SEO and accessibility, use alt. It is the text used for visually impaired users and as fallback if the image doesn’t load. title is meant for tooltips, and can be copied from alt if you want the hover bubble. longdesc is not the standard choice here. If you only want one source of text, write it in alt and, if needed, duplicate it into title for tooltip behavior.

Use a subdomain if you want the blog to be logically separate from the main site. Use a subdomain only when it’s truly a different site or section, like separate support/helpdesk sites. For a blog that belongs to the main business site, the guidance here favors keeping it under a directory, like mysite.com/blog, so the blog stays part of the one site.

If you prefer blog.mysite.com for memorability, a supported workaround is to 301 redirect it to www.mysite.com/blog. That gives users the easy-to-remember address while keeping the content on the main site structure.

The closest guidance here is that having both forms accessible is recommended for user experience and to preserve link/SEO value. This doesn’t directly answer which of those two is better, but it supports using one canonical version and ensuring the other still works or forwards properly.

If your goal is to avoid cross-impact from duplicate meta descriptions, using a main website and a subdomain is supported here as separate sites. The evidence does not compare this setup against having two separate main domains, so it doesn’t say which is better overall for SEO optimization.

Search engines won’t know which domain is the “main” one on your hosting account. They only see the domains themselves, their content, and how other sites link to them.

So based on this, having a main domain plus a subdomain does not make the main domain more SEO-friendly just because it’s the primary hosting domain. SEO depends on the content and links, not the hosting setup.

For SEO, the guidance here is to keep the blog content closely related to your main site. If your site is about web hosting, the best approach is to publish web-hosting-related articles so links back to your main site feel natural and relevant.

If you need more variety, you can include other topics, but they should still stay close to web hosting so you can diversify keywords without losing relevance.

This does not directly answer whether a blog should be on a webpage or a subdomain. It only supports that the blog’s topic should stay related to the main site for better SEO.

Based on this, putting the blog on the main site is the better SEO move than leaving it separate. It does not directly compare a subdomain versus a subdirectory/page, but the supported guidance here is: keep the blog inside the main domain if your goal is to boost the main site’s SEO.

Closest supported guidance: the thread itself suggests subdomains are a topic worth considering, but it gives no evidence for when they help or hurt SEO.

Yes—subdomains can be appropriate for multilingual sites like the example given. Including a few keywords in a URL can help a little, mainly by making links clearer to users. But it’s only a very small SEO factor. Great content, titles, and link text matter much more.

If you already have a URL structure in place, the guidance here suggests not changing it just to add keywords. The evidence supports that keyword-rich, readable URLs may help slightly, but it does not say domain keywords are a major ranking boost.

Keywords in a domain name have limited SEO benefit now. Their impact on search rankings has been reduced in recent years, and there isn’t a specific number of keywords that helps or hurts. Adding more keywords doesn’t have a clearly defined SEO “division of value” in the domain.

The more important benefit is choosing a domain that is easy to remember and easy to type. That is likely more valuable than trying to pack extra keywords into the name.

Using multiple websites for separate services won’t give you special SEO benefits, and it may be a waste of time. The guidance here is that a single website with all services on different pages is better for SEO and user experience. It keeps visitors on one site, makes it easier to find all services in one place, and can give more SEO weight to the main domain.

Google no longer gives special weight to keyword-rich domains the way it once did, so that part of the tactic is unlikely to help much. The “small sites with unique content” approach is often called microsites, and the guidance here is that spending time on many separate sites is usually better focused on the main site. A few microsites could help if they have truly unique, valuable content that isn’t on the main site and is still relevant. Lots of microsites, though, are generally a bad idea most of the time.

So, based on this, the closest guidance is: if your blog and main site both publish the same content, use canonical URLs or redirects to indicate the preferred version. It does not say you’re penalized just for using a subfolder.

There’s no clear sign of a penalty for hosting a blog in a subfolder. The evidence doesn’t directly answer whether the same Google AdSense units can be used for both web and mobile versions.

The supported approach is to use Google’s Responsive Ad Units, which are designed to fit responsive site layouts. That lets the ad adapt to different screen sizes instead of needing separate fixed-size units for web and mobile versions.

A 728x90 header ad is a fixed-size example, but for responsive design the closest guidance here is to use responsive ad units rather than trying to manage different versions for each viewport.

If the deleted page is not being replaced with new content, use HTTP 410 Gone. That tells search engines the page no longer exists. For users, keep the response page helpful: explain why it’s gone and offer links to your home page, sitemap, search page, and similar content if available.

A 301 redirect is not the best fit when the content is simply deleted and not replaced.

For SEO, a 404 is not considered bad just because it means the page is missing. If a URL like `url.com?some_arg=1` has no matching record, returning 404 is supported by this guidance.

If you are deleting a webpage and there is no content for that page anymore, the closest supported recommendation is to use 404 for the missing page.

To check your ranking, search in the search engine for the keywords you want to rank for and see whether your pages appear in the results. If your site shows up, you’re ranking for that term; if it doesn’t, you may not be ranking well or at all.

If you only want to confirm indexing, search for your domain name. If it appears, your site is indexed.

For a more objective and easier way to track rankings over time, use tools that automate keyword rank checks.

Because Google may index the final destination URLs after following 301 redirects, not the redirected sitemap URLs themselves. So if a sitemap contains redirected URLs, Google can end up indexing more live destination URLs than the sitemap seems to list.

The fix is to rebuild the sitemap so it contains only live, final URLs, not URLs that redirect.

There was also a robots.txt issue in the example: it needed a User-agent line.

Yes, that can happen. A sitemap is only a list of URLs you want Google to know about; it is not a complete count of everything Google may index. Google can index URLs discovered elsewhere on the site or from external links, and it may also keep indexed URLs that are no longer in the sitemap.

If Google has indexed more URLs than the sitemap contains, the closest guidance is to check for:
- URLs discovered outside the sitemap
- duplicate or alternate versions of pages
- old URLs still indexed
- Search Console index status for “not selected” or “blocked by robots”

If mobile URLs are all unindexed, that suggests a more serious configuration issue.

Set expiration based on how often each asset changes, not just its type. A practical approach is:

- Rarely changing CSS/JS/images: cache for a week or two
- Daily-changing assets: cache for 24 hours

So in .htaccess, you’d apply expiration times to CSS, JS, and images according to their update frequency. The guidance here doesn’t provide exact .htaccess syntax, but it does support choosing different max-age values depending on how often each file changes.

For a homepage URL, `http://example.com/` and `http://example.com` are equivalent. There’s no rule that you must always add or avoid the trailing slash; the main guidance is to be consistent.

Hyphens are generally best avoided in domain names because they add noise and can be awkward to say or spell. That said, they are not always bad: if a hyphen improves readability or helps prevent confusion, it can be reasonable to keep it. The closest guidance is to use an SMS gateway/API for your website. The suggested phrase is “International SMS Gateway.” Twilio was mentioned as a developer-friendly option for sending SMS, though it was noted as US-limited in the prior discussion. Another option mentioned was cdyne’s SMS service.

Use 301s only when there is a clear, relevant replacement page for the removed URL. If a deleted page has no true equivalent, this does not support sending it to the home page; the closest supported approach is to let it return 404.

So: specific 301 to the best matching new page, otherwise 404.

Keep discontinued product pages useful if they still help users or search engines. The best-supported approach is to leave the page up with a discontinued notice and links to relevant existing products, the home page, sitemap, and contact page. If the page truly no longer exists, use 410 Gone. For items that may return, don’t use 404/410; keep the page indexed and mark it out of stock, with a notification option if possible.

This evidence does not specifically say to redirect to a very similar product, but it supports preserving the page and pointing users to suitable alternatives rather than sending them to a dead end.

If pages are being removed permanently, use a 404 rather than redirecting them to the home page.

Instead, let removed pages return 404 and help users with related content, a search page, sitemap, or links to important pages.

For removed pages, the supported approach is not to 301 everything to the home page. Use a 301 only when there is a clear replacement page for that specific URL. A jQuery checker may help against simpler bots, because many spam bots do not load the DOM or run JavaScript. However, it will not stop all spam, since some bots can run a browser and execute JS, or just submit HTML forms directly with POST requests.

If you can’t change the server-side code, you may not be able to fully fix the form itself. If the submissions go to your email, improving email spam filtering may be the best workaround.

Redirecting non-existing posts to the homepage is not the best SEO practice. The supported guidance here is to avoid sending everything to the homepage; instead, redirect each old or missing URL to the most relevant matching page with a 301 redirect. If several old pages relate to one new page, they can all go there. This preserves relevance better than a blanket homepage redirect.

The safest approach is to set up permanent HTTP 301 redirects from the old URLs to the new ones. This helps Google update the links and keeps existing links working.

If you do not add redirects, old links will break, and Google may treat the new URLs as duplicate content of the old pages, which can hurt ranking.

Use 301 redirects from old URLs to the new ones. If duplicate URLs exist, add a rel="canonical" header or meta tag to point to the preferred URL. It also helps to migrate slowly, keep the old and new sites running in parallel where possible, and introduce the new structure early through sitemaps. For major changes in link structure or site position, make sure the new setup is still in users’ best interest.

If the page is indexed, Google may still not show it for normal searches because of visibility/SEO rather than indexing. The supported checks are to:
